briefings.body:
## Pipeline

A typical Amazon loop runs:

1. **OA** (when applicable, mostly NG / intern / early-career). Two parts: a classic LC-style problem + an AI Assistant Repo Bug-Fix in a multi-file harness. ~70 min total.
2. **Recruiter screen** — process intro + standard BQ, light technical check on title fit.
3. **Phone screen — coding** (60 min). Usually one LC-medium plus an LP-flavored BQ at the front or back.
4. **Onsite / virtual loop** — 4-5 rounds:
   - 2× coding (one of which is often OOD with a multi-step build),
   - 1× system design (or ML system design for AS / MLE),
   - 1× hiring manager BQ deep-dive,
   - 1× Bar Raiser — runs independently of the team, gates the offer.

FAR / Premium loops (frontier-research orgs, Applied Science staff bands) add: **Paper Read Round**, **Science Application (Ambiguous Problem)**, and a **Deep Dive** on prior work.

## Typical timeline

- OA → recruiter → phone screen: 2-4 weeks.
- Phone screen → onsite: 2-4 weeks.
- Onsite → decision: 1-2 weeks (Bar Raiser write-up can extend this).
- Offer → team-confirm: 1-3 weeks.

## Signaling notes

- Bar Raiser write-ups dominate the HC discussion; nailing one LP deep with a quantified outcome can rescue a borderline technical round.
- Several reports describe "strong technical, weak LP" outcomes — Amazon down-levels rather than rejects in this case.
- "Internal references requested early" is **not** a borderline signal at Amazon (unlike at OpenAI) — recruiters routinely ask.
- 2026 NG loops increasingly run as **team-based hiring (“组招”)**: every interviewer in the loop comes from the same hiring team, so the questions and difficulty track that team rather than a fixed company bank — two candidates in the same week can see very different coding bars.
- Intern / NG loops are sometimes compressed: a single screen (most-challenging-project + one coding problem) or two back-to-back 60-minute interviews, increasingly held **in person** at an Amazon office with a 15-min resume/AI-grill segment bolted onto each technical round.

- MLE loops can apply a six-month cooldown after rejection, while separate SDE hiring teams may still be able to proceed independently. Treat cooldown scope as role/team-specific and confirm it with the recruiter.

## Official format anchors

- The SDE II online assessment is officially structured as 118 minutes total: a 90-minute two-question coding block, a 20-minute systems-design scenario block, and an 8-minute Work Style Survey.
- The standard SDE II onsite is officially four 55-minute interviews. Senior bands and FAR / Premium loops layer additional rounds on top of this baseline.
- The phone screen runs in Amazon's internal Livecode editor — syntax highlighting only, code does not execute. Plan to dry-run examples by hand.

## Mid-2026 updates

- NG loops are now frequently **fully in person**: four back-to-back rounds over roughly four hours, most rounds splitting ~30 minutes technical / ~30 minutes LP with a pure-BQ final round, and coding done on a whiteboard.
- L5 team-based phone screens can add an unannounced, team-scoped mini system-design after the coding problem — even when the recruiter frames the round as coding-only.
- When a recruiter moves an application to a different Req / Job ID, a completed OA does not always carry over; a repeat OA on the new requisition is possible.

## Boomerang Loop Flexibility (2026 Q3)

Returning L5 candidates can see a compressed two-interview loop: roughly 20 minutes of Leadership Principles plus 30 minutes of coding, followed by another 20-minute BQ segment and 30 minutes of design. A team-fit follow-up may then become a project-architecture whiteboard and hiring-manager conversation rather than a full restart. When a competing offer deadline is documented, the team can add that conversation quickly and return a decision within hours.

## August 2026 process signal

- An NG loop may split three back-to-back virtual rounds from a separately scheduled Bar Raiser several weeks later; a long gap before the final round is not itself a rejection signal.
- A post-VO SDE II rejection can now carry a one-year cooldown rather than the historically common six months. Cooldown scope can vary by role and hiring team, so confirm the exact end date and whether another requisition is eligible with the recruiter.

## Front-End NG loop variant (August 2026)

Front-end / full-stack new-grad hiring can use a phone screen followed by two virtual onsite rounds and a separately scheduled Bar Raiser. The technical mix is front-end UI implementation, JavaScript/browser fundamentals, one general data-structure problem, and LP coverage throughout; the Bar Raiser remains pure behavioral.

## Late-summer 2026 scheduling variants

NG onsite scheduling varies by team: Vancouver can spread four rounds across two days, while Boston can run four back-to-back interviews. One Boston timeline ran from July 31 OA to August 24 availability survey, September 4 onsite, and September 10 verbal offer; this is an example timeline rather than a response-time guarantee.

A Summer 2026 intern path matched the candidate to a team before interviewing and used two one-hour interviews after the OA, with the hiring manager and an L5 SWE. Both mixed coding and behavioral questions; the manager emphasized behavior and GenAI experience. The eventual offer was for the interviewing team.

For SDE II, a filled requisition can interrupt progress after the OA and lead the recruiter to offer other openings. An onsite availability survey may require a response within 24 hours, while the detailed schedule can arrive only the day before the interviews.

## September 2026 interview-format variants

An Applied Scientist one-hour phone screen can begin with roughly 30 minutes of Leadership Principles before moving to a project deep dive and coding, even when the recruiter describes a half-ML, half-coding agenda without behavioral questions. Prepare behavioral examples alongside the technical material and leave room for changes to the advertised split.

An SDE II phone screen can put technical work first and LP questions last, with an initial coding exercise followed by two separate design discussions. Finishing the first problem quickly does not necessarily end the technical portion.

A four-round virtual loop can also separate a pure behavioral round and a pure coding round, then combine behavior with system design and coding in later rounds. The presence and placement of LP questions varies across individual interview schedules.

## Additional September 2026 team formats

An AI infrastructure hiring path can use a phone-screen object-design exercise followed by five onsite interviews: three coding rounds, one ML round and one system-design round. This differs from the four-round general SDE format; check the team-specific schedule when planning preparation.

An SDE II phone screen can allocate the first 20 minutes to a resume deep dive plus two LP questions, then 40 minutes to coding. Technology choices, trade-offs, business logic and personal responsibility are part of that opening discussion. Continued explanation during coding can consume substantial time: one candidate spent about half of the coding allocation discussing the approach and finished without time for a dry run.

## October 2026 format signals

- SDE II onsites can let candidates choose remote (Zoom) or in person; the in-person version is four back-to-back rounds with roughly ten distinct LP questions spread across them. Recruiters may warn of LeetCode-hard coding, but the actual mix can be standard — a scheduler-style coding problem, a topological-sort variant, a classic system design, and an OOD/LLD round — so do not skip design and OOD prep.
- If you tell an interviewer you have already seen a problem, expect them to switch to a different one on the spot.
- Team-based L5 phone loops (e.g. an AWS security team) can run three one-hour rounds, each splitting roughly 30 minutes technical and two LP questions.
- A Canada SDE II virtual round can run 2 minutes of introduction, 30 minutes of whiteboard coding, 20 minutes of BQ with detailed follow-ups, and 5 minutes of Q&A.
- Annapurna Labs ML kernel engineer screens test kernel implementation and optimization rather than LeetCode, even when the recruiter describes LeetCode-style coding; the LP portion centers on kernel-optimization experience and ownership.
- Amazon Robotics and AWS intern loops use two one-hour rounds (hiring manager plus engineer), each mixing coding and BQ; the manager round can spend about 30 minutes on behavioral, including a GenAI question.
- AWS SDE II onsite loops can be team-matched before the onsite, with the interviewer schedule arriving only about two days ahead and no option to switch teams. Each of the four rounds pairs about 30 minutes of whiteboard coding or design (code does not need to compile) with LP questions, one round is the hiring manager's, and a decision can arrive within about a week.
- SDE II phone screens can be an incremental OOD exercise instead of a LeetCode problem: start with two classes and extend the model as the interviewer adds requirements.

## November 2026 format signals

- SDE II virtual onsites can run four 60-minute rounds, each split roughly 25 minutes of LPs and 35 minutes technical, with 3–4 follow-ups dug into every STAR story. One loop mapped the rounds as: Ownership / Dive Deep + grid BFS coding; Invent and Simplify / Insist on the Highest Standards + LLD; Bar Raiser with Customer Obsession / Have Backbone + system design; hiring manager with Deliver Results / Bias for Action + streaming data-structure coding.
- SDE I NG virtual loops (one of them in Canada) can run four ~1-hour rounds, including one pure-LP round (about 55 minutes in one loop) and one round pairing GenAI BQs with coding or LLD; LLD prompts (parking lot, ticket reservation) can take the place of a LeetCode slot. An automated rejection can arrive about five days after a loop the candidate felt went well.
- PhD Research Intern loops: an OA with two basic coding problems plus a ~5-minute personality survey; round 1 pairs two BQs (a deadline trade-off, handling harsh conference reviews) with a light coding task followed by deep questioning on the code; round 2 has no coding — an open discussion of LLM post-training methods plus an introduction to the internship. The internship runs about 5–6 months, starts from a high-level project proposal, has a primary mentor (sometimes several) and weekly research guidance, usually targets a strong-venue publication, and does not touch customer-facing production systems.
- The embedded SDE intern OA can arrive the day after applying and runs Coding Challenge ~100 minutes (one algorithm problem plus the AI-assisted repository task in HackerRank's VS Code-style IDE), Work Simulation ~45 minutes, and Work Style ~6 minutes.
- Senior firmware/BIOS loops can be two rounds: a hiring-manager-plus-teammate screen with small coding warm-ups, then a five-interviewer panel covering linked-list coding, memory reservation, ring buffers, and bootloader update design, with a strong LP component throughout.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Shape of the loop

Apple's engineering loop is highly team-dependent. A common path is recruiter screen -> hiring-manager or peer screen -> one or more technical screens -> onsite / virtual onsite -> manager or director wrap-up. Some MLE and hardware loops start with the hiring manager and only later add coding; some SDE loops go straight into coding with no project warm-up.

## What to expect

Most technical rounds are 45 minutes. Onsite loops commonly contain 4-6 rounds; MLE loops often mix project deep-dive, ML fundamentals, ML coding, ML system design, and behavioral. Storage / infra loops skew toward classic coding plus distributed-system design. Hardware DV / ASIC loops are their own track with SystemVerilog, constraints, architecture, and debugging.

## Timeline

Fast loops can close in under three weeks from recruiter outreach to decision. Intern hardware loops can also move quickly after a school event or team referral. The slowest part is not the scheduling itself but the lack of precise round labels: candidates often learn only minutes before a round whether it is coding, ML case study, project deep-dive, or behavioral.

## Variants by org and geography

Loop shape varies sharply by team and region. Multimodal / generative-AI teams run a phone screen (ML coding plus transformer fundamentals) followed by a four-round virtual onsite: ML coding (e.g. a regression task), ML system design (a chatbot), an ML-fundamentals barrage, and an AI-assisted coding round. Domestic (China) MLE pipelines can compress to three rounds total, sometimes initiated directly by the hiring manager rather than a recruiter, with the next-round decision landing the following morning. Vision-team MLE phone screens follow the same shape — a general conversation about the team's work plus a from-scratch coding task such as implementing multi-head attention — and a booked onsite is not a guarantee: a hiring manager can decide not to move forward even after the next-round prep call has already been scheduled.

A recent full SWE loop shows the classic Apple pattern: code screen first, then an onsite with system design, multiple coding rounds, resume deep dive, and behavioral. Fast loops can proceed from code screen to onsite quickly, with verbal offer roughly one to two weeks after onsite and written offer/background-check paperwork about a week later.

In ASE data-infrastructure pipelines, the second screening round can compress a full coding problem and a system-design prompt into a single hour — a recent round paired a trie-flavored dictionary-lookup task with designing a system to process very large JSON payloads. Candidates describe the intensity as well above a standard 45-minute screen, so treat this round as two complete exercises and budget time accordingly.

Senior software pipelines can place a senior-manager conversation immediately after the hiring-manager screen, before any confirmed final round. Do not infer stage solely from interviewer seniority: the sequence can move from an HM résumé deep-dive with light coding to the HM's manager for a technical conversation as early as the next day.

A July 2026 senior SWE process split five 45-minute virtual-onsite rounds across two days. Positive feedback arrived two days after the final round, followed by a verbal offer the next day; the official offer arrived 12 days later after internal approvals. A long recruiter silence during that approval window did not signal a reversal, so treat post-verbal communication gaps as possible approval lag rather than a definitive outcome.

Another 2026 SWE sequence used two separate phone screens — implementation followed by distributed-system design — before a four-round onsite mixing code debugging, storage design, hiring-manager behavioral questions, and algorithmic coding.

Engineering-manager loops can start with the direct hiring manager, continue to a peer technical interview, and then expand into a four-person panel split between technical design and behavioral or business-partner sessions. A final 30-minute hiring-manager Q&A may follow the panel. HR may provide broad preparation themes before the panel, while a holiday period can stretch the decision to roughly two weeks.

## Accessories Software QA variant

The Accessories QA process can begin with an HR location discussion and a hiring-manager project interview, followed by an in-person portfolio presentation in Cupertino, interviews with team members and managers, and another coding session with San Diego colleagues the next day. The role itself can require working onsite in San Diego even when the interview takes place in Cupertino. Candidates encountered a two-to-three-week pause attributed to reorganization before receiving onsite invitations. Presentation panels ranged from six to eight people, with approximately 30–60 minutes allocated to the presentation or discussion. Strong alignment in the project interviews does not remove the final coding assessment.

## ML-oriented summer internship variant

A summer 2026 SDE internship process conducted in 2025 used two interviews, despite the work being closer to MLE. The first combined introductions and motivation for Apple with custom coding and a follow-up; explaining complexity and possible improvements mattered. The second began with research experience and moved into ML and mathematics/statistics. The candidate received a verbal offer the next day, within roughly a week of starting interviews, and a formal offer one to two weeks later. This is a team-specific example, not a standard timeline for every internship.

## iCloud screening variants

An iCloud ToolKit process used two separate coding phone screens. An iCloud senior MLE process for a time-series and operations-research optimization team instead began with a hiring-manager résumé deep dive, followed by a 45-minute ML forecasting discussion. In that MLE process, the recruiter sent a rejection within hours of the second interview. This is a possible decision timeline, not a guaranteed turnaround for other teams.

## September 2026 screening variants

For an Ads Staff opening, the recruiter first called the screen coding, then system design. The actual interview spent approximately 30 minutes on behavioral questions and the final 15 minutes on a technical design discussion. A Services hiring-manager screen after recruiter contact was entirely behavioral. A separate ASE Cloud Infrastructure opening used a 55-minute first interview with the hiring manager: conversation first, then just over 20 minutes of high-level design, followed by candidate questions. These sequences illustrate why a calendar label alone is an unreliable guide to the round.

Decision timing also varied: the Ads Staff rejection arrived three days after the screen, while the ASE Cloud Infrastructure rejection took about two weeks. For a 2027 software internship, recruiter contact came three days after an online application and the first interview went directly to a technical screen, opening with introductions and a brief résumé discussion.

## October 2026 infrastructure loop variants

A compute-infrastructure SDE team ran three phone interviews one at a time, each gated on passing the previous one, followed by three virtual onsite rounds. Almost every round centered on multithreading implementations and OS, networking, and distributed-systems fundamentals; there was very little system design or behavioral. The recruiter did not share round topics in advance, and the onsite topics provided turned out to be wrong. The rejection email arrived the evening after the final round.

An ASE storage-infrastructure phone stage used two 45-minute interviews: first the hiring manager (behavioral plus two easy coding questions with required test cases), then a tech lead (behavioral plus a distributed-cache design).

For a fully remote Kubernetes role, the screening result came back on the spot and the recruiter moved to schedule the phone screen within half an hour. After the phone screen passed, the process stalled a week later: an internal-transfer candidate took priority, and the external candidate would be contacted again only if that person did not pass.

A 2026 virtual onsite ran four rounds: system design, a coding round with a deliberately vague prompt, an LRU-cache coding round that turned into design follow-ups, and a behavioral round focused on project depth.

## Late-October 2026 decision delivery

As of late October 2026, some teams deliver onsite rejections by phone instead of email. In one case, the recruiter scheduled the call about a week after the onsite, and this happened for two separate onsites in a row. A recruiter call booked several days out does not signal an offer. Treat it as a neutral decision call. Ask the recruiter for the expected decision date so the wait is not open-ended.

## November 2026 loop variants

**ICT4 services engineering.** Two coding phone screens ran about ten days apart. The virtual onsite was split across two days: three rounds on the first day (concurrent-data-structure coding, a permissions-system design, a document-sync design) and two on the second (an ingestion-service design and a project architecture deep-dive). Every onsite round also carried one targeted behavioral prompt. Positive feedback arrived four days after the final round, and a verbal offer followed two days later.

**New grad.** The process opened with an HR call to confirm graduation date and location preference. It then ran three back-to-back rounds: Java fundamentals plus a coding problem, a roughly 90-minute hiring-manager behavioral interview, and a friendly behavioral round with a long-tenured HR partner. The coding round and the manager's impression appear to carry the decision. A team may interview several new-grad candidates in different cycles and pick one per opening, so an offer can be a choice among multiple finalists.

**Senior screens.** An Ads senior SWE phone screen produced a rejection about one week later. An ASE screening stage used two separate phone interviews, each a single coding problem with behavioral questions at the start of the first.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Google's full-time loop is split into two big sessions with a hiring committee (HC) gate in the middle, then a team-match phase before any offer.

## End-to-end pipeline

1. **Recruiter reach-out** — usually triggered by referral, application, or LinkedIn outreach. A 15–30 min chat covers background, target level, and timing.
2. **OA (optional)** — 90 min, 2 problems on HackerRank for SWE Early Career; sometimes skipped for senior or referred candidates. See the Coin-Collecting Board and Group-by-Digit cards.
3. **R1 — Phone / virtual** — 1 coding round + 1 BQ round, each 45 min. Sometimes combined into a 60-min slot (15 min BQ + 45 min coding). Pass-through rate is the loop's first hard filter.
4. **R2 — Onsite** — typically 2 back-to-back rounds. For SWE: two coding rounds. For MLE / AI-ML: one coding + one ML domain. For L5/L6: adds 1–2 system design + leadership + project deep-dive. As of late 2025, R2 has shifted back to in-person at a Google office for most US loops; coordinator handles flights and hotel.
5. **HC review** — package goes to hiring committee. No candidate-facing event; 1–3 week wait.
6. **Visa check** — recruiter call to confirm work authorization. Does not imply HC has passed yet (most candidates get this call regardless).
7. **Team match** — pass HC and you enter a 1–8 week phase finding a team. Some orgs pre-allocate a team (no team match needed); most loops require browsing open roles and interviewing with HMs.
8. **HM call** — once a team has interest, the hiring manager runs a final fit chat. Offer follows.

## Typical cadence

- Recruiter reach-out → OA: 1–2 weeks
- OA → R1: 1–3 weeks
- R1 → R2: 2–6 weeks (longer if onsite scheduling spans a holiday)
- R2 → HC outcome: 1–3 weeks
- HC pass → team match offer: 2–8 weeks
- End to end: **2–6 months** from first contact to signed offer; 6+ months is not unusual.

## Onsite logistics

- The in-person VO uses a Chromebook in a small conference room; you sign into your own Google email account to take notes.
- Coding happens on a shared whiteboard plus the Chromebook for Google Docs. Bug-free code is not required — interviewers prefer dialogue.
- Each round has a 5-min intro from the interviewer, 35–40 min of problem work, and 5 min for candidate questions.
- Lunch is hosted by a Google employee mid-day and is **not evaluated**.

## Cooling period

- A clean fail at VO triggers a **~12-month cooling period** before you can re-interview for SWE.
- The cooling period applies per company-wide, not per team. Reapplying to a different org during the cooling period typically gets auto-rejected by recruiting tooling.
- If you only failed team match (HC passed), you can usually retry team match within 6–12 months without redoing the loop.

## 2026 R2 scheduling update

Recent L4 / Early Career loops still treat R2 as an onsite session by default, but coordinators can move individual R2 days back to virtual when logistics require it. Candidates should prepare for the same two technical rounds either way: an in-person R2 usually uses office logistics and a Chromebook, while the virtual version keeps the Google Docs / Meet format. Recruiters may be firm about in-person attendance even when the candidate asks to convert; if a health or travel issue exists, expect the coordinator to prefer delaying the onsite over replacing it outright.

## 2026 role-specific paths

- One L5 SWE path uses a 45-minute virtual coding round followed by a 45-minute leadership round as the first gate; the later session is planned as two coding rounds plus one system-design round.
- Google DeepMind Research Engineer recruiting for Gemini post-training starts with a background-and-motivation recruiter conversation, followed by two medium-to-hard algorithmic coding rounds and an ML quiz.
- Team-match conversations for internal ML tooling groups can include technical prompts about model design and anomaly detection. Treat these conversations as both fit discussions and lightweight technical screens.

## PhD new-graduate AI/ML and L4 examples

A 2026 PhD AI/ML path uses two technical-stage interviews covering ML and behavioral questions, followed by two in-person coding interviews. One candidate reached the phone screen around day 60 after applying, technical interviews around day 90, onsite around day 120, and team match around day 135. These are individual timings, not scheduling guarantees. The onsite offered a choice of Bay Area or Seattle locations; itemized personal receipts were required for reimbursement.

An L4 path moved from R1 to scheduling R2 in three days, then from onsite to positive feedback and HC submission in roughly one week, with HC approval and team match another week later. HC approved that candidate at L3, illustrating that a positive interview outcome need not preserve the level initially targeted.

## September 2026 L4 design variation

An L4 loop can include a design interview alongside coding, so the earlier two-coding-round description is not universal. One sequence ran from a July 27 questionnaire to an August 11 recruiter conversation, August 24 R1, and September 17 R2; R2 was arranged on the day of R1. Treat this as one scheduling example and confirm the exact round mix with recruiting.

## Late-2026 path examples

- **Early-career L3:** a first online coding round, a separate online behavioral round about a month later, then two in-person coding rounds roughly two months after that (one reschedule included). The four interviews spanned about four months; HC passed, but team match remained open afterward — at L3, team match can be the longest and least certain stage.
- **New-grad general hire:** the OA can arrive many months after the application (one candidate applied in September and received the OA the following year). Virtual interviews followed two to three weeks after the OA, as four rounds that each combined behavioral questions with a coding problem rather than a dedicated behavioral slot.
- **Applied AI, senior level:** the onsite ran as two coding rounds plus one system-design round, with no standalone behavioral interview. Recruiter feedback was given per round, identifying which specific rounds fell short.

## Late-2026 two-round format and solutions design

- Some L4 team-specific loops (including referral-driven ones) now run as just two sessions. **Round 1** pairs a standard coding problem — written in an editor that does not compile — with a behavioral interview. **Round 2** pairs a **solutions design** interview with another coding problem. Solutions design resembles system design but is less ambiguous; one example prompt was an LLM-based review-ingestion and summarization platform with emphasis on trust and safety, prompt injection, input sanitization, and PII handling.
- The onsite for this format can be in person with a virtual option, and the whole process can total as few as four interviews.
- An L5 timeline after a referral: recruiter contact and Hiring Assessment two weeks later, R1 within about two weeks, R2 (onsite at a New York office) about four weeks after that, HC approval roughly four weeks after R2, team match three weeks later, and the offer one month after matching — about four and a half months end to end.

## Communication can sink an otherwise strong onsite

An L4 onsite ended in no-hire with "lack of communication" as the stated reason, even though both coding problems and their follow-ups were solved optimally and an earlier phone screen had rated communication as outstanding. Feedback beyond that phrase was not shared. Treat communication as a separately scored axis in every round: narrate clarifications, decisions, and trade-offs explicitly, and check in with the interviewer instead of assuming that a correct solution speaks for itself.

## October 2026 notes

- **L4 timeline:** application in late August, Hiring Assessment in mid-September (passed on submission), then R1 scheduled about a month later. R1 combined one behavioral and one coding interview, and the pass notice arrived the next day with a hand-off to a new recruiter for the next stage.
- **L5 onsite is in person:** a request to switch the onsite to virtual was declined. One L5 onsite ran system design plus two coding rounds; another ran two coding rounds plus an AI-flavored design round.
- **L6 direct loop:** a recruiter-sourced L6 candidate went straight to four virtual rounds — two ML system design (one with the hiring manager), one coding, and one behavioral — with no separate phone screen.

## November 2026 notes

- **Positive round feedback does not guarantee HC approval.** One candidate received "positive feedback, move to next steps" after the onsite, and the next recruiter relayed "strong performance in code comprehension, data structures and algorithms; BQ also good" — yet the hiring committee rejected roughly four weeks later, citing "mixed" coding performance (both coding rounds had needed hints). Requests for an additional interview or a down-level were declined as a final decision, with a **12-month cooldown**.
- **Pre-onsite verification can delay scheduling.** A name mismatch in background checks can hold up onsite scheduling; use your legal name consistently across the application and all paperwork from the start.
- **L4 with Solutions Design:** phone screen of LeetCode + Googleyness, then an onsite (Kirkland) of LeetCode + Solutions Design, where the design slot ran as a detailed deep dive on a shipped project rather than a system design prompt.
- **L3 onsite:** three technical coding rounds plus one Googleyness & Leadership round with resume deep-dive questions.
- **L5 onsite:** two coding rounds plus a system design round with a data-pipeline flavor (e.g., finding the slowest query each day over fixed daily windows).

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Uber's loop is short by FAANG standards: one OA, one phone screen, one onsite. The recruiter side is the main scheduling pain.

## End-to-end pipeline

1. **Recruiter screen / referral intake** — 15–20 min. Covers level target, location preference, visa status, comp expectations. Some loops skip this and go straight to OA when a referral is in place.
2. **OA** — Hack2Hire HackerRank-style or CodeSignal. 70–90 min. SDE2 / Senior typically 2 problems (90 min); some older SDE2 loops saw 3–4 problems (70 min, CodeSignal). Camera + screen share + mic required; ID check at start. No external IDE.
3. **Phone screen (tech screen)** — 60 min. Usually 1 coding round (1 medium + 1 follow-up or 2 short problems), occasionally an OOD prompt instead. MLE loops fold an ML knowledge check or ML coding into this slot.
4. **Virtual onsite (VO)** — 4 rounds, 60 min each, in one or two consecutive days:
   - 2 × coding (one is often OOD: parking lot, meeting scheduler, expression evaluator)
   - 1 × system design (L5+) or project deep-dive (L4 / NG)
   - 1 × hiring-manager BQ (often combined with a short BQ + previous-project walkthrough); this combined deep-dive + BQ round commonly runs ~75 minutes, noticeably longer than the other rounds
5. **Result & team match** — Most teams are organized as direct hire, not a separate team-match phase. Outcome lands in 1–2 weeks via the assigned recruiter.

## Typical cadence

- Application / referral → recruiter contact: 1–3 weeks.
- Recruiter → OA: 3–7 days.
- OA → phone screen: 1–2 weeks.
- Phone screen → VO: 2–4 weeks.
- VO → outcome: 1–2 weeks (longer if the recruiter is slow — see below).
- End to end: **6–10 weeks**; some pipelines slip to 3+ months when recruiters reschedule.

## Recruiter caveat

A recurring pain point: several Uber recruiters are notorious for sitting on results, double-rescheduling phone screens, or cancelling interviews when the candidate pushes back. Multiple candidates have lost a loop because the recruiter cancelled after two reschedules. If recruiter ghosting persists for more than 10 business days, escalate through a referrer or directly to the assigned coordinator — internal referrers can usually surface the result faster than a portal status check.

## Cooling period

- Failed phone screen → typically 6 months before re-applying to any Uber engineering role.
- Failed VO → 6–12 months depending on the team; recruiters sometimes set this explicitly in the rejection email.
- The cooling rule applies company-wide, not per team. Changing the application email is not a workaround — internal ATS dedupes by phone and identity.

## In-person vs virtual

Almost all loops in 2025–2026 remain fully virtual via Zoom / Google Meet, regardless of level. A few rare onsite VO conversions have been seen for staff-level candidates relocating to SF or NYC.

## 2026 Team-Match Timing Signal

Recent senior loops can still depend on team interest after a positive interview signal. A candidate may clear the loop, wait while the original team chooses another person, and later match to a different group. Treat the post-VO phase as active until the recruiter gives a final answer: keep recruiter communication warm, ask whether other teams can review the packet, and use internal referrers when scheduling stalls.

## 2026 SDE II BPS-style loop variant

A current SDE II sequence uses five named checkpoints after recruiter intake: a BPS-style screening round, DSA coding, runnable low-level design, high-level system design, and a hiring-manager behavioral round. The screening round can begin with high-level object modeling before expanding into executable code. The low-level-design round emphasizes design patterns and concurrency handling, while the high-level-design round explicitly grades architecture trade-offs and non-functional requirements such as storage and latency.

## 2026 phone-screen split variant

One current 60-minute phone screen allocates about 5 minutes to introductions, 20 minutes to coding, 30 minutes to a project deep-dive, and 5 minutes to candidate questions. Prepare the project narrative before the virtual onsite: this format moves architecture choices and ownership probes into the screen itself.

## 45-minute accelerated VO variant

Some four-round virtual on-sites run in 45-minute blocks. The main prompt is expected to be completed in roughly the first 15 minutes, leaving most of the round for changing requirements: concrete allocation instead of a count, streaming input instead of a sortable batch, moving data, or production-scale distance semantics. Practice finishing the base implementation quickly enough to discuss and code at least one extension.

## September 2026: 45-minute technical phone screen

A 45-minute technical phone screen can open with a resume walkthrough, the most challenging project, the candidate's usual technology stack, and an introduction to the hiring team's business. The remaining approximately 30 minutes are reserved for coding. Budget for both the project conversation and implementation within the same session.

## September 2026: L5a infrastructure backfill variant

An L5a infrastructure/backend backfill loop can proceed from a phone screen to a three-round virtual onsite: one coding round, one system-design round, and one hiring-manager behavioral conversation. In this shortened format, the hiring manager may already have feedback from the two technical rounds and use the conversation to discuss staffing urgency and expectations for getting up to speed quickly. This is a team-specific loop variant.

## October 2026: Staff phone screen with a design segment

A Staff-level phone screen can run as 45 minutes of coding followed by 15 minutes of free-form design. The coding half may be a known recurring prompt; candidates discuss a brute-force approach, then optimize, and the interviewer may accept a verbal dry run of the provided example instead of asking for written test cases. The design half does not necessarily follow the published guideline of discussing a past project's challenge and decisions. Instead, it can ask where ML or LLMs could add leverage across one of the hiring team's end-to-end operational workflows, such as a task flow running from customer request through driver execution to evidence upload. Prepare a structured answer that walks the flow stage by stage and names concrete ML insertion points.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Standard Loop Shape

The default loop is a strict **one-round-at-a-time** funnel. Each round is scheduled only after the previous round passes; failing any round closes the loop immediately (early-break model). Typical shape across SWE / MLE / SRE reports:

- **Recruiter / HR call** (optional, sometimes skipped when recruiters reach out directly via LinkedIn)
- **Phone screen / R1** — 60 min, project deep-dive (15-30 min) + 1-2 coding problems (30-45 min), occasionally with 八股 in the front quarter
- **R2** — 60 min, same shape; can be a second coding round or pivot to system / ML system design
- **R3** — 60 min, often hiring-manager round (HM): heavier behavioral + one more coding / design problem
- **Team match call** (HR) — once technical rounds clear, the recruiter pitches a team and confirms terms

End-to-end typical timeline: 3-6 weeks from first contact to verbal offer, depending on rescheduling friction.

## Variants by Org

- **TikTok USDS (US Data Squad / SRE)** — 4 rounds scheduled in one batch (coding, network/linux, system design, HM). All four scheduled up front but later rounds are cancelled on failure of an earlier one. Frequently finishes in 2 weeks.
- **TikTok Intern / NG SWE** — typically 3 rounds + HR; the third round sometimes adds a "code-reading + design" hybrid.
- **MLE / Monetization / Commerce / E-Commerce** — 3 technical rounds, each blending project deep-dive + ML 八股 + 1 coding problem. The third round may be HM with deeper project drill rather than fresh coding.
- **ByteDance Research Scientist / Volcano Engine AML** — 2-3 rounds. Coding is sometimes nominal (Lark editor, no compile) — the bar is on research depth and design conversations.
- **TikTok Backend / Live Service Arch** — 1 HR + 1 coding + frequent ghosting between rounds; reports of being dropped after 1 round are common.

## Scheduling Friction

- Recruiters frequently reschedule mid-loop; multiple reports of rounds being rebooked 2-3 times before they actually happen.
- HR sometimes ghosts after a round for 1-2 weeks before either matching to a team or rejecting; do not interpret silence as decline-pending.
- Mismatched JD-to-org placement is common — candidates with K8s background end up paired with Hadoop teams, frontend candidates with backend deep-dives. Confirm the actual interview content with the recruiter before each round.
- Bar for "team match" after technical pass is its own gate: some candidates pass all loops but spend weeks waiting for a team to claim them, then get re-shuffled.

## Recent process signals from 2026 Q2

Recent loops continue to be strictly one-round-at-a-time, but team-level hiring state can override good feedback: candidates can clear early rounds, then have the role filled or be redirected to another group without restarting the original feedback trail. Some senior loops are group-specific rather than company-standard: three rounds may all be project deep-dive / module design, while another group for the same candidate may start over with a peer design round.


As of mid-2026, per-round cadence in slower loops runs roughly two weeks apart with results about a week after each round. Recent rounds — including frontend screens — increasingly gate on conceptual follow-up depth even when the coding is fully solved: writing correct code is no longer sufficient if you cannot reason about an adjacent concept the interviewer probes (e.g. how to act when a cache's miss rate is high).

## 2026 Q2 Signal

Ads and Growth loops continue to run as a strict pass-one-round-then-schedule-next-round funnel: technical screen first, then system design, then HM. Recent Growth feedback also shows the second round can pivot fully to recommendation-engine design after a resume-heavy opening.

## 2026 Q3 Dense-Loop Variant

A recent SWE loop compressed five rounds into two days and added a sixth "check another direction" round on the second afternoon. That sequence mixed two hard coding rounds, a data-structure round, recommendation system design, behavioral plus resume drill, and an extra coding check. Treat the nominal round count as flexible and keep one additional project and one additional coding block ready even after the scheduled loop appears complete.

## 2026 Q3 Mixed-Round Compression

Second-round structure can be highly compressed: roughly 30 minutes of resume deep-dive, 15 minutes of system design, and 15 minutes of coding, with only the principal coding logic expected before time expires. A 2027 summer-intern screen used a similarly explicit 5 / 25 / 25 / 5 split across introduction, resume plus design fundamentals, coding, and candidate questions. Ads screens can return a next-day pass and still stall for two weeks while the next round is scheduled, so keep parallel processes active until a concrete calendar invite arrives.

## September 2026 Team-Specific Scheduling

A USDS JV senior MLE process can schedule two consecutive one-hour interviews after the recruiter conversation: an introduction/project discussion plus coding, followed by a background and technical-fit discussion. Another USDS loop proceeds roughly one round per week, with two coding rounds and then an HM round that still includes coding.

An already planned HM interview can be cancelled because hiring priorities or business needs change. Early-round completion therefore does not guarantee that the remaining interviews will take place.

## September 2026 Three-Design-Round Variant

A ByteDance loop can consist of three system-design rounds conducted entirely in Chinese, with the hiring manager leading the first round. In this variant, the first two rounds include live AI-assisted implementation after the candidate writes down the design approach. Invitations to the next round arrived roughly two days after each of those interviews; the candidate was still awaiting a decision one week after the third round. That sequence establishes the interview format, but does not establish an offer, rejection, or waitlist outcome.

## Late September – October 2026 Loop Shapes

A USDS SWE loop ran three technical rounds: a two-problem coding round, a second round with one modified coding problem followed by monitoring / tracing / telemetry questions, and a third round pairing a quick high-level system design with project deep-dive. About a week later the recruiter scheduled an additional HR call focused on immigration status, said a decision would come within the week, and then went silent. An extra HR call after the technical rounds is a logistics step, not a confirmation of an offer.

A 2027 new-grad SWE loop opened with a graph / topological-sort coding round followed by a system-design round. Interviews completed just before China's National Day holiday (October 1–7) can sit without feedback until the holiday ends.

A 2027 summer e-commerce backend intern process ran: application on August 6, OA the next day, HR scheduling on August 23, a one-hour technical interview on September 11, and a rejection on September 26 — roughly two weeks from interview to result.

## October 2026 Loop Signals

A USDS SWE onsite ran three rounds: two coding rounds (a fast two-problem round, then one tree problem that took most of the hour) followed by a system-design round that drilled further into consistency and failure cases than candidates expected.

Recruiter descriptions of round types are not reliable. In a USDS MLE loop billed as "coding, coding, ML system design", the first round opened with ML 八股 before a NumPy data-transformation task, the second added an ML system-design problem to a data-parser coding task, and the third combined ML system design with hand-written attention. That loop used no LeetCode-style problems at all. Interviewers were US-based and courteous; prepare every round for coding, ML knowledge, and ML design together.

Failing a round does not always end the process: some candidates are re-routed to a new team and start another loop. One candidate went through three such single rounds, each with resume deep-dive, 八股, BQ, and 20-30 minutes of coding, before stepping away. Treat each re-route as a fresh evaluation rather than a continuation.

Research Scientist new-grad screens open with a research presentation, then questions on recent model technical reports, multimodal understanding, and normalization choices, before a single coding problem where the interviewer pushes past the first working complexity.

## Late October 2026 Loop Shapes

- **Infra onsite (four rounds):** three coding rounds and a project deep dive that ended with a short arithmetic puzzle, with infrastructure fundamentals (Kubernetes networking, DNS, HTTP versions, 5xx debugging) and "how do you use AI at work" asked in every round. A verbal offer came immediately after the loop and was withdrawn the next day because another candidate had accepted — get the offer in writing before treating it as final.
- **AML new-grad (two rounds):** a team-lead round and a hiring-manager round, each with about 30 minutes of resume deep dive (which method, why, and concrete implementation details) plus one coding problem. The process can still end in a "headcount filled" rejection after both rounds go well.
- **Phone screen:** one North America screen split time roughly half project discussion, half coding.
- **Coding + SD loop:** another loop ran two coding rounds plus one system-design round.

## November 2026 Loop Signals

- **SWE onsite (three coding rounds):** one problem per round, each on the hard side: a constrained string-construction greedy, a multi-day grid quarantine simulation, and a nested-formula parser. Passing the onsite does not finish the process. Team match follows, and hiring managers in team-match calls may ask system-design questions without warning, so keep design skills warm until an offer is signed.
- **USDS one-hour first round:** interviewer introduction, self-introduction, a project deep dive, a HackerRank coding problem, then ML-foundation questions with no coding. Results can come back within hours: one rejection arrived the same evening.
- **Data-engineer new-grad:** applied in September, interviewed in early October. Round one was in English (resume, one Python LeetCode problem, one SQL problem). Round two, a week later, was entirely in Mandarin: resume plus open-ended questions on reconciling metrics between upstream and downstream tables, and on scheduling tasks with ready times and execution times on limited resources to minimize the final completion time.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Common Pipeline

A typical Snowflake SWE loop runs:

1. **Recruiter / HR screen** (~30 min). Process intro, resume walk-through, location, work authorization. Snowflake's HR screen is unusually high-impact — candidates are rejected at this stage with no technical signal, sometimes after only superficial conversation. Treat it as a real round, not a formality.
2. **Work-authorization form**. Sent before any technical interview once the recruiter advances the candidate.
3. **Phone screen — two back-to-back coding rounds**, usually 45-60 min each. Same day or split across two consecutive days. Each round is one coding prompt with deep follow-ups; almost always pulled from the recurring bank (multi-source BFS grid, course-schedule variants, tree-deletion height, transactional KV).
4. **Virtual onsite**. Usually 3-4 rounds: an additional coding round, a system-design round (often KV store, job scheduler, or ACL service), and a behavioral round. Some loops slot in a fourth coding or replace BQ with an HM-style conversation.
5. **Hiring manager call**. Confirmation that the loop has passed; not always purely informational, depending on level.

## Timing

From referral to onsite scheduling is typically 2-4 weeks. Loops with no scheduling friction can complete in under a month. Rejections after the technical screen often arrive within 1-3 days; HM call to offer can take an additional 1-2 weeks. Recruiters generally do not give technical feedback after a rejection.

## 2026 Updates

Two shifts have surfaced in mid-2026 loops:

- **In-person onsite.** Some recruiters now require an in-person onsite after the phone screens rather than the older virtual onsite. Confirm the format when scheduling so you can plan travel.
- **AI-conducted pre-screen for general SWE.** Applicants to the general SWE pipeline may receive an automated AI screening interview before any human round — a ~20-minute voice interview to be completed within a week of the invitation. It deep-dives your experience and asks how you use AI tools at work; treat it as a real evaluated round, not a formality.

By late summer 2026, the back-to-back technical screen was not uniform across teams: one loop paired a coding round with a system-design round rather than two coding rounds. Confirm the round mix with the recruiter and be ready to switch directly from implementation to architecture discussion.

## Intern Loop

A fall-intern virtual onsite used two coding rounds. One centered on isolating the prerequisite route for a target course in a dependency graph; the other began with linked-list cloning and added a random-pointer follow-up. This is a useful format signal, but scheduling and round composition may vary by team.

## Data Engineer Loop

The Data Engineer pipeline differs from the SWE loop. Instead of algorithmic coding, the two technical rounds (≈1 hour each) center on SQL and Python: the first pairs SQL queries (joins, duration filters, per-entity aggregation) with a Python data-manipulation task; the second adds a data-modeling / pipeline-design exercise — for example, consolidating multiple SaaS application sources into a single analytics layer — alongside more SQL and Python. The onsite is lighter on coding, typically a conversation with the hiring director plus an informal session with team members, so behavioral fit carries more weight at the final stage.

## When the Phone Rounds Aren't Clean

If the two phone coding rounds are solved but not cleanly bug-free, Snowflake sometimes schedules an extra coding round a few days later rather than rejecting outright. Recent additional rounds have paired a quick string-manipulation warm-up with a math / construction prompt, and interviewers may favor the simplest working solution over a clever one.

## Late-Stage Team Evaluation

For higher-level candidates, the process may continue after the formal onsite with another hiring-manager conversation and a separate prospective-teammate chat. These are still evaluative: strong onsite feedback does not guarantee an offer, and the team may continue comparing candidates through the final conversation. Clarify who owns the final decision and whether each post-onsite chat contributes interview feedback.

## September 2026 IC1 Screen

An IC1 technical screen used two virtual coding rounds with multiple prompts in each round. The first combined two separate problems; the second extended its initial problem into a path-returning follow-up. Allow time for a second task even after completing the opening implementation. One timeline ran from an August 3 referral to an August 7 recruiter call and September 3 technical rounds, with technical scheduling initiated on the day of the recruiter call.

## September 2026 Coding-Round Format

A two-round online coding loop allocated approximately one hour per round, including an opening self-introduction or project conversation, implementation time, and candidate questions at the end. Budget for that opening and closing discussion rather than assuming the entire hour is available for coding.

## Agent-Focused AI Engineer Loop

An agent-focused AI Engineer hiring path uses a standard algorithmic coding screen and an ML-fundamentals interview called **ML Expertise** before an in-person onsite. The onsite has three rounds: **AI Augmented Coding**, a second **Expertise** discussion aligned with the team's agent work, and a **behavioral conversation with the hiring manager**. This path hires directly into a team, so the Expertise discussion follows that team's work rather than a uniform general-hire syllabus.

The office visit includes an advance QR code and parking instructions. This hiring path also requires **two professional reference contacts before an offer is issued**. Arrange those contacts in advance and confirm the reference-check timing with the recruiter; these details describe the AI Engineer path and do not establish a uniform sequence for every Snowflake role.

## October 2026 Notes

- **Phone screen mix.** A backend loop again paired a system-design round (a pipeline that loads data from S3 into a database) with a coding round (transactional key-value store) at the phone stage; its onsite then consisted of an AI-enabled coding round, a project deep dive, and a behavioral round.
- **Interviewer no-shows.** Interviewers sometimes cancel minutes after the scheduled start; the recruiter then adds a replacement round a few days later. If an interviewer cuts a round short on their own schedule, asking the recruiter to reschedule is reasonable rather than accepting a truncated evaluation.
- **In-round reassurance is not a verdict.** Candidates have been rejected the day after an interviewer said in the room that a round clearly went well. Treat every round's follow-ups as decisive and do not read the outcome from interviewer tone.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Microsoft runs two parallel hiring tracks that share a recruiter pool but very little else.

## Traditional Loop (Azure / Copilot / Cloud / Office)

Most non-MAI teams use either a **team-specific virtual onsite (VO)** or the standardized **Hiring Event (HE)** track. Both formats land in the same place — four 60-minute rounds — but HE is back-to-back from roughly 8:00am to 1:30pm Pacific with 30-minute breaks, and the slot cannot be moved (HE batches run on fixed weekdays; candidates pick the week, not the time of day). Team-招 VOs are more flexible on time.

Typical four-round shape:

- 3 × coding + BQ (45-50 min coding after 10-15 min behavioral)
- 1 × system design (sometimes substituted with an OOD round)

The HE bar is roughly L61/L62 (SDE II). Failing HE triggers a **6-month freeze on HE re-entry**, but you can still apply through team-招 postings during that window. Team-招 has no such global freeze.

Phone screen, when present, is a single 45-60 minute technical round. Recruiter screens are short logistics calls — process intro, level expectation, location.

After the loop, decisions usually arrive within 1-2 weeks. Team-match for HE candidates can stretch significantly (weeks of org shopping) because HC approval is decoupled from team selection.

## MAI / Microsoft AI Loop (Mustafa Suleyman's org)

MAI runs its own loop and recruiter pool. Structure varies by sub-team (Copilot, pretrain, post-train infra, Bing, Super Intelligence) but the common shape is:

- HM phone (background + level routing)
- 1-2 technical phone screens (often ML-coding, OAI-style problems)
- 4-6 round onsite: project deep dive + 2-3 coding + 1-2 system design (sometimes ML system design) + HM/culture

Onsite is one day rather than HE's two-day option. Recent Copilot / MAI onsites (2026 Q2) increasingly label the coding rounds as "AI Coding Agent" rounds, sometimes paired one with-AI and one without-AI (see the tooling briefing); the deep-dive round may ask you to send a PR link and walk the live diff. MAI coding consistently uses OpenAI-style prompts (in-memory DB, beam search, batch dataloader, stop token detection, DNA sequence reconstruction) — candidates who only prepped LeetCode are blindsided. Recruiters do not pre-share the topic list.


2026 Principal loops can be scheduled as a phone screen followed by a two-day virtual onsite rather than a single HE block. The shape is still four main VO rounds: behavioral plus system design, AI-fluency / applied-AI discussion, another behavioral plus system design, and an OOD coding round.

**September 2026 — a three-round senior SWE onsite variant.** A senior SWE process can consist of a technical phone screen followed by three onsite rounds. One such loop combined a project-based behavioral opener and implementation discussion in the first round, two technical exercises in the second, and a library implementation in the third. The four-round formats above do not cover every team-specific loop.

**September 2026 — a five-round SDE II variant.** A team-specific loop can span five rounds: coding with basic data-structure discussion; an AI-assisted design and coding exercise; system design with a hand-written implementation component; an operating-systems and C++ discussion tied to resume projects; and a behavioral review of past work and achievements. Round count and the balance between coding, design, and domain knowledge vary by team. This format does not establish a replacement for the Hiring Event schedule above.

**Late 2026 — MAI principal applied-scientist loop (data platform team).** A Microsoft AI web-data-platform team (separate from Superintelligence) ran a phone screen on ML fundamentals, background, data questions, and some design. The four VO rounds each split roughly in half between coding and system design, with brief data-focused ML questions on class imbalance, evaluation, and data drift. The round topics shared by the recruiter did not fully match the actual interviews. In one case, the requisition was canceled hours after the final round; a completed loop does not guarantee that headcount remains open.

**Late 2026 — a Windows + Devices SWE II loop.** One process began with a resume and behavioral screen, then four same-day rounds: behavioral plus coding, behavioral plus system design, a standalone behavioral round, and resume discussion plus coding. The same coding problem family appeared in both coding rounds. A not-selected status appeared four days after the onsite.

**October 2026 — an SWE II / Senior SWE four-round final loop.** The candidate chose a morning or afternoon block, then ran four consecutive rounds of about an hour each: behavioral plus a rapid-fire CS-fundamentals quiz plus coding; introduction plus coding; a Principal SWE round opening with career-direction questions before system design; and behavioral plus a second system design. Two system-design rounds in one loop is possible at this level. If you do not join on time, the recruiter calls to check whether you are still attending — double-check the start time in your own time zone.

**October 2026 — Azure Compute loop.** The phone screen paired an Azure control-plane system design with a coding problem. The onsite had four rounds: a load-balancer design for the compute layer (scaling for high load, fault tolerance), a behavioral round centered on why Microsoft, and two coding rounds built on variants of familiar interval-scheduling and permutation problems. A rejection can arrive as a generic email with no feedback.

**October 2026 — a three-round SDE loop.** One SDE loop ran a system-design round that starts from a single-client design and scales out through load balancing, horizontal scaling, and database sharding; an object-oriented design round with class modeling followed by an implementation function; and a data-structures-and-algorithms round packing three problems into one session. Expect several short problems per round in this format, not one long one.

**Hiring-manager screens and round gating.** A hiring-manager phone screen for a closely matching role can spend about 45 minutes on detailed project discussion before a short coding question. Later rounds are not guaranteed: in at least one onsite, failing a round led to cancellation of the final scheduled round.

briefings.title: Round Format & Pacing
briefings.body:
Karat runs the first technical screen for a number of companies. The hiring company decides whether to use Karat, but the round itself — the prompt, the interviewer and the pacing — follows Karat's own format.

## What a round looks like

- **Multi-part problems.** Expect a sequence of parts rather than one problem. One format is a staged extension of existing code: fix a bug in a provided method, implement a new method, then implement a harder method. Another is two independent problems back to back (for example, a string-validation task followed by a table-joining task).
- **Not finishing is expected.** Interviewers may say upfront that you are not required to complete every part. Bank the early parts cleanly before starting the hardest one.
- **Coding time is short.** About 40 minutes of coding time is typical, and long prompts with starter code eat a large share of that in reading alone.

## Pacing advice

- Skim the whole prompt and the provided classes once, then re-read only the part you are working on.
- Get the quick wins (bug fix, simple method) correct and tested before moving to the open-ended last part.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Pipeline

A typical OpenAI loop runs:

1. **Recruiter / HR screen** (~30 min). Process intro + standard BQ (why OpenAI, why leave, salary expectations, location). HR will not share interview-specific feedback later — this is a stated company policy, not an oversight.
2. **Phone screen — coding** (60 min). Almost always one prompt occupying the entire hour, with 3-5 progressive sub-parts. The interviewer expects the first 2-3 parts done with clean code and edges handled. Most SWE pipelines pair it with a separate system design screen, on the same day or a different day.
3. **Final loop** — by the company's own framing, "4–6 hours of final interviews with 4–6 people over 1–2 days." On a SWE / RS / RE pipeline this concretely lands as 4-5 rounds:
    - 1-2× coding (sometimes a separate ML programming round for RS / RE),
    - 1× system design or ML system design,
    - 1× technical deep dive (slide-based, on your strongest project),
    - 1× HM behavioral — the final gate.

XFN / PM / cross-functional pitch rounds appear on some loops.

## Typical timeline

- Resume review window after application: roughly one week.
- Recruiter reachout → HR call → phone screen: typically 2-3 weeks apart.
- Phone screen → final loop: 1-2 weeks scheduling, then the loop runs over 1-2 consecutive days.
- Final loop → decision: target is "within one week of final interviews," though team-match cases can stretch this to 1-2 weeks longer.

## Format

The default mode is **virtual** (video calls with screen-share for technical rounds). Candidates may request to interview onsite in San Francisco; that's the documented opt-in, not the default. Pre-loop, the recruiter confirms which rounds use Colab vs the standard coding platform.

## Signaling notes

- The HM BQ + technical deep dive are **gated** — they only "unlock" if the technical rounds passed. Reaching them is itself a positive signal.
- HR asking for internal references on Day 1 after the interview is widely read as a borderline-status signal — not a guaranteed pass.
- Quiet HM in the BQ round ("HM not selling the role") is widely cited as a negative signal. Counter it by proactively pitching role fit rather than passively answering.

## What the bar emphasizes

The published hiring philosophy is explicitly *not* credential-driven: the company flags collaboration, communication, openness to feedback, and mission alignment as core axes alongside the technical bar. Practically this maps onto the deep dive (collaboration + communication signals) and the HM BQ (mission alignment), which is why "Why OpenAI / AGI / safety" gets its own dedicated round and is treated as a real gate, not a formality.

## Post-loop add-on: the 15-minute HM call

A short (≈15 min) HM call sometimes appears between the loop pass signal and the team-match phase. Recruiters frame it as "no prep needed, just a chat," but it is graded: candidates have moved forward after positive technical feedback only to be rejected after a flat HM call. Treat it as a compressed HM round — have a sharp 'why OpenAI' and one timeline-pressure story ready, even though the format reads casual.

## Compensation & process signals (mid-2026)

- **Recruiter speed**: outreach can land within ~2 days of applying, weekends included.
- **Three-stage framing** a recruiter recently laid out: Stage 1 — two technical rounds (~60 min data-structures/coding + a system-design round); Stage 2 — virtual onsite (60-min coding, a live refactoring/optimization round, and the slide-based technical deep dive); Stage 3 — hiring manager.
- **Base salary** quoted in a recent recruiter call: roughly up to ~$327K (L5) and ~$385K (L6) base; total comp adds equity on top.
- **Debrief cadence** is commonly Tuesday / Friday, so the wait between the final round and a decision tends to bucket around those days.
- **Performance review** is framed loosely around 90-day and 1-year checkpoints.

## Late-stage rejection patterns

Positive mid-loop feedback does **not** predict the outcome. Multiple candidates cleared the technical loop with explicitly positive signals, then either (a) were given a surprise add-on round (e.g. a director "match" conversation) and rejected afterward with "not enough positive signal to send to hiring committee," or (b) sat in limbo while the team decided. Treat every round — including casual-sounding add-ons — as graded, and don't read a smooth technical loop as a done deal.

## Infra / AI-infra track

Candidates applying to AI-infra roles report a five-round virtual onsite that differs from the standard SWE shape: an **ML coding** round (60 min) *in addition to* a **systems coding** round (75 min), a **system design** round (60 min), a **hiring-manager** round, and a **technical deep dive**. The extra ML coding slot is the distinguishing piece — SWE loops usually pair a single coding round with system design, whereas infra loops carve out a separate ML-flavored coding round on top. The 75-minute systems round tends to lean on concurrency, so prepare for that explicitly.

## Team match (mid-2026)

Even after a passing hiring-manager chat, team match in mid-2026 is frequently slow, with candidates pointing to tight headcount rather than their own performance as the bottleneck. A representative recent onsite combination was BQ + technical (slide) presentation + a payment-system design + the plant-infection coding problem, followed by a separate HM team-match conversation that dragged on for weeks. Keep your own pipeline warm during this window — a clean loop does not guarantee a fast match.

## Hiring-committee spike signals

A late-June loop adds a sharper version of the team-match signal: after a positive onsite, the recruiter said the original team was full and the packet needed 1-2 clear "spike" / strong-hire signals before going to hiring committee. Read this as a reason to make one or two rounds unmistakably distinctive rather than merely solid across the board; a clean but flat loop can still stall at HC or team match.


## Group-specific offers

Some team-owned openings skip the long team-match phase entirely. In that shape, a move-forward decision can go directly to reference checks and offer negotiation because the candidate is already interviewing against a specific team rather than a general hiring pool. Keep both paths in mind: general-pool candidates should plan for match latency, while group-specific candidates should be ready with references immediately after a positive loop.

## Recruiter-screen calibration (July 2026)

For infra openings, the 30-minute recruiter screen can align the target level immediately and may lead straight to a single-day coding-plus-system-design block. Ask explicitly which level the recruiter is calibrating, whether the opening is tied to a specific team, and whether a work trial exists for that requisition. Scheduling can remain flexible when another interview process is active; requesting a focused later loop is not inherently treated as a negative signal.


## Applied / Product full-stack track (August 2026)

A product-facing full-stack loop can run fully virtually over roughly three to four weeks: a 30-minute recruiter screen, a 60-minute practical coding screen, then four or five rounds covering coding, a live full-stack build, product-oriented system design, and mission/values. Team match follows the loop.

The initial technical stage is team-dependent. One format uses a single coding screen; another uses a two-hour back-to-back block with one coding round and one system-design round before a four-round virtual onsite of coding, design, technical deep dive, and hiring-manager discussion. Confirm the exact block structure with the recruiter before scheduling.

## Team-owned behavioral gate (August 2026)

Some team-specific pipelines insert a 45-minute hiring-manager behavioral round immediately after two successful technical phone screens and before the virtual onsite. In that shape, the onsite may omit a separate BQ round. Treat mission alignment and AI-safety questions as a full gate even when the recruiter presents the next step as a manager conversation.

For RE / security loops, the two 60-minute technical screens can run back-to-back with no break: general coding in CoderPad followed immediately by ML coding in Colab. Schedule a full two-hour mock and plan a deliberate mental reset between rounds.

## Scheduling variation (September 2026)

A planned single-day, four-round virtual onsite can be rescheduled into one round per day over four days, with repeated interviewer substitutions. A behavioral conversation originally assigned to an org head may also move to a different interviewer. Prepare examples that stand on their own when the interviewer changes.

Interviewers may not know which prompts were used in the phone screen. If a prompt repeats, say so immediately; choosing a replacement can consume several minutes of the round.

## Recruiter screen and late-stage outcomes (October 2026)

- The recruiter screen is a real gate. Be ready to state what you are working on in concrete terms, what you are looking for next, your current level, and your promotion history. A recruiter may promise a scheduling link at the end of the call and still send a rejection a few days later.
- The recruiter screen commonly asks for your view on AGI and AI safety. A weak answer can end the process before any technical round.
- An infra team-owned loop ran: phone screen (coding + system design) → HM chat about a week later → onsite of coding, system design, technical deep dive, and an HM chat with an adjacent team's manager. Feedback was positive, but the team went with a candidate whose background matched more closely; the rejection came about three weeks later. Team-owned openings compete on fit, not only on bar.
- Level is set when the packet goes to hiring committee, not during the interviews. Behavioral performance weighs heavily in that decision.
- Cooldown periods are inconsistent: 6 months, 12 months, and no cooldown have all been quoted, likely depending on team and timing. Confirm with the recruiter instead of assuming a year.

## Mid-October 2026 signals

- **ML-track screens come in pairs.** One recent pipeline ran a first stage of two coding rounds (general coding + ML coding), and on passing the next stage was again a general-coding + ML-coding pair. The move-forward email can arrive the same afternoon, but calendar invites for the next stage can lag well over a week after availability is submitted, especially around holiday weekends. A short follow-up with the recruiter is normal.
- **Add-on system-design round.** When a phone-screen system design leaves the panel without enough signal, the recruiter may schedule an extra design round rather than reject outright. Treat it as a full gate: the add-on can still end in rejection.
- **New-grad SWE online assessment.** The new-grad SWE pipeline uses a multi-problem OA (four problems in one recent cycle) of self-contained algorithmic tasks with small inputs — graph traversal, path counting, and rule-heavy simulation. Precise reading of tie-break and edge-case rules decides the score more than asymptotic complexity.
## Late-October 2026 signals

- **Phone screen = coding + system design pair.** Most SWE pipelines run the screen as two rounds, one coding and one system design; they may land on the same day or on two different days.
- **Staff-level loop shape.** A recruiter-sourced Staff-target pipeline ran a screen of coding + system design, then a virtual onsite of coding, system design, a manager BQ (why OpenAI, AI safety, how you coordinate large projects across teams), and a project deep dive. The rejection came three days later with no feedback, despite every round feeling positive to the candidate — at this level, small gaps (needing a hint to finish the last coding step, rushing into the design before requirements) can be enough.
- **MLE onsite design rounds.** Recruiter prep material for MLE onsites lists two design rounds: one ML system design and one backend system design.
- **Full-stack track moves fast.** The recruiter call can be under ten minutes, with a team identified on the spot and the two-round screen (coding + system design) scheduled the following week. Decisions often arrive the next business day.
- **Shadow interviewers.** A screen may have two interviewers on the call — one leading and one shadowing.

## Mid-November 2026 signals

- **Screen can grow by a coding round.** A SWE screen that started as one system design plus one coding round added a second coding round afterward. Prepare as if the screen may be three rounds, not two.
- **Team match can still end the process.** A research candidate who passed the loop moved into team match and was then rejected because the matching teams had very limited headcount and only took candidates with a close fit. Passing the loop is not an offer.
- **Bank size and rotation.** The pool of coding prompts is now large, and new prompts roll out roughly every month while retired ones stop appearing. Candidates who prepared for under three weeks reported running short; about a month of preparation is a more comfortable budget.
- **Coding speed.** Coding rounds demand high speed. If your day-to-day coding relies heavily on LLM assistance, practice writing multi-part solutions unassisted under a timer.
