briefings.body:
## Pipeline

Meta runs two parallel loop formats in Q2 2026:

1. **Traditional loop** (scheduled before April 16, 2026): recruiter screen → CodeSignal OA (some pipelines) → 1× phone screen (Tag-list, 45 min) → onsite (2× coding + system design + behavioral, often spread across 3 days).
2. **AI-Native loop** (mandatory on or after April 16, 2026): same front-end, but onsite swaps to **2× AI-Enabled Coding (60 min each)** + **AI-Enabled SWE System Design (45 min, new)** + **AI-Oriented Behavioral (45 min)**. A few pipelines still preserve one traditional SD slot.

MLE / RS tracks substitute one or both coding rounds with **ML System Design** plus a **project deep-dive**. Data Engineer candidates go through a separate **AI-Native Full-Stack** round.

## Typical timeline

- Recruiter screen → phone screen: ~1 week.
- Phone screen → onsite: 2-3 weeks scheduling; the onsite itself spans 3-5 days.
- Onsite → HC decision: 1-2 weeks.
- Team match after HC: 1-8 weeks depending on req availability.

## Reject + cooldown signal

Q2 2026 reports show a noticeable uptick in "passed every round but rejected at HC + 1-year cooldown," attributed to ongoing reorgs and tightened HC. Team-match-stage stalls are also common — recruiters often go silent for 3-6 weeks before either a team match or a final no.

By late May–June 2026 the freeze hardened further: some candidates who cleared every round received a follow-up that the specific role they interviewed for is no longer being filled, and team match has stalled for weeks with recruiters citing limited open headcount. Outcomes are uneven, though — other candidates in the same window still reached team match within days of HC, so a strong loop is not wasted. Ask the recruiter directly about open-req availability both before and after the loop.

## New-grad cohort variation

A 2025 new-grad pipeline used OA → three onsite coding rounds → one behavioral round, with no separate system-design slot. The loop occurred two weeks after the OA and the offer arrived by portal email about two weeks later, without a verbal-offer call. Treat this as cohort-specific: confirm the exact round mix with the recruiter rather than assuming the experienced-hire template.

## September 2026: round mix by role

A SWE onsite can include two AI-coding rounds, two AI-enabled system-design rounds, and one behavioral round after the phone screen. Confirm the number of design slots for the specific opening.

Data Engineering can use a 30-minute Leadership interview plus a separate 60-minute Fullstack session, without a preliminary recruiter call. Production Engineering can instead start with one coding interview and one scenario-based troubleshooting interview.

## September 2026: MSL Research Scientist and MLE tracks

An MSL Research Scientist loop can include a hiring-manager discussion of personal background and prior experience, a coding round, two research-design sessions centered on a previous project and follow-up questions, a separate AI-design interview, and a behavioral interview. Despite the research-design label, the two project sessions can focus on work you have already done. Round durations and ordering were not specified for this format.

The MLE track can combine a coding phone screen, ML-focused coding, ML system design, and behavioral assessment. ML system design is a central part of that track; do not assume its round mix matches the SWE loop. Explain your reasoning during coding, and prepare three or four behavioral stories covering conflict, ownership, and disagree-and-commit situations.

## October 2026: Data Engineer technical screen refresh

The SQL question set for the Data Engineer technical round was fully rotated in October 2026, and one of the Python questions was replaced, so older DE question lists are no longer a reliable preview. The problems are not especially hard, but the prompts are wordy and convoluted — budget real time to parse the schema and the question before writing anything. The Python portion is multi-part, and running out of time before the final part runs end-to-end can sink an otherwise solid round; keep the early parts lean. Interviewers may offer substantial guidance during the session, which by itself does not signal a pass.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Standard Loop

A typical Oracle SWE loop runs:

1. **HR / recruiter reach-out** (cold or post-application). HR often emails a short skill-rating form first; recruiter then schedules a 30-minute call covering motivation, expectations, and basic role intro.
2. **Hiring Manager phone screen** (~30-45 min). Sometimes purely behavioural + light fundamentals ("what is immutable software?"); sometimes one small coding / OOD probe. Outcome from this screen heavily influences the eventual leveling decision.
3. **Technical phone screen** (45-60 min, HackerRank or shared editor). Format: ~10 min resume / behavioural, ~30 min one coding or OOD problem, ~5-10 min Q&A. Java fundamentals or domain trivia frequently appear as warm-ups before the algorithmic problem (abstract class vs interface, HashMap collision resolution, immutable software).
4. **Virtual Onsite (4-6 rounds)**. Most loops run 4 rounds; some OCI loops have stretched to 5-6 (one tech screen + 5 VO). Composition varies by org:
   - **OCI**: typically 2-3 coding + 1 system design + 1 hiring-manager BQ + 1 bar raiser.
   - **OHAI / Oracle Health**: 2 technical (heavy OOD slant, occasional code-reading), 1 system design or HM project deep-dive, 1 bar raiser BQ.
   - **Oracle Labs (AI/ML)**: 4 rounds mixing ML knowledge + coding; project deep-dive is a major component.
   - **NetSuite**: a back-to-back virtual or in-person onsite with multiple SDEs interviewing simultaneously, plus separate HM and director chats.
5. **HM / Director final chat** — usually behavioural-only, sometimes light culture / motivation. Some loops conclude here, others fold this into the VO block.
6. **Offer / down-level discussion**. Recruiters frequently come back with an offer at a lower level than originally targeted; see the leveling briefing for patterns.

## Timing

From HR reach-out to a decision typically runs 3-8 weeks if the team is actively hiring. Recruiter responsiveness is the largest variance — multiple candidates report being ghosted post-VO for weeks, even after positive in-round feedback. One Oracle Labs candidate was ghosted four months before receiving a rejection. Plan accordingly: do not stall other pipelines waiting on an Oracle decision.

## Process Quirks

- **Recruiter pre-loop framing is often inaccurate**. Candidates who were prepped for "system design only" have walked into LC-medium coding rounds, and vice versa. Treat the recruiter brief as low signal.
- **Interviewer punctuality varies**. Late starts of 5-20 minutes are reported with some frequency, especially with senior IC and India-based interviewers; the loop's available time is reduced accordingly without explicit re-extension.
- **Camera-off interviewers** appear occasionally, including in screens that should be face-to-face. Some candidates have walked through a full screen without seeing the interviewer.
- **Down-leveling at offer stage** is one of the most common reported outcomes — see leveling notes.
- **Re-investing in repeat applications**: a 6-12 month cool-off before re-applying is the usual cadence; some teams reach back out faster if the prior loop was close.

## Round-Agenda Opacity (August 2026)

Some OCI loops provide no per-round agenda and do not identify whether the next interviewer is an engineer, hiring manager, or bar raiser. A single round can also mix behavioural discussion, coding, and system design, including a design prompt in the final ten minutes after a long project conversation. Prepare for each virtual-onsite slot as a mixed-format round, keep the environment ready for coding, and reserve enough time to switch modes quickly.

## IC4 Four-Round Mix (August 2026)

A Seattle IC4 onsite used two system-design rounds, one algorithmic coding round, and one low-level-design coding round after the phone screen. In a separate four-round loop, the hiring-manager slot was expected to contain system design but instead became a resume and project deep dive. Treat nominal round labels as a plan rather than a guarantee, and prepare both architecture stories and implementation-ready coding for every technical slot.

## Five-Round IC4 Loop

One IC4 process combined a technical phone screen with five virtual-onsite rounds: a hiring-manager conversation, a design round with pseudocode, a dedicated behavioral round, and two coding rounds. Behavioral questions also appeared in the screen and technical rounds. The hiring-manager conversation focused on the team and prioritization, without coding, design, or resume deep-diving.

## IC3 Remote Final Loop (September 2026)

One IC3 final loop reserved 8 a.m. to noon Pacific for four rounds, each scheduled for 45 minutes: two coding rounds, one behavioral round, and one expected design round. The order was not provided in advance. The design slot instead spent roughly 30 minutes on the resume and the final 13 minutes on client-server troubleshooting. A director led the dedicated behavioral round, and behavioral questions also closed both coding rounds. The recruiter confirmed that the candidate had cleared the final loop the following day.

## Fast OCI Loop and Changed Round Content (September 2026)

One OCI candidate received a recruiter call the day after applying, a phone screen about a week later, and a virtual onsite about another week later. The four onsite rounds were spread across two days, with a rejection communicated the following day and no feedback provided. The loop contained two coding rounds, a director conversation, and a cross-team round described as Bartender. The scheduled 60-minute system-design slot became a behavioral-only conversation lasting under 45 minutes, while the cross-team round introduced low-level / object-oriented design that had not been included in the recruiter's outline. This is a team-specific example of both a fast timeline and changing round content.

## Senior Phone-Screen Split

Senior OCI phone screens can split the hour between behavioral questions and coding, with behavioral first: one senior principal SDE screen used 20 minutes of behavioral questions and 40 minutes of coding, and another OCI screen used 30 minutes of each, with the solution required to pass test cases on HackerRank. Because the coding problem gets only part of the hour, rehearse concise behavioral answers so they do not crowd out the implementation.

## IC3 Five-Round Loop with a Project Thread (October 2026)

One IC3 process ran a technical phone screen followed by four rounds, and every round opened with a discussion of the candidate's current project:

1. **Technical phone screen** — project discussion, one graph algorithm problem, and a few basic system-design questions.
2. **Technical interview** — project discussion, one algorithm problem, and an object-oriented design exercise.
3. **High-level design** — project discussion, a domain-specific design prompt tied to the interviewer team's own business, and an algorithm problem in the same slot.
4. **Hiring manager** — a full architecture diagram of the current project, behavioral questions centered on leadership and ownership, and the business impact of past work.
5. **Bar raiser** — a classic high-level design prompt, a discussion of architectural decisions in current and past projects, and behavioral questions.

Two takeaways: design appears in three separate slots (phone screen, the HLD round, and the bar raiser), and the domain-specific prompt rewards researching the target team's product before the loop. The bar raiser is not purely behavioral here — prepare a standard design walkthrough for it as well.

## OCI Storage and Late-2026 Loops (October 2026)

- **Recruiter screen**: a senior core-infrastructure storage recruiter screen lasted 15-20 minutes and checked basic fit — experience, a difficult problem you solved, and location. The scheduling email for the next round arrived about three days later.
- **Location**: many OCI teams are now concentrated in Nashville; expect the location question early.
- **Three-round storage onsite**: two technical rounds, each with behavioral questions, followed by a hiring-manager round of short operations-design questions about the storage data plane (host patching, bug-fix deployment, host images).
- **Phone screen plus four rounds**: a coding-plus-BQ phone screen, then two coding rounds with BQ, a hiring-manager slot billed as system design that became a project deep dive and ended 15 minutes early, and a behavioral-only round run by a data scientist from another team. The rejection arrived by email.
- **Another phone screen plus four rounds**: a classic hard coding problem plus BQ in the screen, then a project deep dive with BQ, a DP coding round, a URL-shortener design round with BQ, and an expiring-token coding round. Behavioral answers and trade-off reasoning carried the most weight; the coding problems did not follow a recognizable fixed bank.

## OCI Loops (November 2026)

- **Four-round virtual onsite over two days**: about a week after the recruiter call came a coding phone screen, then four rounds split across two days. Every round opened with roughly ten minutes of behavioral questions, and the content of each round was not announced in advance. The rounds were algorithmic coding, low-level / object-oriented design (no code execution, focused on interface design), a URL-shortener system design with heavy trade-off probing, and a hiring-manager slot billed as system design that became a resume deep dive on on-call work and the hardest project. Behavioral answers and trade-off discussion carried the most weight.
- **VMI (VM infrastructure) team**: three rounds — a standard LeetCode problem, a string coding problem, and a hiring-manager round combining a VM-provisioning service design with a deep dive on your current project's hardest problem. This team expects low-level system design and working knowledge of hypervisors and VM internals; a candidate without that preparation was rejected the following morning. For infrastructure teams, prepare VM lifecycle and hypervisor fundamentals, not only distributed-systems design.

The standard pipeline is recruiter screen (15-20 min, non-technical, salary + why-C1) → CodeSignal OA → Power Day → Team Match. Some senior IC and manager loops insert a 30-45 minute hiring-manager phone chat between recruiter and OA; for MLE / Applied Research, an extra Tech Screen with one or two engineers sometimes precedes Power Day.

Power Day is the entire onsite. Four rounds run back to back the same day with short breaks between them, totalling roughly four and a half hours. Recruiters typically schedule it 1-3 weeks after the OA passes. Candidates can request a prep call with the recruiter beforehand — this is offered as a standard option, not a favor, and it walks through what each round will look like.

After Power Day, candidates who pass enter Team Match. A successful loop becomes a generic offer that is only finalized once a team commits. Team-match cycles run weeks long and can stall, especially in the slower Richmond, McLean, and Plano hubs. Candidates report being asked to interview again with hiring managers during team match even after Power Day approval; this is informal vetting, not a re-evaluation.

Intern and TDP (Technical Development Program, new-grad) pipelines compress the loop into a single Super Day with three 60-minute rounds (code-reading, simple coding, behavioral) and skip the case study; their bar is noticeably lower than full-time SDE.

As of September 2026, a Lead Software Engineer Power Day can be split across two days: case study and behavioral on the first, coding and system design on the second. The four-round structure remains the same.

As of September 2026, an application can receive a CodeSignal OA invitation before any recruiter contact. The recruiter-first sequence is therefore not universal; follow the order in the invitation for the specific application.

As of the 2026 internship cycle, the Technology Internship Program Superday has three parts (behavioral, the Virtual Credit Card case, and an AI-assisted coding round), so the case study is no longer skipped for every intern pipeline.

briefings.body:
## Pipeline

A typical Stripe loop runs:

1. **Recruiter screen** (~30 min). Process intro + light BQ. Recruiter often pre-shares which coding-round flavor (debug vs integration vs refactor) you'll get.
2. **Phone screen — coding** (60-75 min). One realistic prompt in a full IDE (CoderPad with project mode, or HackerRank Projects). Reaching part 2 of 3 is typical; part 3 is a strong signal.
3. **Onsite loop** — 4-5 rounds:
   - 1-2× IDE coding (debug / integration / refactor; sometimes one of each),
   - 1× system design (payments-domain prompt),
   - 1× hiring manager behavioral,
   - 1× cross-functional or values round.
4. **Reference check** — multi-hour, deal-breaker step.

## Typical timeline

- Recruiter screen → phone screen: 1-2 weeks.
- Phone screen → onsite: 2-3 weeks scheduling, then onsite over 1-2 days.
- Onsite → reference check: 1 week.
- Reference check → offer: 1-2 weeks. Several candidates describe offers retracted at this stage.

## Signaling notes

- HM round is often light on technical content. Do not read that as a free pass — the signal it gathers (ownership, why-Stripe specificity) drives the decision more than the round feels.
- A recurring addition is 5-10 minutes of "how do you use AI in your day-to-day" during the HM round. Have a two-minute answer with a concrete example.

## FDE / frontend-calibrated loop

A newer FDE path blends frontend engineering, customer debugging, and product judgment. The early rounds cover React debugging, browser/backend fundamentals, motivation, and building a React interface against an undocumented API. The onsite then extends that interface in a 90-minute AI-assisted session, adds a customer-debugging role-play around an SDK race condition, and closes with leadership plus estimation/project-breakdown rounds. Recruiters describe this path as still being calibrated, so confirm the exact round labels and evaluation criteria before scheduling.

## OA retry timing

A September 2026 candidate was told that an OA rejection carries a one-year cooldown. Confirm the applicable retry date with recruiting before planning another application.

## September 2026 pipeline variations

A senior onsite consisted of debugging, AI-assisted coding, integration without AI, and a manager behavioral conversation, with no system-design round. The manager conversation focused on past projects and leadership. Verify the scheduled round list even for a senior role; a system-design interview is not present in every senior loop.

Another pipeline placed a 20-minute evaluative recruiter call after a passed OA. After rejection at that call, the candidate was told that reapplying within 12 months would not require another OA or HR outreach. Confirm how that advice applies to the next application; it does not establish a company-wide exemption or the same restriction as a cooldown following OA failure.

## September 2026 reapplication exception

Following an onsite rejection, one candidate received feedback about a week later that debugging and integration had fallen short of the team's expectations. Recruiting nevertheless encouraged a new application in early 2027, earlier than the usual one-year interval described to the candidate. Treat such an invitation as specific to the individual application and confirm the retry date directly; it does not establish a shorter company-wide cooldown.

## October 2026 pipeline observations

- **Staff SWE:** after the recruiter screen, two 60-minute "mini onsite" rounds — system design and AI-assisted programming — gate the rest of the loop.
- **New grad:** OA invites can arrive the same day you apply and appear to be sent in bulk; the HackerRank OA allows seven days to complete. A passed OA leads to a recruiter call on background, project scale, and why Stripe, followed by VO scheduling. Book within about two weeks — slots fill quickly. A one-hour first VO precedes a 3–4 hour back-to-back final, which can be split across two days.
- **2027 new-grad team screen:** 60 minutes, roughly 45 of them for coding after introductions and Q&A. Positive feedback on communication and code design did not offset finishing only two parts, so completion count carries real weight.
- **2027 new grad, full sequence:** OA → recruiter screen → technical screen → virtual onsite. The onsite was split over two days, with AI-assisted coding on the first day and Integration plus BugSquash on the second. From application to final decision took about six weeks, including one technical screen that was rescheduled by about nine days because the interviewer had a conflict.
- **New-grad technical screen pacing:** the interviewer may call out remaining minutes throughout the round. Plan to move through the parts quickly rather than refining early ones.

## November 2026 pipeline observations

- **2027 new grad:** a mid-October technical screen on invoice/payment reconciliation led to a virtual onsite about three weeks later with Integration (request replay), BugSquash (Colander), and AI-assisted coding. Another 2027 new-grad onsite drew Bikemap, the rule parser, and Colander. A hiring-manager call follows the onsite, and candidates frequently wait without a stated timeline for that invite.
- **Backend SWE:** the onsite invitation arrived about six business days after a passed phone screen.
- **MLE:** two phone rounds precede the onsite: a coding round and an ML Integration round on a Kaggle-style dataset.
- **Phone-screen rotation refresh:** November 2026 brought brand-new phone-screen prompts that the usual prep sites did not carry yet. Candidates meeting them cold often finished only one or two parts. Settle your data model before you start coding, since later parts build on it.

C3 AI's experienced-hire loop is short and front-loaded on the hiring manager.

## Pipeline

1. **Application → direct interview invite.** Candidates who apply online can receive an interview invite straight from HR with no recruiter phone screen in between. The role description and salary range are not necessarily shared before the first round.
2. **Hiring-manager behavioral screen (30 min).** The first conversation is a behavioral round with the hiring manager. Do not count on getting compensation details here — the manager may not be able to answer salary questions.
3. **Onsite (2 rounds).**
   - **Coding** — one coding round.
   - **System design** — one design round with a manager. The prompt can be a familiar product-style system (e.g. a restaurant reservation system), but the interviewer drives hard into deep dives and interrupts while you are still laying out tables and schema.

## Practical notes

- The system-design round can end early: if the interviewer is not satisfied, they may close the session around the 30-minute mark with direct feedback. Get the high-level architecture and the core data model on the board quickly, then be ready to pivot into whatever deep dive the interviewer picks instead of finishing an exhaustive table design first.
- Scheduling is not always reliable — candidates have had an onsite interviewer not show up. Keep the recruiting contact handy so a missed round can be rescheduled.
- Ask about level, team, and compensation band explicitly and early, since this information is not volunteered.

## New-grad Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE)

The FDE new-grad track starts with an online assessment (see the assessment briefing) before any live interviews.

## Pipeline

1. **Recruiter / HR call** — short process intro. The technical screen is often scheduled on the spot.
2. **Technical phone screen (60 min, CoderPad)** — one multi-part coding problem. About 5 minutes of mutual introductions, then straight into the problem.
3. **Feedback to the hiring manager** — the screen feedback goes to the HM, who decides whether to move forward to the virtual onsite (VO). On some teams the HM does not look closely at the resume until the screen has been passed.
4. **Virtual onsite** — scheduled only after the HM signs off.

Turnaround after the screen can be fast: recruiter follow-up the next day, HM decision a day after that.

## Senior / Staff variant (Cash App)

For Staff SWE on Cash App, the screening stage is heavier and fully remote:

| Round | Length | Content |
|---|---|---|
| Coding | 60 min | CoderPad, incremental practical problem |
| AI Native screen | 30 min | Conversational walk-through of your real engineering workflow and how you use AI |
| Hiring-manager call | 30 min | Resume project deep dive, tech debt, money-movement domain |

The coding and AI Native rounds can be stacked on the same day, with the HM call booked separately.

## Headcount and team-match risk

Hiring is tied to specific teams. A screen rated "very positive" by the HM can still stall if that team closes its role in the meantime — the candidate is then sent back to team matching rather than straight to the onsite. Two weeks of silence after the screening rounds often means the position was filled. Ask the recruiter early whether the role is for a single team and whether a passed screen carries over to other teams.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
A typical Waymo loop runs:

1. **Recruiter call** — process intro, why-Waymo, light project walk. Recruiters reliably preview the loop format (e.g. 'mid-hard LeetCode', 'ML coding on the materials we sent') but the preview is often inaccurate in practice — prepare beyond what's flagged.
2. **Phone screen** — single 45-minute technical, almost always coding. Standard offerings include classic algorithm problems (Dijkstra, BFS on grids, trie autocomplete, decode-string variants, interval coverage) but a notable fraction of screens swap the LC-style problem for an open-ended autonomy-framed prompt (parse a CSV for downstream consumers, OO scheduler for picking up passengers, simulate a pen-on-paper drawing machine). Treat the recruiter's topic hint as a soft signal, not a contract.
3. **Virtual onsite** — typically 4 rounds, sometimes split across two days. Standard mix is 2 coding + 1 system design + 1 BQ / HM, but candidates routinely report 2 coding + 2 system design, or coding + system design + data fluency + BQ. For senior / staff loops a project deep-dive replaces one of the BQ slots.
4. **Add-on round** — feedback is mixed often enough that a 5th round (extra data fluency, extra coding) is common before a decision.
5. **Decision and team match** — strong signals from add-on rounds typically land within a week; full silence past 7-10 days is usually a soft reject.

End-to-end timeline from first recruiter contact to decision is most commonly 4-8 weeks. Compared to Google's pipeline, Waymo skips hiring-committee-style arbitration and the manager has a much larger direct vote — interviewers' written feedback maps almost directly to the outcome.

**Non-technical HM-first variant.** Some direct-apply pipelines (e.g. SWE — Labeling Infrastructure) put a non-technical hiring-manager round first, before any coding. It runs ~45 minutes as a career-profile walk-through — intro, tech stack, projects you've owned and delivered — plus light domain probing (for a labeling team, e.g. the distinction between annotation and labeling) and a manager-led pitch of the team and roadmap. There is no algorithm content, but it is a real gate: failing it ends the process, and a failed HM round can also block other Waymo teams' recruiters from advancing you for separate roles. Recruiter follow-up after this round is often slow (a week-plus), so silence here is not necessarily a reject. The 2026 loops also coincide with an active multi-city expansion push, which recruiters reference when describing headcount. A lighter HM behavioral screen can also be decisive: expect a complex-project walkthrough and direct probing on why the project was challenging, with fast no-hire feedback possible after the call.

**Senior frontend variant.** The phone screen can combine an algorithmic tree transformation with a small UI built on top of it. The virtual onsite may then stay frontend-focused across all four rounds: framework-specific UI debugging, JavaScript or TypeScript asynchronous coding, frontend-oriented system design, and a search-input implementation exercise. Framework fit can be evaluated literally; a role advertised for production Angular proficiency may use Angular even when the candidate's résumé emphasizes React. Confirm the expected framework before the loop and prepare to reason about unfamiliar syntax at a design and pseudocode level.

**Simulation-team fit (September 2026).** A simulation-team loop can open with a simulation system design exercise even after the recruiter has said simulation knowledge will not be tested. Clarify the distinction between domain-specific knowledge and a system design scenario drawn from the team’s work; a reassurance about the former does not rule out the latter.

**Domain-driven system design (late 2026).** Onsite system design prompts increasingly come straight from the interviewer's own team, such as designing a vehicle fleet to collect map data. Interviewers probe their internal scenarios rather than generic scaling, so a stock web-scale design template tends to fall flat. Before the loop, review autonomy-adjacent basics (sensor data volume, fleet operations, offboard data pipelines) for the team you are interviewing with. Rejections after a full loop can arrive about a week later as an automated email with no feedback.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Pipeline (post-2025 reform)

A typical full-time loop runs:

1. **Recruiter screen** (~30 min). Process intro, leveling alignment, salary expectation. AI / coding role context is set here.
2. **Phone screen** — usually one round, 55–60 minutes. Recent loops report a **packed** screen that splits the hour into 3 segments: 5–10 min behavioural, 30–35 min coding (usually one problem from the recurring `Coding Q` family), and 15–20 min mini system-design or ML-foundation. Staff candidates may get a *two*-phone-screen variant: a coding round and a separate Project Retro (4-axis behavioural deep dive).
3. **Onsite loop** — five rounds, virtual or in-person, often spread over two days. Recent template:
   - Coding (algorithmic, no AI tooling)
   - AI Coding (in-IDE assistant — see the AI Coding Round briefing)
   - System Design (general or ML SD)
   - Project Deep-Dive (40–60 min conversation + diagram)
   - Host Manager / Tech Experience (behavioural + project depth, often with a domain probe)
- A 6th round (BQ-only) is occasionally added for Staff candidates and dropped without notice for Senior.
4. **Team match** — for non-org-aligned candidates, post-loop team-match decides which org makes the offer. Some loops compress this into the host manager round.
5. **Offer / decline / downlevel discussion** — see the Leveling & Downlevel briefing.

## Pre-loop OA (some tracks)

Some new-grad and general SWE tracks add a self-paced, multi-level online assessment (Karat/CodeSignal-style) before the phone screen. As of 2026 it has reused the same problem set from 2025, so prior-year OA write-ups remain accurate — the Recipe Manager versioning/rollback problem is one recurring instance. Notification timing after submission is inconsistent; assume a multi-week gap.

## Calendar time

- Recruiter → onsite is commonly 2–4 weeks; some teams have hit 8-week delays.
- Onsite → feedback is 1 week if positive; ghosting is reported when negative.
- Total end-to-end commonly 4–8 weeks; freezes lengthen this materially.

## Current freeze signal

Multiple candidates in April 2026 reported the interviewer mentioning an internal hiring freeze "not yet officially announced". Expect schedule slips and team-match stalls until this clears. Have a plan B.

## August 2026 loop variants

Current SWE loops do not always follow the five-slot template above. One five-round variant used three conventional coding rounds, one system-design round, and a 45-minute host-manager conversation, with no separate AI-coding or project-deep-dive slot. A Staff platform variant used four rounds: behavioral plus domain depth, AI-assisted coding, CI/CD system design, and conventional coding. Confirm the exact round labels and tool rules with the recruiter instead of assuming every nominal "five-round loop" has the same composition.

## September 2026 phone-screen format

A 60-minute technical phone screen can start with a short introduction and a resume-project discussion, then move into two coding questions. One such session had a lead interviewer and a shadow interviewer. Another phone screen also used two coding questions, so the earlier coding-plus-design split is not universal; confirm the agenda for the specific team.

## September 2026 round labels and track differences

A six-round onsite route includes coding, two system-design sessions, Host Leader, Craftsmanship, and Execution. Another route schedules Technical Communication and Project Deep Dive separately, alongside coding, system design, and Host Manager. Confirm the actual agenda and the purpose of each named session; a familiar round count does not identify its contents.

Applications phone interviews can use a short smoke-test coding question followed by a main problem. An MLE phone screen can instead combine coding with a personalized-feed ML design discussion. These track differences coexist with the two-coding-question format above.

## Late September 2026 formats

A five-round virtual onsite can consist of AI coding, conventional algorithm coding, Host Manager, system design, and Technical Communication. In this format, the Host Manager session combines behavioral questions with resume discussion, while Technical Communication also explores resume projects. The two conversations are separate sessions.

Infra phone screens can place systems and Java fundamentals before the coding problem. A separate phone-screen format uses a systems-fundamentals block followed by two coding questions. These variations further broaden the possible agenda beyond a coding-plus-design split.

## October 2026 MLE phone-screen formats

MLE phone screens are tightly packed. One 60-minute format starts with a brief introduction, which the interviewer may cut short, then three behavioral questions, one coding problem, and an ML system-design prompt. The session leaves little time to discuss the candidate's own research or ML background. A Senior MLE format splits the hour into a 30-minute ML-code debugging exercise and a 20-minute ML design discussion. In both formats, pacing matters more than depth on any single segment.

## Mid-October 2026 formats

A Senior backend route can run a technical screen (brief project discussion, then one live coding problem) followed by a four-round onsite: system design, two coding rounds, and a Hiring Manager round centered on behavioral and situational questions. Other Senior routes involve five to six rounds after the screen.

Senior phone screens vary widely in shape. One hour can be split evenly between resume discussion and a single coding problem; another screen skips BQ and project discussion entirely and moves straight into two easy coding problems. Some screens are dry-run only — code cannot be executed — and interviewers probe code structure as well as correctness. A Staff screen can instead open with three behavioral questions before coding.

Phone-screen results can take about a week to arrive. One Staff candidate received no reply after a week, even to a follow-up email, and treated the silence as a likely rejection.

MLE phone screens can pair behavioral questions with a data-metric design prompt (summarize a heavily skewed distribution for a leadership audience) and a compact ML design.

## Late October 2026 formats

- **Staff AI Engineer onsite:** five 60-minute rounds — Staff AI Modeling & Fundamentals, Staff AI System Design, Staff Coding – Data, Host Leader – AI, and Staff Coding with AI. The Host Leader session can open with a case-study problem meant to draw out behavioral signal rather than a technical design discussion.
- **Senior applications-track virtual onsite:** coding, system design, AI coding, behavioral, and Technical Communication. Results arrived about two weeks after the onsite.
- **Senior Infra route:** a phone screen with two LeetCode problems, then a virtual onsite with behavioral, algorithm coding, AI coding, and system design. Infra preparation should also cover multithreading and concurrency — locks, thread safety, synchronization primitives, producer-consumer — alongside the usual algorithms and design.
- **Developer Infra phone screen:** no coding. A senior manager runs a behavioral and experience deep-dive conversation for the hour.
- **Staff MLE phone screen:** two behavioral questions, one coding problem, and a small ML system design, in that order.

## November 2026 formats

- **Senior Staff onsite:** five rounds over two days — one coding round (AI allowed), two system-design rounds, and two behavioral rounds, one of them with the hiring manager (a director). Design interviewers can be very senior: one design round was run by the org's Distinguished Engineer. The hiring-manager conversation can run well past its slot — one scheduled hour stretched to ninety minutes of technical discussion.
- **MLE virtual onsite:** Modeling & Fundamentals, behavioral, ML system design (video recommendation), AI-assisted coding (train a model on a provided dataset, several parts), and data coding. The result arrived about a week later.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
The Airbnb engineering loop follows a consistent shape across SWE and MLE roles:

- **Recruiter screen** — 15–20 minutes. Process intro, role overview, salary expectations. No technical content.
- **Tech screen** — 45-minute coding round. One algorithmic problem from a small, well-known pool (split-stay, text justification, terrain water-drop, smallest permutation, account merge). Bug-free output and self-written test cases are explicit graded signals.
- **Hiring manager screen** — 45-minute background conversation. Sometimes inserted before onsite, sometimes after. The output is a binary team-fit signal, not auto-advancing.
- **Onsite (virtual)** — typically 4–5 rounds:
  - Coding (1–2 rounds): more questions from the same coding pool.
  - System design (1 round at G7+; 2 rounds at G9+ where the second is often more open-ended).
  - Code review (60 min, Python or Java): the candidate reviews 2–3 escalating PRs with the interviewer largely silent.
  - Experience / project deep-dive (60 min, occasionally runs to 90 min): one resume project explored in detail.
- **Core values** — 45-minute culture round, scheduled separately after the technical loop. Conversational, mission-aligned, less STAR-heavy than peer companies.
- **Team match** — after hiring-committee approval, the candidate enters a team-match pool. This stage can take 4–8 weeks; multiple candidates report ghost periods of 1–2 weeks between updates. A "passed but no team" outcome is common — candidates can stay in the pool for up to a year before the file is closed.

Total elapsed time from first recruiter contact to offer letter is commonly 8–14 weeks, dominated by team match. Candidates report scheduling slippage of multiple weeks between onsite and core values, and again between core values and team match.

- **Recruiter prep calls are part of the loop.** Recruiters often hold short coaching calls before the system-design / experience rounds and again before the hiring-manager / core-values rounds, explaining each round's format and expectations. Counting these touchpoints, candidates report 8–10 total meetings end to end.

- **Recoverability differs by round.** Candidates are told that a weak coding round can be appealed for an extra coding attempt, but a weak system-design round generally cannot be re-tried — and the system-design signal is treated as a key input to the hiring-committee decision. When a loop is otherwise solid but the SD signal is borderline, the recruiter may schedule one additional system-design round before the final decision rather than rejecting outright. The onsite typically runs as four rounds (coding, code review, system design, project deep-dive); the separate core-values round is only scheduled once those four pass.

As of the 2026 new-grad cycle, a compact SWE path is also in use: OA → recruiter call → two 45-minute coding interviews → project deep-dive → core-values. The deep-dive and core-values rounds can be scheduled together after positive coding feedback, without separate system-design or code-review rounds. One recent schedule took about five weeks from OA to the final interviews, followed by final feedback one week later.

As of September 2026, a U.S. onsite schedule includes a round labeled “AI coding interview.” The label alone does not establish the task format or whether AI tools are permitted; confirm both with the recruiter.

### Data engineering analytics loop — September 2026

The data engineering analytics path can start with an OA containing SQL and Python, followed by four virtual onsite rounds: SQL, coding, behavioral, and data modeling. The behavioral discussion centers on end-to-end project details. The modeling interview can extend into query and table optimization. This is a separate role-specific schedule; confirm the round list for the position being considered.

### Strategic finance & analytics loop — 2026

Business-side roles such as strategic finance & analytics run a longer, multi-month loop with no coding:

- **Recruiter phone screen.**
- **Take-home case study** — raw data in a spreadsheet; deliver a 4–6 page write-up of insights and recommendations. AI assistance is explicitly prohibited.
- **Hiring manager round** — present the case study and field follow-up questions.
- **Cross-functional panel** — four interviews with stakeholders such as strategic finance, product, and data science. Mostly behavioral, mixed with mini-cases and hypothetical questions that probe product sense.
- **Core values** — two interviews with employees outside the hiring team.
- **Skip-level fit interview**, then a **final interview with a director or VP**.

End to end this ran about three months. The final stage can be a head-to-head between two finalists, with the decision arriving roughly two weeks after the last interview.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## SWE / Data / Infra loop

A typical full-time pipeline runs **recruiter intro → phone screen → onsite (4–5 rounds) → offer**, with end-to-end timing around 6–8 weeks. Rescheduling between rounds is common and onsite slots are frequently split across days; budget a multi-week onsite window rather than a single block.

- **Recruiter intro (30 min)** — background, target team, comp range, process overview. Principal/Staff candidates may be asked role-specific domain questions (e.g. fraud, ads) directly in this call.
- **Phone screen (45–60 min)** — single coding round in the candidate's preferred language. The rate-limiter problem dominates this slot; runners-up are the function-call-path coding problem and a like-button system design (when the recruiter routes to a phone-SD instead of phone-coding). Hidden test cases run automatically on submission; passing all visible cases is not enough.
- **Onsite loop (4–5 rounds, virtual or in-person)** typically combines: one coding round, one or two system-design rounds (regular SD + product/feature SD), an HM behavioral round, and a director or staff/principal culture round. Senior+ candidates are split into a regular SD and a deep-dive on a prior design.
- **HM / director rounds** are scheduled last and are explicitly weighted; multiple candidates have reported strong technical performance but a non-aligned HM/director chat tipping the loop to a reject.

## Recruiter pre-loop call

A growing number of candidates report a 20–30 minute pre-onsite call with the recruiter that walks through the loop slot-by-slot, names the interviewers, and previews the format of each round (sometimes including the prompt family). Use it aggressively: ask which SD theme each interviewer typically picks, and ask whether the HM has a specific signal axis to brush up on.

## After the onsite

Decision turnaround is fast — most candidates hear back within 2–7 days. Detailed feedback is not provided on rejection; a follow-up recruiter call is sometimes available but is not a debrief. Down-leveling to a more mid-level role can be requested proactively if a single round felt weak, but is rarely granted retroactively.

## Frontend (UI) loop

Frontend-specialized candidates run a UI-flavored variant of the same pipeline: a phone screen (the function-call-path coding problem and rate-limiter still appear here), then an onsite of **frontend coding + frontend system design + HM behavioral**. The system-design slot is a frontend SD prompt (image feed, feed-status app, notification UI). At staff / principal level the frontend SD interviewer will drill well past the component tree into backend delivery detail — e.g. a "real-time notification system" prompt that turns into fan-out, push transport, and delivery-guarantee questions. Prepare the backend contract behind your UI, not just the rendering layer.

## Frontend / Fullstack matching wrinkle

Frontend-labeled openings can still route fullstack candidates through a frontend-heavy onsite, then switch to team matching if the hiring manager feels the prior experience is too backend/fullstack for the original team. A strong technical onsite is not always enough to close the loop; final matching and executive conversations can still reject on ownership posture or career-decision signal.

## Frontend screen variant — 2026 Q3

Frontend candidates may instead receive a **45-minute first technical screen** built around implementing a real-world UI component with state and user-event handling. TypeScript, JavaScript, and React are accepted choices. Recruiters may disclose this format during the intro call, so confirm whether the screen is UI implementation or the general coding rotation before choosing a preparation track.

## Vanilla frontend variant — August 2026

A senior frontend phone screen may require a browser widget built in vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with frameworks and third-party libraries explicitly disallowed. Expect held-state behavior, physical-keyboard events, mouse events, and simultaneous inputs to be part of the evaluation. Confirm the allowed frontend stack before the interview rather than assuming React or TypeScript is available.

## Fast team-specific MLE loop — August 2026

A senior MLE team can run two first-round conversations followed by a four-round virtual onsite. The first wave combines a 60-minute project presentation with a 45-minute HM conversation. The onsite then covers practical ML modeling, one CodeSignal coding round, a second HM conversation, and a director calibration round; the four slots can be split across two days. Scheduling and decisions can move unusually quickly, including onsite scheduling within days and a verbal offer on the next business day.

## Game-based assessment for experienced hires — October 2026

The interactive game assessment (factory optimization, vehicle assembly, and a situational-judgment section) is not limited to new grads: experienced hires with around three years of full-time experience can also be routed through it before the phone screen, and the Roblox app must be installed to play the modules. The following phone screen can contain **two coding problems** in one session, so pace the first one to leave time for the second problem's follow-up.

## SWE IC3 phone screen — October 2026

The IC3 SWE phone screen can be a single 45-minute coding session with a two-part problem (for example, find matches on a grid, then clear them and apply gravity). Results can arrive the same day, and the next step is an HM round. Rate-limiter screens in the same period also used a two-part, 45-minute format, with the second part adding per-field limits; the time is tight for both parts.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Pipeline

A typical Pinterest SWE or MLE loop runs:

1. **Recruiter screen** (~30 min) — role fit, timeline, compensation expectations, and process overview.
2. **Technical screen** (~60 min) — usually one coding problem; MLE screens may add a short ML-fundamentals segment.
3. **Interview round** — commonly five interviews for SWE and four to five for MLE:
   - SWE: three coding, one system design, and one behavioral interview.
   - MLE: one or two coding, two ML design interviews, and one behavioral or hiring-manager interview.
   - Staff loops may add Leadership & XFN Collaboration or a deeper competency round.
4. **Add-on round** — used when one signal needs clarification, often as another coding or design interview.
5. **Debrief, hiring review, and team match** — the interview team evaluates the competency signals; team alignment can remain a separate offer gate.

## Calendar time

Recruiter-to-screen scheduling is often about a week, with another one to two weeks before the full interview round. Debrief and team alignment create the largest variance, so plan for a multi-week process and communicate competing deadlines early. The official candidate guidance directs timeline and scheduling questions to the recruiter or recruiting coordinator.

## Format notes

- Recent technical loops commonly run virtually, but role location follows Pinterest's PinFlex policy and the specific job's office requirements. Confirm the expected interview medium and work location with the recruiter.
- Coding uses a shared editor; confirm whether execution is enabled and state the language before the round.
- University engineering funnels officially use CodeSignal before recruiter and technical interviews. MLE assessments may combine coding with ML concepts or hand calculations.
- Prepare one concise project summary before the hiring-manager conversation; the official process treats that discussion as a deeper qualification assessment rather than a scheduling call.

## September 2026 timing variant

An IC14 loop used a 60-minute phone screen followed by 45-minute onsite interviews, including two algorithm rounds, system design, and an AI-assisted coding round. One candidate received the screen result the same day and the onsite result a week later, then entered team matching. These timings describe an individual loop rather than a guaranteed turnaround.

## September 2026 five-interview variant

Another SWE onsite format has two coding interviews, two system-design interviews, and one behavioral interview. One loop placed behavioral first, followed by the two coding rounds and then the two design rounds. A phone-screen-to-onsite path with the same five-round mix proceeded to team matching after a successful interview decision. Confirm the actual round allocation for your loop, since the coding/design split varies.

## September 2026 additional loop formats

A SWE onsite can combine two conventional coding interviews, one system-design interview, one behavioral interview, and one AI-assisted coding interview. The AI exercise is a separate part of that five-interview mix.

A Senior Staff backend-infrastructure process began with a recruiter conversation and a primarily behavioral hiring-manager conversation, followed by a separate technical-depth interview after nearly two weeks. That candidate received a rejection two days after the technical-depth round. This sequence illustrates an early senior-level evaluation path, not a complete onsite schedule or a guaranteed response timeline.

## October 2026: Data Engineer and IC15 notes

Data Engineer roles carry the SDE title and run the same interview process as SDE, including the same coding phone screen — prepare the standard SDE coding question set rather than SQL- or pipeline-specific material. An IC15 loop paired a graph-search phone screen with a virtual onsite whose first interview was a data-structure design-and-implement exercise followed by complexity discussion.

## October 2026: ML intern OA and onsite follow-up

ML and PhD MLE intern funnels start with a 70–75 minute CodeSignal assessment mixing ML multiple-choice, one easy coding problem, and hand-written ML implementations from given formulas. The bar is not all-or-nothing: one candidate advanced without every problem fully correct, so prioritize getting each part working over perfecting one.

A SWE onsite in October 2026 again used two coding and two system-design interviews. Post-onsite communication can be slow — one candidate had to nudge the recruiter two weeks after the loop before receiving a templated rejection, so follow up proactively if you have not heard back within about two weeks.

## November 2026: ML intern and PhD new-grad ML loops

The MLE intern funnel runs CodeSignal OA → phone screen → technical virtual interview, usually followed by a hiring-manager conversation. Candidates matched to the ATG team at the recruiter stage get an extra ML Practitioner interview. The technical virtual interview opens with introductions and about ten minutes on prior experience, then three short ML-fundamentals questions (about five minutes), then a hard original coding problem. The ML Practitioner interview starts with a ~10-minute project discussion and moves into an open-ended modeling scenario where a structured walk from problem definition onward matters most.

A PhD new-grad ML loop ran four technical interviews over two days, each day pairing one coding interview with one ML discussion. The ML discussions are open-ended product-modeling scenarios that still probe details; one opened with a short walk through the candidate's prior paper. Interviewers offer hints and treat the session as a joint discussion, but a loop that feels positive can still end in rejection.

A SWE phone-screen rejection arrived about three weeks after the screen, with no recruiter replies in between. If an interviewer arrives late or the screen is badly disrupted, asking the recruiter to reschedule is a reasonable option.

briefings.body:
## Every team runs its own loop

Disney hires through individual organizations: Streaming (Disney+), Experiences, and others. Each hiring manager decides the format, so two loops with the same title can look completely different. Experiences loops are said to be noticeably easier than Streaming loops. Ask the recruiter for the exact round list, and verify it, since recruiter descriptions are sometimes wrong.

## Typical pipeline

1. **Application** through Workday.
2. **Recruiter call.** Resume screen, tech-stack and tool check, light cloud questions, work authorization (some roles do not sponsor visas), pay range, and location. Common prompts: most proud project, why Disney / this role.
3. **Hiring-manager or phone screen.** Usually a background and project conversation plus a short coding problem. Some screens run on HackerRank with two interviewers; some teams run two separate HM conversations.
4. **Technical round(s).** Coding, code review, or (for data engineering) pipeline design with a tech lead and senior engineers.
5. **Onsite.** Format varies widely:
   - **Software engineering:** system design, an algorithm problem, a front-end coding exercise, and BQ.
   - **Lead SWE (front end):** Disney has started running in-person onsites, and this one was held at the Seattle office. Four rounds: a TPM collaboration chat, a code review with a principal engineer, and two front-end system designs on a whiteboard.
   - **Senior Data Engineer (Experiences):** a single 1v6 panel of about two and a half hours covering pipeline design again, Python OOP and resume-driven tech questions, an hour of BQ, and a personal culture-fit segment.
   - **Product engineer:** two coding interviews (one AWS-focused), then a culture-fit onsite.
6. **Post-onsite.** Hiring managers sometimes request an extra conversation to probe a specific area such as stakeholder management.

## Timeline

A Senior Data Engineer loop ran from a mid-August application to a late-September onsite: recruiter call at the end of August, tech round in early September, HM round mid-September, and the panel at month end.

## Headcount risk

Disney has had rolling reorganizations and layoffs. In at least one recent loop, a candidate received good feedback after the onsite, but the position was then put on hold because of an organizational change. Some teams also lean heavily on contractors, and contractor loops (for example in data engineering) run a similar structure: system design, coding, and an HM video interview.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Major Pipelines
briefings.body:
## Common Shape

Most Netflix engineering loops follow this shape:

1. **Recruiter / HR screen**. Role fit, compensation expectation, work authorization, culture memo, and sometimes language constraints. Some teams explicitly ask for Python or Java and do not accept C++ for coding rounds.
2. **Phone screen**. Usually one 60-minute technical round. Depending on org, this can be coding, technical problem solving, SQL + pipeline design, or a light system-design discussion.
3. **Virtual onsite**. Commonly 5 rounds: coding, system design, data modeling or domain design, and two manager / culture / behavioral rounds. DataEng and ML Infra loops can stretch longer when multiple stakeholders are involved.
4. **Team match / HM alignment**. Ads hiring is often centralized. Passing the technical loop can still lead to additional HM conversations before an offer.

## Pipeline Differences

- **Ads**: the most standardized path. Expect topological sort, Ads Frequency Cap, Ads Data Modeling / demand intake, and two HM / BQ rounds.
- **Member, Commerce & Games**: usually coding plus a Technical Problem Solving round around homepage viewport dedupe. Requirements are intentionally under-specified.
- **Data Platform / Infra**: cache, latency, thread-safety, config rollout, and reliability trade-offs show up frequently.
- **ML Infra / MLI**: blends service design, ML platform design, stakeholder partnership, model monitoring, and manager culture rounds.
- **Data Platform (three-stage example)**: phone screen = problem solving (duplicate detection series) + HM; first VO = general system design (ML job scheduler) + problem solving (title rotation) + partnership; second VO = team-specific system design + a second HM round. Round names such as "problem solving", "domain expertise", and "partnership" map to coding, system design, and behavioral respectively — prepare them the same way.
- **Applied GenAI (Research Engineer)**: the screen is split into 30 minutes of ML fundamentals (attention / KV cache / normalization) and 30 minutes of practical coding, where the candidate reviews a feature-pipeline pull request whose tests already pass and explains what would break in production, then discusses serving those features under different freshness requirements.
- **DataEng**: SQL, data modeling, production pipeline concerns, event-stream coding, and heavier BQ / culture calibration.

## Leveling & 2026 Hiring Context

- Netflix runs a famously flat senior band: recruiters have declined Staff (L6) requests outright, telling candidates that an external L6 maps to L5 here and that L5 still owns L6-scope work. Plan to interview at L5 even with a senior external title.
- A company-wide hiring freeze was in effect through 2026 Q2, yet recruiters continued to reach out on LinkedIn for Ads and Data Platform roles — an active pipeline does not guarantee an open req, and at least one candidate finished the full loop only to have the freeze announced the following week. Confirm the req status early.
- Some Ads requisitions are fullstack rather than backend. On top of the standard coding / SD / data-modeling / BQ rounds, these add two frontend rounds — one UI implementation ("UI doing") and one UI design — so confirm the stack with the recruiter before you prep.

## VO1 / VO2 Phase Split

Some loops explicitly divide the virtual onsite into two phases. VO1 emphasizes general engineering signal; VO2 shifts toward the target team's domain. Prepare reusable fundamentals for VO1 and role-specific deep dives for VO2.

## Time Management in Team-Specific Design

The team-specific system-design round is graded on reaching a complete design within the slot. Broad prompts make it easy to spend time on areas the interviewer considers secondary; if the interviewer gives a time warning, treat it as a signal to move on and cover the remaining components at a high level.

description: Citadel and Citadel Securities run two distinct loops sharing one brand. Citsec (the market maker) hires for HFT software, quant research and quant dev; its phone screens lean on small, sharp coding prompts (merge-K, ring buffers, stock-DP ladders) and the loop is famously single-fail — any weak round and the next interview is cancelled within a day. Citadel (the hedge fund) and its sub-orgs (GQS, EQR, NXT) lean harder on probability brainteasers, deep resume drilling and a multi-week team-match stage where coding bar drops but cultural and PM-style fit dominates the offer decision.

briefings.title: Citadel vs Citadel Securities — Two Different Loops
briefings.body:
Candidates routinely confuse the two entities and get caught off-guard when interviewers explicitly ask "what's the difference between Citadel and Citadel Securities?" during phone screens.

- **Citadel Securities (Citsec)** — the market-making / liquidity-provision arm. Core teams: Equity Market Making, Fixed Income, Options, HFT Software Engineering, Quant Research (QR), Quant Development (QD). Loop is engineering-heavy with low-latency / OS / concurrency questions. Single-fail policy is universal here.
- **Citadel** (the hedge fund) — multi-strategy investment firm. Sub-orgs include GQS (Global Quantitative Strategies), EQR (Equity QR), Fixed Income, Commodities, NXT (rotational engineering program). Loop emphasizes brainteasers, resume drilling, and a separate team-match phase after technical clearance.

When recruiters reach out, ask explicitly which org and which desk — the prep priorities diverge significantly. Citsec coding rounds focus on data structures, low-latency idioms, and order-book mechanics; Citadel QR/EQR loops weight statistics, alpha-factor methodology, and quantitative reasoning much more heavily.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
The standard Goldman Sachs engineering loop runs in four serial phases:

1. **Recruiter screen / submission** — for campus pipelines, the next touchpoint is the Hirevue video interview within 1-2 weeks of applying. Experienced-hire flows often skip Hirevue and go straight to a coding screen.
2. **Online Assessment (OA)** — 90-120 minutes on HackerRank or CoderPad, typically two problems pulled from a small recurring bank (see the LeetCode-style OA bank in the question list). Hidden test cases; full-credit submissions still get rejected, so partial credit alone is not a strong signal either way.
3. **CoderPad technical screen** — one 45-60 minute live coding round, typically two LeetCode-equivalent problems from the Goldman-tagged list (string compression, trapping rain water, decode ways, merge k sorted lists are recurring picks). Experienced-hire candidates can receive a second CoderPad request after the first live-coding screen; use it as a signal to stay prepared for another practical coding round rather than reading it as a final outcome.
4. **Superday** — back-to-back virtual or in-person rounds with engineers and managers. Most loops are three rounds: two coding + one mixed (resume deep-dive, system design lite, or technical fundamentals). System design appears unevenly — some candidates report a stock-trading-system prompt, others get an algorithm pop-quiz instead. Final round usually overlaps with manager fit.

Typical end-to-end timeline runs 4-8 weeks from application to verbal offer. Background checks and offer approval add another 6-8 weeks before the start date is locked.

**Locations:** New York, Salt Lake City, Dallas, London, Bangalore, and the Beijing engineering hub all share the same loop template. Salt Lake City has a heavier campus pipeline and runs Superday in larger cohort batches.

As of October 2026, an experienced-hire engineering loop in New York ran: recruiter outreach (with repeated confirmation that the role is five days a week in office) → a 40-minute proctored screen with camera and screen recording on (two SQL queries plus debugging a Java Spring API against failing tests; looking down to think drew a warning) → two team phone rounds (a team lead's rapid-fire PostgreSQL / message-queue questions, then a senior engineer's tree coding problem that drifted into B-trees and database indexing) → a four-round onsite. A verbal offer came within about 30 minutes of finishing the onsite, so the end of the loop can move much faster than the earlier stages.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Standard SMTS / MTS Loop

A typical Salesforce SWE loop runs:

1. **Recruiter / HR reach-out** (cold or post-application). Sometimes paired with a recruiter prep call; treat the prep call's advice as low signal — preparation guidance can diverge from the actual rounds, so prepare across the bank rather than relying on a single forecast.
2. **Hiring Manager screen** (one short screen). Mostly behavioural and resume walk-through, but some HMs slip in a coding problem mid-conversation. Treat it as a leveling round — the HM's read shapes the eventual offer level.
3. **OA (HackerRank)**. Usually a timed set of medium-difficulty coding problems; the recurring families are linked-list dedup, longest-subseq-substring, palindromic strings, sliding-window time-window, string-compression, min-ops-to-zero. See the question cards for the full list.
4. **2 virtual VO rounds** — one coding, one system design (or one frontend coding + one backend SD for fullstack candidates). For AI Engineer loops, this expands to three rounds: HM chat + Project Deep Dive + AI Fundamentals.
5. **Onsite (SF / Bellevue office)** — usually two more rounds: typically one coding + one system design, occasionally one OOD or one frontend coding. Held in-person at Salesforce Tower (SF) or the Bellevue office; for hybrid candidates this is the friction point.
6. **Team match** — Salesforce sequences team match **after** the loop is approved, not before. Even with a successful loop, candidates have waited weeks-months for the right team. Visa-check / leveling can also re-open at this stage.
7. **HR offer call** — when an offer materialises, the result often arrives within about a week of the final round.

## Timing

The process usually spans several weeks when team matching is quick and can run longer when scheduling or matching stalls. Early screens often move faster than the final onsite and team-match stages. Clarify the expected decision window with the recruiter instead of assuming a fixed turnaround.

## Two Recent Process Changes

- **In-person onsite re-emerged**: many recent loops require travel to SF Tower or Bellevue for the final two rounds. Candidates without proximity should clarify travel expectations early.
- **Re-interview at offer stage** is rare but possible: a hiring manager can still reject after the loop closes, and post-loop calibration can reduce the proposed level.

## Research Scientist Loop

A recent Research Scientist process used four interview rounds. Coding carried substantial weight and mixed conventional algorithms with design-oriented coding and handwritten basic PyTorch modules. A separate research presentation focused on the candidate's latest work, followed by discussion around AI agents. Because exact module interfaces and the presentation rubric can vary, prepare both a concise research narrative and implementation fluency with foundational PyTorch components.

## Team-Specific General-Hire Variant (2026)

A general-hire application can route into a team-specific process immediately after the Futureforce HackerRank OA. In one current flow, recruiter outreach arrived about a month after the OA and introduced a newly formed iOS / Swift team with an August–September start-date target. The sequence was recruiter team introduction → hiring-manager discussion → team-related OOD technical round → planned San Francisco onsite.

Treat this as a separate branch rather than assuming pooled matching. Confirm whether the requisition is still general hire or already bound to a team, what stack is expected, whether onsite travel is required, and whether the original application remains usable if the team stops the process. Holiday and PTO scheduling pushed the planned onsite back repeatedly; the process then ended without feedback while the application remained "in progress," blocking a switch to another team.

## Hiring-Manager First-Round Variant (August 2026)

A 30-minute first-round HM screen may contain only a self-introduction, project and tech-stack discussion, the manager's team overview, and candidate questions — with no explicit behavioral prompt. Treat this compact format as evaluative: strong stack alignment, a warm conversation, and explicit discussion of next steps do not guarantee progression. Prepare concise evidence of scope, technical judgment, and impact even when the manager does not ask standard BQ questions.

## September 2026: Cross Cloud SMTS and MTS Variants

A Cross Cloud SMTS process began with a VP conversation, followed by an OA, two virtual interviews covering coding and system design, and then an in-person stage with another coding interview and another system-design interview. Behavioral discussion occupied about 20 minutes of each round except the final onsite stage. One candidate completed the onsite on a Wednesday and received confirmation the following Monday that team matching would begin; matching was still pending at that point.

A separate MTS sequence consisted of two coding rounds followed by a system-design round. Confirm the sequence for the specific team and level rather than assuming every MTS interview follows the Cross Cloud SMTS structure.

## Intern Loop (2026)

A 2026 SWE intern process started with HR picking up a mass application, then an OA of two problems at modest difficulty. Team match happened **before** the formal interviews here — the reverse of the full-time sequence — and the formal loop was only two rounds:

1. **Hiring-manager round** — self-introduction, a deep dive into one project the candidate picks (tech choices, architecture, hardest problem, personal contribution, how to optimize or scale), "why Salesforce", and how much the candidate knows about Salesforce's Cloud products.
2. **Coding round** — three short fundamentals problems: two linked-list problems and one basic SQL query.

The offer arrived three days after the final round. Intern questions skew toward fundamentals, so preparation time is best spent on linked lists, basic SQL, and a well-rehearsed project deep dive.

## October 2026: Auto-Routed Requisitions and Director-Led First Screens

Applications are not always evaluated only for the role applied to: a batch of September applications led to a 30-minute SMTS interview for a requisition the candidate had never applied to, assigned internally. The first call was with a long-tenured Director who assumed a recruiter screen had already happened — in fact it was the first stage. The conversation was technical rather than a light chat: a resume deep dive focused on the parts closest to the team's work (Cloud, Terraform, CI/CD), with "have you actually implemented this?" probes. Treat any first call as evaluative even when it arrives unannounced for an unfamiliar role, and research the team before the call so you can steer toward overlapping experience.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Bloomberg's SDE loop is one of the more standardized in the industry, especially for new-grad hires. Expect a five-step pipeline:

- **Recruiter / HR phone screen** — 20–30 minutes. Behavioral only: walk-through resume, why-Bloomberg, visa and timeline. Decisions arrive within a day or two.
- **Technical phone screen** — 45–60 minutes. 10–15 minutes of project / BQ chat, then two coding problems. Both problems must be reachable in the time slot; running out of time on the second is a common failure mode.
- **Super Day onsite** — three back-to-back technical rounds plus an HR conversation, typically all in one afternoon. Each technical round is 45–60 minutes with two interviewers, two coding problems, and 10–15 minutes of resume / BQ at the top. New-grad campus loops compress this into 2–3 in-person rounds run from school. Decisions between rounds are fast — candidates routinely get "you're moving to the next round" or a polite end within the hour.
- **EM / hiring manager round** — 45–60 minutes with the manager whose team is sponsoring the headcount. Most candidates report it as resume deep-dive plus behavioral; system design only surfaces when the role is mid-senior. A non-trivial fraction of EM rounds drop in a surprise hard coding problem, so going in cold on data structures after a long behavioral stretch is risky.
- **Offer call** — usually within a week of the EM round; written offer follows shortly after.

Tokyo and Dublin loops follow the same shape but are slower to schedule and feature mixed-region interviewer panels (e.g., Hong Kong shadow plus Tokyo team lead). End-to-end timeline from recruiter outreach to offer is typically 4–8 weeks for new-grad, longer for senior in-office roles.

**Experienced-hire team loops** — candidates interviewing with specific teams repeat the later rounds per team: each team's second round pairs one hour of coding (two mediums, standard pace) with one hour of system design, so being in process with two teams means going through the pair twice. The system-design hour carries most of the differentiation at that stage.

**Parallel team processes (as of late 2026)** — a candidate can be in process with at most two teams at the same time, and each team runs its own independent technical phone screen. A job posting generally maps to a single headcount, and those fill quickly, so passing a team's phone screen does not guarantee the seat is still open. When a headcount fills, the recruiter can forward the candidate to a sister team that is still hiring; the passed phone screen carries over, and the candidate goes straight to that team's virtual onsite. In these team loops, a virtual onsite comes first and a separate in-person onsite follows it.

**AI engineering general hires (as of late 2026)** — some senior Applied AI Engineer openings in the AI department are recruited as a general position rather than for a specific team: team match happens only after the offer. The phone screen is a single 60-minute session run by an experienced manager — process overview, self-introduction, a background question (career switchers should expect "why did you change fields"), then one multi-stage class-design coding problem. Time is tight, and the interviewer actively guides rather than silently grading. Teams in this department include AI services centered on RAG — indexing documents so clients can retrieve company-specific documentation.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Recruiter Call
A short behavioral conversation. Some candidates are contacted by recruiters or agencies; others apply online.

## Phone Screen
Two 45-minute rounds, back to back with no break. The pairing varies by team:

- **Coding + system design** — the most common pairing for general SWE hires.
- **Systems coding + algorithm coding** — two coding rounds, one of each track.
- **ML infrastructure design + coding** — for ML-platform roles; the "ML design" round is really ML infra (e.g. an inference pipeline), so prepare infrastructure, not modeling.
- **Infra screen** — a light coding exercise plus detailed Kubernetes / Docker questions.

If one track does not produce enough signal, the recruiter may add an extra round (for example, a second algorithm round) before deciding.

## Onsite
Recent onsites are **in person**, with lunch provided. A typical loop has about five rounds:

- Algorithm coding (LeetCode style)
- Systems coding (concurrency)
- One or two system design rounds (often job scheduling or large-scale vehicle data; ML system design for ML roles)
- Hiring manager round (project deep dive + behavioral, sometimes a surprise team-specific design question)
- AI-assisted coding — working through tickets in an existing codebase with an AI assistant (seen in recent loops)

## After the Onsite
Passing the onsite is not the end: candidates then meet senior leadership — described as **two more rounds** or a meeting with three senior leaders. Leadership questions can be open-ended technical design (e.g. how you would design ChatGPT from prompt to output), so prepare for them like a design round, not a chat. After the onsite, HR may also ask about your current level, pay expectations and reasons for leaving.

## Pace and Decisions
Decisions are fast and often terse: rejections commonly arrive the same day or the next day after a phone screen, sometimes even when candidates felt both rounds went cleanly. A "no suitable role right now" response also happens. Treat each round as needing a clear, strong signal on its own.

The bar swings sharply with the interviewer — multiple candidates report bug-free coding rounds that still ended in rejection — so prepping the canonical question set cold matters more than chasing breadth.
