briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
DoorDash's loop is short on paper but slow to schedule in practice. Recruiter delays of multiple weeks between stages are the most common pain point, including mid-loop ghosting when the assigned recruiter switches teams.

## End-to-end pipeline

1. **Recruiter outreach / referral intake** — usually email-only; a non-trivial share of candidates report never speaking to a recruiter live. Some recruiters disappear mid-loop and a replacement picks up weeks later.
2. **Phone screen (Code Craft)** — 60 min, one engineer (occasionally a shadow). The default format is a Code Craft coding round on the DoorDash HackerRank-based platform; a minority of loops put a project deep-dive in this slot instead, especially for MLE and Staff candidates.
3. **Virtual onsite (VO)** — 4 rounds, 60–75 min each, in one day for SDE / 1.5 days for some EM and Staff loops:
   - 1 × Code Craft (one of the recurring originals — Dasher Pay, Bootstrap API, AI Code Craft Challenge — or a new variant)
   - 1 × System Design (3-day Donation, Notification, Food Review, or a level-appropriate variant)
   - 1 × Debugging (Pick Dasher / Round Robin is the dominant prompt; consistent hashing is the standard follow-up)
   - 1 × Hiring Manager BQ (often paired with a 15–25 min project deep-dive)
   - Staff and EM loops sometimes add a fifth round (Architecture or Scope deep-dive)
4. **Result & team match** — most teams hire direct; some pipelines add a HR call to negotiate level / package before final.

## MLE variant

Senior MLE loops increasingly use a four-round VO mix: HM / values, ML domain-knowledge discussion, ML system design, and AI Code Craft. Store or restaurant recommendation remains the core ML system-design prompt, while the domain-knowledge slot is resume-grounded and asks which methods the candidate used in production work. Shadows may join every round.

## Typical cadence

- Application / referral → recruiter contact: 1–4 weeks.
- Recruiter → phone screen: 1–3 weeks.
- Phone screen → VO: 2–4 weeks; multi-week schedule slips are common.
- VO → outcome: 2 business days for fast rejections; 1–2 weeks for offers.
- End to end: **6–12 weeks**; loops that span recruiter changes routinely hit 3+ months.

## Q2 2026 hiring freeze

Multiple candidates received "happy to continue the process once things reopen" closings during April–May 2026, indicating a soft hiring freeze on backfills. Existing pipelines were finished out, but new requisitions slowed dramatically. Treat any in-progress loop as still real, but expect added delay to a final offer.

## Cooling period

- Failed phone screen → ~6 months before re-applying to the same role family.
- Failed VO → 6–12 months depending on the team.
- Recruiters sometimes re-engage rejected candidates from the cooldown pool when a similar req opens; do not rely on it.

## In-person vs virtual

Almost all SDE / MLE loops in 2025–2026 run fully virtual (Zoom / Google Meet). A small number of EM and Staff loops have moved to an in-person final round in San Francisco or Seattle.

## Mid-2026 observations

Some SDE virtual onsites now run the four rounds across two consecutive days (two per day) rather than a single day, with panelists drawn from several different teams. Cross-team panels mean less shared context on your domain — calibrate how much background you give before diving into project details. Candidates also encounter panels that consistently answer questions with "what do you think? You make the decision" — decision ownership is being graded, so commit to a recommendation instead of asking the interviewer to choose.

## September 2026 Staff loop variation

A Staff pipeline can include both coding and a project deep dive before a four-round virtual onsite. One such onsite comprised AI-assisted coding, system design, incident investigation, and a 45-minute hiring-manager conversation. Confirm the scheduled round mix rather than assuming every Staff panel includes debugging or an extra architecture round. The rejection in this pipeline arrived two weeks after the onsite, so a delayed response alone does not establish the outcome.

## Post-offer immigration timing

For candidates on an H-1B, the transfer petition is filed by external immigration counsel after the offer is signed, and that step can take more than a month even with HR, the hiring manager, and the skip-level escalating. Expediting is not guaranteed. If a grace-period deadline is approaching, raise it at the offer stage and plan a fallback status in advance. Offers are generally not rescinded during such delays, but the start date can slip by several months.

## October 2026 cadence note

Phone-screen turnaround can be much faster than the typical range above: an onsite invitation can arrive on the fourth business day after a Code Craft phone screen. The four-round SDE onsite mix (HM, system design, AI coding, debugging) remains the standard shape.

## November 2026 observations

- Two-day onsites are now common: one pattern is system design + debugging on day one and AI Code Craft + HM on day two; another runs AI Code Craft + system design on day one and debugging + HM on day two. The HM slot can be rescheduled repeatedly, sometimes landing more than a week after the other rounds.
- Outcomes typically arrive between three days and a week after the last round; rejections often come without feedback even when requested.
- A pass can still require matching to a different team than the one that interviewed you; candidates describe this re-match as quick and not difficult.
- Full-stack E4 loops follow a different shape: a frontend coding phone screen and a separate HM chat (covering the role split, roughly 80% backend / 20% frontend, and how you work with AI agents) precede an onsite of system design, engineering values + AI usage, Code Craft, and a full-stack AI Code Craft round — with no debugging round.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Pipeline

A typical Anthropic loop runs:

1. **Recruiter screen** (~30 min). Either a referral handoff or a cold reachout. Why-Anthropic and AI-safety screening start here.
2. **Phone screen — coding** (55 min). One prompt from the Coding Q1–Q6 catalog. Recruiter emails the prompt blurb a few days before; matching the blurb to a Q-number is half the prep.
3. **Onsite loop** — five rounds, usually spread across two consecutive days:
   - Coding (a different Q than the phone)
   - System Design (Q1–Q5)
   - Project Deep-Dive (20–25 min presentation + Q&A)
   - Hiring Manager / Behavioral
   - Culture / AI-Safety
4. **Hiring Committee** review.
5. **Reference check** — Anthropic asks for **two coworker references** (typically one manager, one peer/senior IC). This happens *before* the offer and the package is finalized post-HC.

## Calendar time

A fast path goes recruiter → onsite in ~10 days; the full loop including HC and references commonly closes in 3–5 weeks. Some candidates wait 1–2 weeks for a verdict after onsite with no interim signal.

## Common variants

- **Research Engineer / Scientist & Fellows**: replace the standard coding phone screen with a 4-of-N or 6-of-N self-select menu (Coding & Design, ML Programming, ML Configuration System, RL Fundamentals, Prompting/Engineering with LLMs, ML Take-Home).
- **Recruiter-adjusted screens**: recruiters can change the screen order and format when a candidate profile calls for a more engineering-heavy evaluation; an Alignment Research Engineer candidate may receive Agentic Coding as the first technical screen.
- **Performance Engineer**: no phone-coding screen — a 2-hour take-home kernel optimization gates straight into the onsite, which adds a Performance Modeling round.
- **EM / managers**: swap one technical round for a Design Doc Review and one for Execution & Leadership; the Culture and Project Deep-Dive rounds stay.
- **AI Safety Fellow**: CodeSignal OA → 5-hour in-home PyTorch assessment with live review.
- **Senior / Staff via strong referral**: the loop can skip the OA and phone screen entirely — recruiter call → a first-round hiring-manager conversation → onsite. That onsite can run five rounds (1 coding, 2 system design, 1 technical project discussion, 1 culture) spread across three days, and the culture round is sometimes run by a non-engineer.

## Tooling & screen-share

Throughout every technical round you are expected to share your screen. Looking things up in language docs or on the web is explicitly permitted — interviewers want to see how you research, not whether you've memorized standard libraries. AI assistants (Copilot, Claude, ChatGPT) are *not* allowed; they're the line everyone watches for. Stay fluent enough in basic syntax and idioms that you don't burn the round on lookups.

## Pre-round recruiter blurb

A defining feature of the Anthropic loop is that the recruiter emails a short paragraph **before** each technical round describing what the upcoming prompt looks like — without naming the specific question. Two examples of the genre:

> "Q is about familiarity with handling concurrency, ability to evaluate tradeoffs between threads, processes, and async, and IO-bound vs CPU-bound reasoning."

> "Q is a standard algorithmic-style round in Google Colab; the interviewer will ask you to write code that compiles and runs, and to iterate based on test failures."

The blurb is the single most useful prep signal Anthropic gives candidates. Map the blurb to a prompt family before the round (the families and their blurbs are documented in the Coding Q & SD Q Portal briefing), and structure your warm-up around the specific data structures and tradeoffs the blurb foreshadows. Candidates who arrive having drilled the blurb-matched family typically clear the round; candidates who treat the blurb as boilerplate often realize mid-round that they could have prepared more narrowly.

## Verdict signals

- Verdicts are usually delivered by email with little to no feedback ("touch design, cannot provide more details"). The no-feedback rule is a stated policy, not an oversight — do not write back asking for resume or round-level critique. Even all-hire loops can end without an offer if no team match exists.
- Reaching reference check does **not** guarantee an offer — HC can still reject after references come back.

## Two-day VO split

Recent candidates report the five rounds frequently split as **day 1 = coding + system design (both Q1-style), day 2 = three non-technical rounds (HM, Project Deep-Dive, Culture)**. A poor day-1 performance can lead to day 2 being cancelled outright, so the technical bar is largely set in the first 24 hours.

## Mid-2026 flow variations

- Loops increasingly run the **full interview first, team match after** — the reverse of the earlier match-then-interview order. In this flow a Hiring Manager conversation lands at the end as the final gate, and a background-vs-team-direction mismatch there can end an otherwise strong loop.
- If the culture signal from the onsite is judged insufficient, an **additional culture round** may be scheduled before the HM conversation rather than an outright reject.
- Some loops swap the catalog system-design prompts for **two domain-specific design rounds** tied to the hiring team's area, and run the HM round as a phone call before the onsite.

## Late-August 2026 recruiter sequence

One current full-stack sequence starts with a system-design technical screen, then advances to the full loop; the recruiter explicitly calls out multithreading as the coding theme. Another end-to-end loop moved from recruiter contact to technical screen in roughly two weeks, then ran system design, coding, project deep-dive, HM, and culture across two onsite days, with the decision arriving two days later.

## September 2026 role-specific sequences

A performance/infrastructure SDE path skips the OA but keeps a coding phone screen: recruiter → hiring-manager screen → technical coding screen → onsite. One candidate advanced after waits of two days, two days, and nine days respectively; the performance-engineering take-home path above is not universal across infrastructure roles. Design-document review can also be the technical phone screen. Recruiters may switch the design track from Product to Data Infrastructure based on the candidate’s experience, even shortly before the scheduled interview.

An infrastructure onsite can instead consist of four rounds: Distributed Coding, Programming / Problem Solving, Culture, and Performance Modeling. A candidate on this path received a reference request nearly a week after the onsite; the request did not guarantee an offer.

## October 2026 sequences

- Some virtual onsites run **four rounds with no system design**: an agent-building coding round (hand-written agent loop), Project Deep-Dive, HM, and Culture — with the phone screen itself being the LLM-inference design question.
- The frontend track runs CodeSignal OA → a frontend coding phone screen → onsite with an AI-assisted "Code with Claude" round, a chat-app system design, and HM / Culture / Project Deep-Dive.
- For RL-focused teams, the first technical step after the recruiter call can be an **RL-fundamentals screen**, with the rest of the loop scheduled only after its feedback.
- Decisions can be fast in both directions: phone-screen results within four to seven days, and onsite rejections as early as the next business day.

briefings.body:
## Common Pipeline

A typical Databricks SWE loop runs:

1. **Recruiter / HR screen**. Motivation, current search status, location, level, and resume fit. New-grad candidates often get timeline and internship questions here.
2. **Technical phone screen** (~55-60 min). One coding prompt, often from the recurring bank: IP/CIDR Firewall, Optimal Commute, Fibonacci Tree, KV QPS, Snapshot Set, or related variants.
3. **Virtual onsite** over Google Meet. Usually four technical / behavioral rounds: algorithm, coding or low-level programming, architecture / system design, and hiring-manager behavioral. Some loops split the onsite across two days.
4. **Redo / extra round**. If one round is weak but the rest is strong, Databricks can schedule a redo algorithm or coding round instead of rejecting immediately.
5. **References + hiring committee**. The official pipeline runs seven explicit stages: identify opportunity → apply → talent acquisition → skill assessments → interviewing → reference checks → decision and offer. Several candidates clear the technical loop and still fail later at reference or HC. Treat the process as unfinished until the written offer is signed.

## Timing Notes

Technical screen feedback can arrive same day or after a week. Onsite feedback can arrive in 2-7 days, but reference and HC can add multiple weeks. Team match and headcount can also hold a candidate after passing interviews.

## Experienced-Hire Variants

Some experienced-hire processes can route from recruiter screen into a system-design screen, then director and team conversations. Recruiters may ask current level, promotion timeline, and a current project mapped to the job description.

Staff-level loops can start directly at the onsite after a hiring-manager introduction. One AI-platform loop used five initial rounds—compression coding, high-level design, low-level storage programming, project deep dive, and hiring-manager behavioral—followed by two extra design / system-programming rounds. Extra rounds can repeat an already-seen prompt family when interview packets are not coordinated, so restate assumptions and solve the assigned variant cleanly instead of relying on context from an earlier round.

A full-stack experienced-hire screen may be framed as frontend-aware product design yet still evaluate ordinary schema and API design with no frontend coding. The onsite can then contain one system-design round, two coding / system-programming rounds, and two behavioral rounds.

## Senior Loop Shape (2026 Q4)

- The HR screen can walk through every prior employer in turn: why you left each one and whether you were promoted there.
- For L6 applicants, the phone screen can be the system-design prompt rather than coding.
- The onsite can run as four rounds over two back-to-back days: coding, cross-functional behavioral, architecture, and systems programming.
- Team-specific senior roles (for example distributed systems) can get a domain-flavored algorithm screen — such as a MapReduce-style data-flow problem — with team match only after the tech screen. Language choice is open in that round.

## Early Termination (2026 Q4)

Onsite rounds are not always held as one block. When the earlier rounds are scheduled first, a clear fail can end the loop: one candidate failed the systems-programming round and was told the next day that the remaining behavioral and coding rounds were cancelled.

questions.overview: Implement Connect-N on a board unbounded both horizontally (any integer column, including negatives) and vertically: insert(col, player) places a piece and reports whether a player now has N consecutive pieces along a row or a column. A push-from-bottom variant shifts the whole column up on each insert, so several rows change at once and both players can win on the same move.

### Trading & research internships

Most candidates enter through recruiter outreach. A typical software engineering pipeline:

1. **Technical screen (about 60 minutes).** Starts with introductions and a conversation about your career, why Anduril, and a past project (tech stack, hardest problem, and for senior roles design questions about it). ## Problem style

Screen problems are practical and moderate in difficulty: manufacturing-style optimization word problems, a garbage-collector reachability exercise, an in-memory transactional key-value store, and a public string-expansion problem. Expect a follow-up that extends your first solution, so write code that is easy to grow.

## Timeline and decisions

- Screen results arrive quickly — within 24 hours by email, or the next day from HR.
- Rejections come with **no feedback**; company policy is to give none.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Pipeline

1. **Online assessment** (pre-screen) — a level-based implementation task for many roles; see the OA briefing.
2. **Recruiter call** — a 30-minute slot, usually scheduled within days of passing the OA.
3. **Phone screen** — a coding round in some pipelines (for example, a folder-permission problem).
4. **Virtual onsite**, split across **two days**.

Some candidates go straight from a recruiter reach-out to the two-day onsite without an OA. Overall the process moves quickly once it starts.

## Two-day onsite

Day 2 is scheduled only after Day 1 is done, so treat Day 1 as a gate.

A typical SWE onsite covers:

- **Project deep dive** — one large project you owned, examined in detail.
- **Two coding rounds** — practical, multi-part problems such as the word-guessing game and the file crawler, or a key-value store plus a concurrency round (token bucket).
- **System design** — for example, an S3-like object store.
- **Behavioral** — a standalone behavioral round in addition to the deep dive.

One common Day 1 is the deep dive plus both coding rounds.

## Research-track loop

Research roles follow a similar two-day shape with different content:

| Day | Round | Length |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Live coding | 60 min |
| 1 | Live architecture / system design | 60 min |
| 2 | Research deep dive | 60 min |
| 2 | Behavioral | 45 min |
| 2 | Hiring-manager wrap-up | 30 min |

The architecture round is run by engineering-leaning interviewers who push into implementation detail. Candidates with a research background name it as the round that most needs extra preparation.

## Practical notes

- Some loops ask candidates to sign an NDA covering the interview content.
- The hiring-manager conversation, when present, is relaxed and focused on the team and role.

description: Pure Storage (now also hiring under the Everpure name) reuses a small, well-known set of coding questions, so loops are decided by depth rather than novelty: interviewers press hard on concurrency, lock discipline and read/write optimization. Experienced loops close with a hiring-manager conversation and an architect-led design round built around real storage problems.

questions.title: Event Fire / Callback Registration (Trigger System)
questions.overview: Implement an event that callers register callbacks on: callbacks registered before fire() are queued and run when the event fires; callbacks registered after it has fired run immediately. Then make it thread-safe. The follow-ups (register racing with fire, never invoking callbacks under the lock, where the fired flag is set relative to the critical section) decide the outcome, and the expected final version varies by interviewer.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Experienced hires

A typical end-to-end process:

1. **Recruiter outreach → hiring-manager call (~30 min).** Background and behavioral questions; the manager may mention how many open headcounts the team has.
2. **Coding rounds.** Two phone screens, or three separate coding interviews on consecutive days. Each round is one well-known question with heavy follow-ups.
3. **Final pair (back to back, ~1 hour each).**
   - **Hiring manager:** mostly your questions for them, then a short, high-level design discussion based on your background and the team's work.
   - **Architect system design:** about half the time on resume projects with the architect's questions, the other half on a real problem the team has faced: how you would solve and optimize it.

Some loops instead bring candidates to the Bay Area office for a two-round in-person onsite after the screens. On-site visits no longer include travel reimbursement or a meal.

## Timing signals

- From application to first recruiter contact can take about 6 weeks; each later step moves within 1–2 weeks.
- After the coding rounds, the final rounds can be scheduled weeks later if you ask (for example around holidays).
- Headcount fills during the process: the manager may say one of two openings was filled while you were interviewing.

## Outcomes

- Rejections arrive either as a phone call or as a next-day email with a generic "not a match", sometimes with no call at all.
- Candidates who felt they solved both screen questions well have still been rejected, so communication and how you handle follow-ups weigh heavily.

description: Snap interviews are highly interviewer-dependent: candidates report classic graph and cache problems, open-ended backend coding, product-heavy system design, and MLE loops that dig into recommendation systems, ranking, fundamentals, and project judgment. The safest preparation strategy is to be fluent in BFS/DFS, cache/data-structure implementation, feed and ads design, and concise behavioral stories around innovation, ambiguity, and execution.

questions.title: Maximum Island Perimeter
questions.overview: Given a binary grid, find islands with BFS or DFS and return the largest island perimeter rather than just the island count.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Signal
briefings.body:
## Common loop shapes

SWE candidates commonly see a phone screen with 10-20 minutes of behavioral or project discussion, followed by one coding problem. Virtual onsite loops usually contain two coding rounds, one or two system design rounds, and a Q&A or culture round. Some L5 loops are described as five rounds, with four evaluated rounds and one lighter Q&A / culture conversation.

MLE loops are more specialized. A typical loop includes ML fundamentals, ML system design, applied ML or product modeling, one coding round, and a project deep-dive or behavioral round. Senior and staff candidates should expect project challenge questions, not just textbook ML definitions.

## Signal to prepare for

Snap puts unusual weight on bug-free execution and interviewer-defined follow-ups. Coding questions often start from a known graph/cache/search shape but add a product or concurrency twist. System design rounds tend to stay close to Snapchat product surfaces: Stories, Spotlight, ads, short video recommendation, ranking, metrics, and content ingestion.

## Timing and logistics

Several candidates report all-day virtual onsite loops around 5 to 5.5 hours. Rescheduling flexibility can be limited, and some candidates report being asked to finish onsite within a short timeline. Prepare enough breadth that a random, non-tagged question does not derail the round.

## Tech-trivia warm-up in coding rounds

Some onsite coding rounds open with 20-30 minutes of networking and systems trivia before the actual coding problem starts. Candidates report being asked about OSI layers, WebSocket vs Server-Sent Events, and TCP vs QUIC ahead of a BFS-on-grid round. Treat the first half of a coding round as potentially conversational and budget time accordingly — practice a clean 30-minute coding template so the truncated window does not push the implementation off the cliff.

## September 2026 loop variants

An L5 virtual onsite can contain four rounds: two system-design rounds, one conventional coding round, and one AI-coding round. Behavioral questions and resume discussion can be embedded in a design round, leaving approximately 30 minutes for design. An MLE phone screen can divide its hour into 15 minutes of introductions and behavioral discussion, 15 minutes of ML fundamentals, and 30 minutes of coding.

## MLE onsite round format

As of September 2026, an MLE onsite can run each round as roughly 10 minutes of values and project discussion followed by about 50 minutes of round-specific content. The rounds cover ML (driven by the candidate's own project), coding, Applied ML, and ML system design. Applied ML and system design can both start from the same ads or recommendation case and then examine the candidate's framework block by block. Applied ML focuses more on modeling.

## SDE ML-infra loops

As of fall 2026, an SDE ML-infra loop can include a phone screen with one coding problem, then an onsite with one system design round, two conventional coding rounds, and one AI-coding round. Recruiter prep meetings and emails may frame the design round as ML-infrastructure design: a multi-org distributed training platform, a feature-extraction pipeline and feature store, or a general ML platform. The actual prompt can still be a conventional infrastructure problem, such as CI/CD with separate control and data planes and region-level host distribution. Prepare classic distributed-systems design alongside ML-infra topics instead of betting the whole prep week on the advertised theme.

## October 2026 updates

An MLE L4 onsite covered ML fundamentals, coding, system design, and Applied ML. After the debrief, the hiring team added one more system-design round (a harmful-content identification system) before moving the candidate to team match. Keep some preparation in reserve for a possible add-on round, and treat an extra round as a request for more signal rather than a rejection.

Security Engineer (IAM) L4 loops start with a 60-minute first round: about 5 minutes of introduction, a behavioral portion, about 25 minutes of IAM domain knowledge, about 25 minutes of coding, and 5 minutes of Q&A. Coding runs on HackerRank CodePair, and the interviewer may not ask for screen sharing. Feedback after this round can arrive within about three days.

## November 2026 updates

A SWE phone screen can run 60 minutes with a behavioral segment first. It covers common behavioral questions and a past project, with follow-ups on details. One coding problem follows, with an in-memory part and a scale-up part.

An MLE virtual onsite can run four rounds: coding, ML design, Applied ML, and ML fundamentals. The ML design and Applied ML rounds can both be recommendation-system rounds. One centers on retrieval and the other on ranking, and both range across system and modeling details. Ads-specific questions, such as how labels are computed, can appear in either. The ML fundamentals round can be a resume-driven deep-dive, so review every resume item in depth.

description: Point72 hires across discretionary, systematic (Cubist) and data-heavy teams, and each role family runs its own loop. Engineering roles reward practical HackerRank fluency and broad, gap-free fundamentals; research roles test probability, statistics and portfolio-construction intuition alongside a close look at your own strategy work.

questions.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II (LC 122) with Trade Report
questions.overview: LC 122 (unlimited transactions, hold at most one share). The data-engineering screen frames it as a 'Portfolio Trading Optimizer': write a `validate_prices` decorator for the stated constraints, a `find_transactions` that returns each buy/sell pair, and a `generate_report` that prints every trade plus total profit. The QR intern screen asks the plain version with complexity; a software screen used a k-transaction (LC 188-like) variant.

briefings.title: Loop Structure and Timeline by Role
briefings.body:
Point72 runs different pipelines for each role family. Cubist, the firm's systematic arm, runs its own screens. The common thread: a phone or HackerRank screen first, then several technical conversations, then an in-office round for experienced hires.

### Data Engineer

- **OA**: HackerRank with SQL (PostgreSQL) and a PySpark job checked by unit tests.
- **Hiring-manager screen**: knowledge breadth across Python, SQL and runtime/memory fundamentals.
- **Two coding screens on HackerRank**: practical tasks (API ingestion with pagination; streaming statistics under memory limits), with data-engineering discussion mixed in. Another format is a 1-hour screen split into 30 minutes of DE/Spark discussion and 30 minutes of coding.
- **Superday in the New York office**: about five hours with four team leads (or a senior stand-in) plus the hiring manager, covering ingestion, Spark, SQL, Airflow and monitoring.
- The whole process can take more than three months. Expect slow replies between stages: one candidate waited over a month after the OA and close to three weeks after the superday.

### Software Developer

- Recruiter call (may ask whether you can interview in C#), then a HackerRank OA with two algorithm questions plus multiple-choice questions.
- Two tech screens, each with one algorithm question plus language fundamentals. Some interviewers are overseas contractors, so slots can fall early in the morning US time.

### Cubist low-latency developer

- From-scratch C++ class-template design (fixed-buffer strings, stable-address containers) plus about 10 minutes of systems fundamentals.

### Quant Researcher (intern)

- Five interview rounds in total. The first two are broad technical screens: motivation questions, probability and game-theory puzzles, statistics, ML concepts, C++ OOP and LeetCode-style algorithms.

### Quant Researcher – ML / MLE / AI Engineer

- Often no OA: HR matches you to a pod and the first round goes straight to a team member or a portfolio manager.
- First rounds are about one hour and mostly resume walk-through with technical probes; some finish early.
- AI Engineer: recruiter phone screen → 90-minute, three-part HackerRank OA → hiring-manager round focused on behavioral questions and your views on AI.
- Decisions usually arrive within a few days to a week after phone screens.

description: Whatnot is a live-stream shopping marketplace, and its engineering loop reflects that: engineers are expected to think like users of the app, with product sense assessed alongside coding and system design. Coding screens favor short, practical problems where finishing and testing the follow-ups matters more than algorithmic depth.

questions.title: User Journey Paths: Action-Log Prefix Tree
questions.overview: Given (user_id, time, action) logs, rebuild each user's time-ordered journey, insert every journey into a trie that counts distinct users per path prefix, and print the trie as an indented tree. Follow-up: logs arrive as a stream. Recruiters may announce two LC mediums, but interviewers often swap in this problem as the only question.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Whatnot's process varies noticeably by role and by how you entered the pipeline, but most loops share the same shape: a short screen, a technical screening stage that often pairs coding with system design, and a final virtual onsite that includes a product-sense conversation.

## Experienced software engineers

- **Recruiter call.** Usually on Zoom with camera on. Expect background, current level, and reasons for leaving. Some recruiters ask how you were rated in recent performance cycles.
- **Hiring manager call (sometimes).** About 30 minutes on background, interest, and ideas for improving the Whatnot app. For some teams the HM call is the first contact, scheduled right after you apply.
- **Technical screen: coding + system design.** Commonly two back-to-back sessions, one coding and one system design. Some candidates get system design as their very first technical round. Recruiters may describe the coding session as two LeetCode-medium problems, but the interviewer can choose a single, longer practical problem instead.
- **Virtual onsite.** Further coding and design, a product-sense round, and in some loops a conversation with technical leadership.

## Machine learning engineers

- Recruiter call, then a 30-minute HM call on background and improvement ideas for the app.
- Then an ML system design round on a live-streaming product problem (with the model treated as given) and a dedicated product-sense round.

## Mobile engineers

- The screen is a time-boxed app build (a small game in about 45 minutes); the recruiter prep doc describes the format in advance.
- The full loop has a larger app-building round, an easy-to-medium algorithms round with mobile domain questions, a product-sense round, and a round with technical leadership.

## Data scientists

- Recruiter call, HM call, a technical screen, a one-week take-home, a presentation of the take-home, then two virtual onsite rounds.

## Timeline and communication

- Scheduling can be fast: recruiter outreach can arrive the day after you apply.
- Post-interview communication is uneven. Some candidates heard back the next day, with system design named as the failing round; others waited one to two weeks, had to chase the recruiter, and received a template rejection with no feedback.
- Not every team is US-based; one frontend team in Shanghai had about nine engineers.

## Late-2026 changes

- The screening system-design pool is no longer limited to the long-circulating set (online judge, e-commerce messaging, donation service, home feed). A metrics monitoring and alerting system now appears as well, centred on how metrics are stored. Prepare a general design toolkit rather than only the known prompts.
- Screening coding rounds still draw heavily on recurring problems; several candidates finished early by having prepared them.

## Late-2026 SWE loop variant

- Some SWE loops now run a two-session screen: a **two-hour AI-assisted coding round** (extend an existing codebase with AI help, then present it) plus a system design round.
- The final round can be as short as two sessions: product sense and a hiring manager values conversation.
- Rejections after this shorter final round arrived about a week later, with brief per-round feedback relayed by the recruiter.

description: Optiver is a market-making trading firm whose interview process is built to find fast, calibrated decision-makers under pressure. The funnel is dominated by a heavy online assessment — a probability/sequence/reaction battery for quant roles and OOP simulation coding for engineers — and the quant loop centers on a live EV betting game where speed and bet-sizing matter more than ending profit.

questions.title: Beat the Odds — Probability Test
questions.overview: The signature Optiver quant assessment: 30 multiple-choice probability questions, ~90 seconds each, no going back. You pick the answer closest to the true value, so speed and estimation matter more than exact computation. Wrong answers are penalized.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Optiver runs distinct loops for its engineering and quant tracks, but both start with a fast, often-automatic online assessment (OA) sent within hours of applying.

**Software Engineer (SWE / SDE / Graduate) track**
1. **OA** — one OOP coding problem (75–90 min on HackerRank) + a 20-question CS-knowledge quiz + the Zap-N reaction games. The experienced-SWE OA instead gives two algorithm problems with a generous (up to 72-hour) window.
2. **HR / behavioral phone screen** — logistics, a project deep-dive, and motivation (~20–30 min).
3. **Virtual onsite** — typically two rounds: one coding (engineering-flavored, large skeleton code, e.g. the OptiCargo scheduler) and one system design (low-latency trading infrastructure, heavy on TCP/IP).
4. **Final behavioral** — values/fit, sometimes paired with an invitation to visit the Chicago office.

**Quant Researcher (QR) / Quant Trader (QT) track**
1. **OA** — the trading assessment: Beat the Odds probability test, Number Logic sequences, and Zap-N games. QR additionally gets three HackerRank coding problems; QT is usually games-only.
2. **Trading game interview** — a live EV/market-making betting game with a trader (often the first technical round, ~25–45 min).
3. **HR behavioral (BQ)** round.
4. **Technical round(s)** — probability/statistics brainteasers and estimation.
5. **Take-home data project** → **presentation round** (QR) drilling your methodology, pandas, and time-series work.
6. **Hiring-manager / culture call** to close.

Timelines are fast: OA invites are typically instant on application, and decisions (including rejections) often come within days of each step. Decisions on individual rounds are frequently communicated within 2–3 days.

**A recent Quant Trader loop.** One recent QT sequence ran four stages of roughly an hour each: (1) an HR round on prior internships, why Optiver, and why trading, with pressure-style follow-ups on résumé details; (2) an online market-making round built on many small dice and card-odds calculations, where you pick out the profitable games; (3) a second online market-making round betting on card sums with private and community cards; and (4) a final stage pairing a live trading game (price adjustment, mental math, logic) with a second HR session focused on drive and collaboration. The two final sessions may be held on the same day or separately.

description: JPMorgan Chase's engineering loop is predictable but operationally uneven: a light HackerRank-style OA is followed by a Super Day with coding, code review, system design, and behavioral rounds rotating across candidates. The technical bar skews practical: simple algorithms, review of production-ish Java code, concurrency/style critiques, and system designs around traffic, search, inventory, payments, and URL routing.

questions.title: Customer Request PR Review
questions.overview: Review a production-style customer-request class or PR and identify engineering issues before coding a small algorithm. The recurring critique areas are hard-coded values, single-responsibility violations, global variables, thread safety, low-level concurrency primitives such as `volatile`, and general maintainability.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
The experienced-SWE pipeline usually starts with an OA, then a recruiter call, then a virtual Super Day. The recruiter touchpoint is short and practical: background, work experience, location / role alignment, and scheduling. Several candidates describe recruiter communication as phone-heavy and light on email follow-through, so treat phone calls as the authoritative channel.

The Super Day is commonly three 45-60 minute rounds in one block: coding + code review, system design, and behavioral. Candidates are often placed into a large waiting-room meeting with many other candidates, then rotated into smaller rooms with different interviewers. Order is not fixed; coding, design, and behavioral can appear in any sequence, with short breaks between rounds.

The coding round frequently has two halves: read or review an existing Java-ish code change, then implement a simple algorithm. The code-review half is not a trick puzzle; the expected signal is practical engineering judgment around hard-coded values, single-responsibility violations, global state, low-level concurrency primitives, thread safety, and naming/style issues. The algorithm half is usually LC Easy / light Medium rather than a deep algorithmic challenge.

After a passed Super Day, candidates can enter team match or a hiring-manager/team conversation. A positive Super Day result does not always immediately convert into an offer; scheduling and HR follow-up can still be noisy.

Recent experienced-hire Super Day scheduling still follows the same pattern: a direct phone recruiter call after OA, a three-round virtual block of coding/code review, behavioral, and system design, and a team-match wait after a passed interview. One practical wrinkle is that candidates can lose setup time while being assigned into breakout rooms, so keep the design-round opening concise and start by locking requirements quickly.

A recent passed Super Day result arrived after roughly one week and opened a 90-day team-match pool. Treat the interview pass and team placement as separate milestones, and keep parallel options active while matching is in progress.

Role-specific experienced-hire loops can be shorter. One recent process used two rounds: a behavioral/project conversation that unexpectedly opened with high-level system design, followed by live coding. This variant is a useful reminder that round labels are porous; be ready to move from a project walkthrough into architecture without a separate design slot.

Coding tools can also vary by interviewer. Even when setup instructions ask for a runnable local environment, the live round may require screen sharing and a plain-text editor with no execution. Prompt delivery may be oral when meeting chat is unavailable. Before coding, confirm the permitted editor, whether execution is allowed, how the prompt will be shared, the input/output contract, capacity semantics, and how much clarification time is available.

A recent Senior SWE process ran as three rounds: one coding round, one system-design round, and a behavioral conversation with the hiring manager. The coding round was a single cache-design problem with a harder extension, and the design prompt was an open-ended large-scale conversational AI product. Be ready to reason about scaling, latency, and serving infrastructure for AI systems in the design round, and treat the hiring-manager slot as a focused conversation on past experience and working style.

description: Reddit's loop runs on a small, slowly-rotating bank of company-specific coding prompts (Tennis Scoring, Report Chain, Chat Message Merge) paired with product-flavored system-design rounds (Game Leaderboard, Live Chat, Notification System). The bar is high on clean OOD and crisp clarification — multi-part prompts are routinely under-scoped on purpose, and rounds end without finishing all parts. Ads and ML Platform orgs add a hiring-manager domain round on top of the standard loop; recent cohorts also report aggressive down-leveling and long team-match limbo after a passing loop.

questions.title: Tennis Match Scoring
questions.overview: Multi-part object-oriented design problem modeling a tennis match. Implement point / game / set / match scoring rules, then extend to best-of-three / best-of-five formats and run-time queries. The most common Reddit phone-screen prompt.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Standard SWE / MLE loop

1. **Recruiter screen** — short call covering background, comp expectations, and target org (Ads, ML Platform, Subreddit infra, etc.). Reddit is fully remote in the US, which the recruiter will usually flag.
2. **Phone screen (60 min)** — one coding problem from the company-specific bank (Tennis, Report Chain, Chat Merge, or a rate-limiter variant). Conducted on CodeSignal with a video call; the interviewer expects clarification + OOD before any code is written. MLE candidates instead get a Jupyter EDA + model-training live coding (post-category CTR).
3. **Onsite / virtual onsite (4–5 rounds)** — typically:
   - 1 coding round (often a multi-part variant of a screen-bank prompt)
   - 1–2 system-design rounds (Game Leaderboard, Live Chat, Notification, Job Scheduler, or an ML-flavored Feature Store / Post-Comment Ranking for ML roles)
   - 1 hiring-manager round (domain-heavy for Ads / ML Platform — see [[hiring-manager-domain-depth]])
   - 1 cross-functional / PM-XFN behavioral
   - Occasionally a product-sense round ("improve Reddit onboarding")
4. **Recruiter wrap + team match** — even a clean loop is gated on team-match. Candidates routinely sit 4–8 weeks in this stage; multiple candidates have been ghosted at this step despite positive interviewer feedback.

## Timeline expectations

- Phone screen → onsite scheduling: 1–3 weeks.
- Onsite → verdict: 1–2 weeks.
- Verdict → team match: 2–8 weeks, frequently inconclusive.
- Cooldown after a reject: **12 months** (confirmed with recruiters).

## Pipeline friction patterns

- Down-leveling is common: staff candidates being moved to senior, senior to mid, sometimes mid-loop. The recruiter usually frames it as "no open headcount at your level."
- A subset of candidates report passing all technical rounds, getting positive cross-functional feedback, and still being soft-rejected after HM — particularly in Ads, where the HM round drills role-specific ad-tech depth that generic SWE prep does not cover.
- The product is fully remote, but Bay Area / NYC team match still tends to clear faster.

## MLE final-loop detail

Recent MLE loops follow a consistent shape: an ML **case-study phone screen** (live Jupyter EDA plus model training on a post-engagement dataset, sometimes with deliberately dirty data — missing values, ~20% positive-class imbalance), then a four-round onsite:

1. **ML Fundamentals** — verbal deep-dive, e.g. how you would build a CVR (conversion-rate) model end to end.
2. **ML System Design** — heavy on inference and feature serving (feature store, online/offline parity, serving SLOs).
3. **Coding** — a bank prompt (e.g. Billing Status) or a backend/protocol implementation.
4. **Hiring-manager BQ** — standard behavioral plus domain depth.

A distinct **"Backend Coding"** round also appears, which recruiters explicitly flag as different from the usual algorithmic screen: implement a small networked service — e.g. a simplified memcached-style TCP key-value server with byte-count-framed `get` / `set` — rather than solve a LeetCode-style problem.

## Fast team-match variant (July 2026)

The long team-match tail is not universal. A recent SWE loop moved into team match the day after the onsite, completed matching within one week, and proceeded directly to an offer. Treat the 2–8 week range as planning guidance rather than a mandatory delay; recruiter responsiveness and an immediately available team can compress the final stage substantially.

## General-pool MLE transition (September 2026)

A team-specific MLE application can move into general-pool hiring after the technical screen when the original opening disappears. One such loop scheduled four virtual rounds of about one hour each: ML Fundamentals, coding, ML system design, and hiring manager. The fundamentals interview focused on ranking despite the candidate's initial generative-AI team application. After an unsuccessful first onsite round, the recruiter canceled the three remaining rounds. Confirm the current hiring pool and expected technical domain when the position changes; completing the phone screen does not guarantee that every scheduled onsite round will take place.

## Recent loop shapes (November 2026)

- A recent virtual onsite ran four rounds: hiring-manager BQ, an **agentic design** round (design an agent over a data warehouse), the backend protocol coding round, and an ML system-improvement design (diagnose an existing prediction service, then redesign it). Three hire votes plus one soft no on design still ended in a reject, so treat every design round as must-pass.
- Android phone screens spend the first 15–20 minutes on a project deep dive with platform questions (Kotlin coroutines, `suspend`), leaving roughly 25 minutes for a bank coding prompt.

description: Adobe has no single company-wide loop: each hiring team defines its own rounds, so a 'coding' interview can turn into system design and an ML screen can mean implementing an algorithm from scratch. Staff loops lean heavily on system design and operational maturity, while MLE loops range from traditional ML to LLM serving and GPU performance.

questions.title: MLE Phone Screen: ML Fundamentals & Resume Project Deep-Dive
questions.overview: Traditional-ML leaning knowledge questions (data leakage, missing data, linear vs. logistic regression losses, MSE vs. MAE) plus a deep dive into two resume projects with ML follow-ups interleaved (recommendation ground truth, evaluation metrics, batch normalization, LLM fine-tuning, applications of research work).

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Adobe does not run a single company-wide interview process. **The loop is defined by the hiring team**, so the number of rounds, their order, and even what a "coding round" means vary from one position to another. Treat whatever your recruiter or team tells you as the source of truth, and ask explicitly what each round covers.

## Typical shapes

**MLE phone screen.** Usually one technical screen before anything else. Some teams schedule it directly, with no recruiter call first. Formats seen:

- Resume deep dive on one or two projects, with ML fundamentals woven in as follow-ups, plus a coding problem that must actually run against a test suite (about 20 test cases).
- Traditional-ML knowledge questions plus a coding portion that is a **from-scratch ML implementation** (e.g. K-Means) rather than a LeetCode problem.
- Two LeetCode-style coding problems back to back.

**MLE fundamentals round.** A dedicated verbal round can go very deep on transformers, KV cache, GPU performance, inference serving, mixed precision, and LLM alignment/evaluation.

**Staff-level SWE onsite.** Four rounds in person at headquarters:

1. A round scheduled as coding that is mostly a **system design** problem, followed by a couple of quick verbal coding questions.
2. An **SRE / operational** round: components, deployment, SLO/SLI/SLA, multi-region, disaster recovery.
3. A **senior system design** round with the most senior interviewer, which pivots into Linux / OS questions and a free-form probe of every technology on your resume — a test of breadth and depth.
4. A **hiring manager** behavioral round (often the org's senior leader), with Q&A about what the team needs.

Some positions **do not require team match** — you interview directly for the team.

**Leadership interviews.** Some loops include leadership rounds where the interviewer opens by saying there will be no technical discussion, and focuses on trust and working style.

## Leveling signals

- At staff level the emphasis shifts strongly to system design and operational maturity; the coding questions in a staff onsite can be answered verbally in a few minutes, while design discussion fills the round.
- Operational excellence (on-call, SLOs, disaster recovery) is an explicit hiring criterion on some infrastructure-facing teams.

## Timeline and communication

- An intern process can run about **one month** end to end.
- Rejections can arrive around **two weeks** after the final round.
- Recruiters sometimes go quiet after an onsite — often because the team is still interviewing other candidates for the same position. A week of silence is not necessarily a rejection.

## Five-round SWE onsite (2026)

Some SWE loops run five one-hour rounds at a noticeably **slow, relaxed pace**. In some rounds, conversation takes up nearly half the hour.

1. **Coding + resume deep dive**: about 15 minutes on one resume project (what exactly you owned), then a classic tree problem. The interviewer probes which assumptions your solution depends on.
2. **Coding**: a classic in-place array problem. You hand-trace a sample before coding, then test edge cases.
3. **Object-oriented / code design**: a short warm-up, then most of the hour on interface design, extensibility and how responsibilities are divided. This round separates candidates more than the algorithm rounds do.
4. **Design**: architecture and API design (for example, product localization) rather than distributed-systems scale. Don't prepare only for distributed-system designs.
5. **Manager chat**: no code, mostly a fit check.

Problems run medium or easier, and solving them only gets you a pass. What separates candidates is explaining the conditions under which your solution holds, and clear thinking about object-oriented design.

description: NVIDIA interviews are highly team-specific and much less LeetCode-bank-driven than most large tech loops. System Software, Linux, Tegra, DGX AI infra, and Deep Learning roles lean toward engineering scenarios: C/C++ debugging, graph validation, GPU / inference fundamentals, small utility coding, and project deep dives; some design and product-facing AI roles add system-design or technical-marketing discussions.

questions.title: FP32 Tensor to Int8 Quantization
questions.overview: Given an FP32 tensor and a floating-point scale, convert the tensor to INT8. Follow-ups add asymmetric quantization with zero point and ask how scale / zero point should change when the input distribution is not symmetric.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
NVIDIA loops vary sharply by team. A common full-time SWE / System Software path is:

1. Recruiter or HM screen.
2. One 45-90 minute technical phone screen.
3. Virtual onsite with 4-6 rounds, usually split across one or two days.
4. Reference checks before final written offer for some teams.

The strongest recent signal is that many teams skip standard LeetCode and instead ask small engineering tasks wrapped in domain context. Even HM rounds can include a short coding or debugging exercise. A typical technical round starts with 10-15 minutes of resume or project discussion, then a 15-30 minute task.

Some loops move extremely fast when the background match is strong: HM outreach can skip phone screen and go directly to VO, with verbal offer and reference request within the same week. Other teams reschedule heavily or go silent after positive-looking rounds. Recruiter guidance is inconsistent; rely on the job description and the team's domain more than on generic NVIDIA tags.

Recent senior / specialist loops show even wider variance. A first technical screen can be only a 45-minute CV and project deep dive, followed by HM discussion and then 4-5 coding rounds; a data-engineering onsite can stretch to roughly nine one-hour conversations across technical assessment, project deep dive, system design, culture fit, and recruiter closeout.

For a team-hired fall distributed-backend internship, both interviews were scheduled together soon after outreach. One round split time between a resume-project deep dive and completing Java object-oriented code under business rules; the other was entirely coding, combining a short stack exercise with an interval-style problem and a trade-off discussion.

Team-defined loops can be much less standardized. One SWE process consisted of two interviews, each combining project discussion with about 30 minutes of pseudocode-friendly problem solving, while a senior autonomous-vehicle integration process scheduled four technical conversations in two-round batches. Recruiters may be unable to describe the total round count or content in advance.

In September 2026, a Research Intern interview used a 45-minute discussion format: about 10 minutes of mutual introductions, about 20 minutes on one research project, and subsequent discussion of daily research practice. The full internship loop and the placement of this conversation within it are unspecified.

As of late 2026, some full-time teams compress the onsite to three rounds after a single phone screen: a director-led behavioral round that pivots into a deep dive across the current and earlier roles, a practical coding round on a live HackerRank virtual machine, and an in-person round combining project discussion with one easy algorithm problem. Decisions in this compressed format can arrive within three days.

New-grad hardware verification loops run longer and more structured. A representative end-to-end path took about eight weeks: recruiter outreach the day after applying, a first technical interview about two weeks later, a second technical interview the following week, then a two-round virtual panel and a three-round in-person panel spread over roughly a week. Positive feedback, verbal offer, and written offer followed over the next two weeks.

As of late 2026, some senior SWE infrastructure loops run as a long ladder: a single coding phone screen, then a stage with two coding rounds, then three infrastructure system-design rounds plus a bar-raiser or director conversation. A further in-person stage can follow within days, with flights booked for the next day: three 45-minute conversations covering a hiring-manager behavioral round, a project deep dive with a senior team engineer, and a senior-manager chat. Even after that, more interviews may still be pending, and the senior-manager conversation can openly discuss the shortlist and level fit — be ready for a down-leveling discussion. Scheduling between stages can be slow; two weeks between a phone screen and the next round is not unusual.

For senior SWE roles, the first round may be led by a principal engineer: a short team introduction, then a resume walkthrough that turns into a design deep dive on systems you built. Past work on authentication (OAuth) or job scheduling gets probed for correctness guarantees: exactly-once execution, preventing duplicate work across executors, and error handling with fallback paths.

Coding rounds bias toward multi-level CodeSignal-style problems (banking system, in-memory database, mining-block knapsack, crypto order management) over canonical LeetCode; bring your own scaffolding because interviewers often hand you a blank file with no class structure or tests. The volume of code is the difficulty; each level is straightforward in isolation but few finish all four in 70 minutes without prior practice. briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Pipeline

Coinbase runs one of the longest pre-onsite funnels in this bank. A typical SWE loop runs:

1. **AI recruiter screen** (~15 min). An LLM-driven voice/chat interview that probes the resume, asks follow-ups, and scores against the JD. Treat it like a real recruiter screen, not a formality — short hard cap and the bot will dig into vague answers.
2. **Pre-screen assessments** — sent as a single email, typically all three:
   - **Criteria Cognitive Aptitude Test (CCAT)**: 50 questions in 15 minutes. Mix of basic arithmetic, GRE-style vocabulary / sentence completion, and visual pattern puzzles. Cannot revisit answers. Only ~1% finish.
   - **Culture / Personality Assessment**: ~150–200 Likert items ("strongly disagree → strongly agree"). Untimed. The same construct is asked multiple ways — internal consistency matters.
   - **CodeSignal OA**: 70 min, see Tooling briefing.
3. **Recruiter call** (~30 min). Process walk-through, salary expectations, why-Coinbase.
4. **Team match**. Even strong loop scores route through TM before onsite is scheduled; weeks of silence here are common and several candidates have washed out at this stage without feedback.
5. **Virtual onsite** (4 rounds, often spread across multiple days):
   - **Coding 1** — multi-level problem (mining block, food delivery, NFT generation, parse log, crypto order)
   - **Coding 2 / Domain** — another multi-level problem (filter+pagination, crypto order management); sometimes the "Domain" round is just more coding rather than a separate domain interview
   - **System Design** — Coinbase Explore (real-time price), crypto brokerage, or wallet/ledger history
   - **Hiring Manager / Behavioral** — project deep-dive + standard BQ; AI-usage questions are now common
6. **Decision** — recruiter typically follows up 2–10 business days later. Detailed feedback is not provided on rejection.

## Calendar time

Fastest reported path is recruiter → onsite in ~2 weeks (MLE loops have been pushed when a team has a hard year-end HC deadline). The typical experience is 4–8 weeks end-to-end, dragged out by team match. Candidates report week-plus gaps with no signal between every two stages.

## Variants by track

- **Frontend**: VO replaces the standard 4-round set with **Tech Execution** (component build with unit tests), **Foundation** (manager BQ), **Domain** (build a more substantial component to a mockup), and **System Design** (frontend architecture). See the Track Variants briefing.
- **MLE**: OA is a ML-flavored CodeSignal (6 MCQ + 1 NN forward-pass calculation + 3 coding incl. classical-ML implementations). VO is 3 rounds: ML coding + SQL, BQ, and Jupyter pair-programming on a messy classification dataset.
- **Senior / Staff**: an additional **Project Presentation** round with slides has been added for some loops in 2026.

## Technical phone screen (2026 update)

As of late 2026, some IC4 referral loops insert a technical phone screen between the recruiter contact and the onsite. It draws from the onsite coding pool rather than a separate LeetCode-style bank — the mining-block problem has appeared here in its full multi-part form — so prepare the onsite coding rotation before the first technical call, not after. Referral-to-recruiter contact can still take ~3 weeks.

## Onsite lineup (late 2026)

A late-2026 onsite ran four rounds in this order:

- **Coding Assessment** — the multi-step ledger / bank system, with steps unlocked progressively and no ready-made tests (you write your own).
- **AI Domain Knowledge** — an AI-assisted conversation over a bug-laden code repo rather than a discrete coding task.
- **System Design** — crypto brokerage.
- **Hiring Manager** — conflict, toughest problem, and "how would you redesign a past system" prompts, then reverse Q&A.

The OA in the same loop was the AI-assisted Flappy Bird strategy problem, scored out of 600 with the in-IDE AI assistant enabled.

description: The Trade Desk's interviews favor practical, simulation-style engineering over puzzle solving, from a levels-based CodeSignal assessment to live rounds drawn from a fixed internal question bank. System design is grounded in its ad-bidding business, where serving read-heavy data at extremely low latency across regions is the central concern.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Typical pipeline (software engineer)

1. **Application.** Cold applications without a referral do get responses.
2. **Online assessment.** A four-level CodeSignal problem (see *Online Assessment & Tooling*).
3. **Recruiter / HR call.** Short and light: salary expectations, what the loop covers, and an introduction to the company.
4. **Phone screen.** Some loops skip it and go straight from the OA to the onsite. When it happens, it can be a 90-minute call (about 30 minutes of behavioral questions, then 60 minutes on one multi-phase coding problem) or a shorter coding-only call.
5. **Onsite.** Usually three to four rounds in one day, or spread over two days.
6. **Decision.** Usually within about a week, sometimes with written feedback.

## Senior onsite shapes

- **Shape A (four rounds):** a 75-minute hiring-manager round combining behavioral questions and a product system design; a 60-minute domain system design about low-latency data for bidding; a 60-minute coding round that opens with about 10 minutes of behavioral questions and requires running code; and a whiteboard coding round **in the office**.
- **Shape B (one day, three rounds plus HM):** two system designs (a step-by-step read-heavy scenario, and the large-dataset / high-QPS read design) and one coding round, plus a hiring-manager conversation about past projects.
- Recruiters have also floated flying the candidate to the team's city for an in-person onsite with two coding and two design rounds.

## Question bank

Interviewers pick from a **fixed internal question bank**. Candidates have watched an interviewer open the bank and select the problem on the spot. Problems repeat across candidates, but any given loop can still be mostly new: one senior APAC candidate prepared earlier problems (string compression, caches) and saw none of them.

## Recruiting experience

Recruiter responsiveness is uneven. Candidates describe recruiters who only reply on their own schedule, prep calls scheduled at the last minute, and results promised in 24–48 hours that arrived about a week later. Follow up in writing and keep your own timeline notes.

description: Nextdoor is a neighborhood-based social network, and its interviews stay close to that product: feeds, posts, comments, and the metrics behind them. The process opens with an unusually heavy two-round phone screen, and decisions are terse and opaque, so polish and speed count even on familiar problems.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Pipeline

1. **Recruiter call.** Many candidates are approached by a recruiter on LinkedIn. This call is a real behavioral screen, not a formality.
2. **Phone screen: two rounds.** Nextdoor's phone screen is two back-to-back technical rounds, not one. Senior generalist SWE candidates get two phone screens as well. The pairing depends on the role:
   - **SWE (backend / generalist):** one coding round plus one system design round, or two coding rounds.
   - **MLE:** one coding round plus one ML coding round. One MLE session ran about 2.5 hours in total, with a 30-minute break between rounds.
   - **Mobile (iOS):** one easy data-structures round plus a debugging round on an existing UIKit project.
   - **Analytics Engineer:** SQL only, no Python, built around product metrics and dashboards.
3. **Virtual onsite.** Candidates who pass the phone screen move to a virtual onsite.

## Small, stable problem pool

Most phone-screen problems repeat. Candidates who prepared the entire known pool, including follow-ups, saw nothing new. The coding pool includes:

- weekday time-interval merging (by far the most common)
- in-memory database with transactions / savepoints
- comparing / sorting version numbers
- flattening a nested comment tree
- photo feed grouping
- a gift-assignment problem
- a newer, harder transaction/lock state-machine problem

Common system design prompts are the Nextdoor neighborhood newsfeed and a job scheduler that has to scale by 100x.

The standard advice: prepare every problem in the pool, with follow-ups, rather than gambling on the odds.

The pool is not fully closed. As of late 2026, a Senior SWE coding screen drew a problem outside the known list: parse a stream of file-system entries and build a tree of nodes with parent/child links, where a child can arrive before its parent. The interviewer supplies sample input; you wire it into your own solution class and run the test cases yourself. The system design round in the same screen was still the neighborhood newsfeed.

description: Tesla interviews are highly team-specific: Autopilot, Optimus, Dojo, data engineering, infotainment, and factory-software teams each run their own practical technical screens. The common pattern is a fast transition from resume/project discussion into runnable code, with interviewers pushing for optimality, clean implementation style, and concrete ownership of past technical decisions.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Tesla loops are less standardized than big-tech committee-driven pipelines. The first human touch is often a recruiter or sourcer screen that collects role fit, project background, relocation, competing-offer, and team-preference information. For interns this screen can be unusually detailed and may ask about favorite projects and personal qualities before a technical interviewer is assigned.

The first technical round is usually 45 minutes. Most teams spend 10-20 minutes on resume or project background, then move into one compact coding, debugging, data, or design-implementation task. Candidates should expect the code to run in CoderPad or an equivalent live environment, including imports, tests, and edge cases. Several interviewers skip extended small talk and start coding quickly.

Follow-up rounds vary by team. SWE and intern loops often run two technical interviews, where the second round may combine coding with team fit. Senior full-time loops can move to an in-person or virtual onsite of four 45-minute rounds: project deep dive, behavioral / manager conversation, and two system-design or technical-design rounds. Onsite invite emails may list interviewer names and titles without labeling which round is system design, past experience, or behavioral.

Decision speed is relatively fast: candidates commonly see next-round movement in a few days and rejections within a week. The flip side is that a single short round has little recovery time; when a deep dive drifts away from the candidate's own work, candidates need to steer the conversation back to decisions they actually owned.

Official candidate guidance reinforces the practical shape of these loops: review the role description, tailor the resume to the position, prepare concrete interview examples, and expect follow-up contact rather than assuming every cycle moves at the same pace.

A compact general SWE screen variant allocates roughly 25 of 45 minutes to behavioral, resume, and project discussion, leaving the balance for an open-ended API implementation. Requirement clarification is part of the coding signal rather than setup supplied by the interviewer.

A newer general SWE onsite variant uses five segments rather than a uniform four-round loop. Behavioral discussion is embedded before technical work in multiple segments, alongside two coding rounds, two product-system design rounds, and one behavioral-only conversation. Treat the invitation as team-specific and prepare to switch quickly between experience stories, implementation, and architecture.

A senior SDE infrastructure loop in Tesla AI used two coding phone screens before an in-person Palo Alto onsite. Five formal onsite interviews and a team lunch were scheduled, then a hiring-manager round was added, bringing the formal interview count to six. The day lasted roughly seven hours, with the decisive manager conversation at the end. This team controlled its own process and interview content.

As of September 2026, a backend hiring process also used an approximately 15-minute AI recruiter screen. Its recruiter email offered a traditional screening alternative on request. The automated option and the ability to switch should be treated as specific to that process.

A November 2026 infrastructure loop ran seven interviews end to end: two phone screens (one behavioral, one coding), then four onsite rounds — a single-project deep dive, a behavioral round, a hiring-manager round of rapid-fire infrastructure fundamentals, and a round from another org made up of technology-opinion questions. Recruiting then added an extra round. It was announced as behavioral, focused on working under high pressure, but in practice it was a CDN system design with no behavioral questions. Treat the stated purpose of an add-on round as a hint, not a guarantee, and be ready for design. The rejection came three days after the last round. Headcount can also pause and reopen mid-process: a candidate told after the phone screen that the role was filled may be invited back days later when a new opening is created.

briefings.body:
## Pipeline

1. **Online assessment (HackerRank)** — usually two coding problems in 65–75 minutes. One version had three problems in 60 minutes. Most candidates rate the problems LeetCode easy to medium.
2. **Phone screen / technical screen** — one coding problem. The two most common are function-signature matching with variadic arguments and word / phrase search over documents; Sudoku validation and solving also appears.
3. **Virtual onsite** — typically three to four rounds:
   - two coding rounds, drawn from a small recurring pool (tail -n, a monster-battle problem, word / phrase search, a random queue, Sudoku, sensor and loading-dock problems);
   - one or two system-design rounds (news feed / RSS / podcast publishing, temporary email service, TinyURL);
   - a values / hiring-manager behavioral round.
4. **Specialty round** — infrastructure teams such as Cloud Traffic add a fast Linux, networking and container fundamentals round.

## Timing

- After a passing OA, HR can reach out the next day; one virtual onsite was scheduled three weeks later.
- Communication after the onsite is uneven. Several candidates were ghosted after the onsite or waited a long time for results, especially during the IBM transition.

## What the pool looks like

The question pool is small and repeats heavily: candidates repeatedly describe most onsite problems as well-known recurring problems. Preparing the recurring problems thoroughly — including their follow-ups — gives the best return. Interviewers sometimes improvise extra follow-ups if you finish early.

## Feedback and reapplication

Recruiters may share per-round outcomes. One Senior II candidate learned both coding rounds passed while both design rounds narrowly failed, and was told they could reapply earlier than the usual waiting period.

## Common shapes

Akuna runs different loops by track. Quant trading and quant research intern paths can start with multiple online assessments: mental arithmetic and sequence recognition, probability and expected-value betting, then a harder market-making or video assessment. Developer and quantitative developer tracks usually start with a coding OA, then a technical phone or virtual onsite.

## Quant tracks

Trading-facing tracks reward speed before depth. Candidates see short windows, many small questions, and answer formats that require fast arithmetic rather than long derivations. The Sneak Peek Week track has appeared as a replacement for a standard trading internship opening, with three OAs and a superday after the online rounds.

## Developer tracks

SWE, C++ developer, and QD/QS loops are more implementation-heavy. Recent samples include HackerRank coding, C++ object-pool debugging, exchange order matching, streaming statistics, and rate-limit class design. The interviewer may also revisit the candidate's OA and ask follow-up questions rather than introduce a completely new prompt.

## Recent shifts (late 2026)

- Quant Research intern: OA1 is followed by a separate OA2, and the phone screen can come after a long wait. The phone screen pairs a short research conversation with two live coding tasks on HackerRank (an ML-optimization implementation and a probability question turned into code).
- Junior Quant Researcher: the OA is three LeetCode-style problems at roughly medium-to-easy difficulty, mixing hashmap counting, BFS, and grid DP.
- Quant Developer (Shanghai): the OA can be a single 24-hour take-home that asks for a complete order-matching system rather than a set of short algorithm problems.
