briefings.title: Loop Structure and Team Variation
briefings.body:
eBay interview structure varies substantially by team. One senior candidate completed a recruiter screen, a technical coding challenge, and a manager behavioral conversation. Another process scheduled two consecutive screening sessions for coding and hiring-manager discussion. A data-infrastructure candidate had separate technical and system-design screens before the later process. The number of preliminary interviews varies with the hiring process.

Onsite loops can also differ. An MTS1 candidate described system design, two coding rounds, and a manager session that itself included a design problem. Another MTS loop contained system design, conventional coding, behavioral discussion, and AI-assisted coding. A more recent onsite instead used shopping-cart implementation, data-structure discussion, shopping-search design, and behavioral questions, without a conventional LeetCode-style task.

Internship hiring includes practical formats as well. One candidate encountered a class implementation and testing exercise, then a second session mixing infrastructure knowledge, debugging, and regular expressions. The candidate described spending substantial time understanding the specification and debugging the class. This path cannot be inferred from the standard four-question CodeSignal OA described by a different internship candidate.

SDE-2 interviews have included a coding round, a product-design discussion, and a manager design session with detailed aggregation follow-ups. Behavioral questions can appear within those technical rounds, including motivation for joining eBay and examples of conflict. A hiring-manager label therefore does not necessarily mean that the entire session is nontechnical.

Candidates also describe variation in recruiter follow-through. Some received further scheduling shortly after a screen, while another senior candidate did not receive a clear outcome after several rounds. One MTS candidate was told both that the position had been filled and that coding had not met the level expectation. These are individual process outcomes, not a fixed response-time or progression policy. The most useful organizing principle is the hiring team and the actual round instructions, because the observed sequences and formats differ materially.

An applied-scientist loop (Berlin office) ran six rounds, including a recruiter conversation about the package and the three-day return-to-office requirement; a coding / software-engineering round; a statistics / ML / AI round; an ML / AI system design and big-data round; and an eBay DNA / product / business-reasoning round with the hiring manager. Nearly every round turned into a project deep dive, and the content differed substantially from the recruiter's preparation instructions. After the full loop the position was placed on hold and cancelled a month later, so a completed loop does not guarantee that the headcount is still open.

A recent phone screen consisted of one algorithm problem with a short verbal follow-up, after which the remaining time went to résumé and experience questions.

A backend virtual onsite (late 2026) ran three rounds split across two days: a coding round that opened with roughly 30 minutes of technical questions (cryptography, Spring Boot, Kubernetes) before the problem, a system-design round, and a hiring-manager conversation that introduced the team and then moved to behavioral questions. The rejection arrived about two weeks later, with the recruiter offering to reach out about similar openings.

An Applied Researcher 2 loop had four rounds: ML breadth (fundamentals from bias–variance through transformers and KV cache), coding (two problems), a hiring-manager behavioral round on the most challenging project, and a director round combining behavioral questions with a résumé deep dive.

description: xAI's loop is built around speed and founder-style intensity: a single 15-minute video screen often gates the entire pipeline, the take-home assumes you will use Cursor / Claude Code, and onsite rounds run in person in Palo Alto with offers decided minutes after the final round. Bars are calibrated less for algorithmic novelty than for raw shipping velocity, low-level systems instincts (concurrency, GPU/inference, distributed numerics), and willingness to work 60–100 hour weeks RTO5.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Pipeline

A typical xAI loop runs:

1. **Recruiter / coordinator outreach** (LinkedIn, cold email, or sourcer relay). Often skips a formal HR screen — the 15-min tech screen is itself the first real signal.
2. **15-minute video screen.** The single most common stage. Self-intro + most-challenging project + why xAI; some screens tack on a basic CS verbal question (process vs thread, GIL, multi-threading) and an increasing number now insert a short live coding question into the same 15 minutes.
3. **4-hour take-home** (CodeSignal, Exceptional Engineer / Backend Specialist / Junior SWE tracks). Covered separately under the take-home briefing.
4. **Phone-screen rounds.** Either a single 45-minute coding round or a triple (back-to-back, same week) of 45-minute rounds mixing coding, ML coding, and project deep-dive. Recruiter typically schedules all three in one week with 24-hour turnaround between rounds.
5. **Onsite (Palo Alto, in-person).** Two to three rounds, usually 1×SD + 1–2×coding, plus a hiring-manager / project deep-dive. Flights and ground transport reimbursed.
6. **Founder / sell call.** For Exceptional-Engineer and senior tracks; final confirmation and offer pitch.

## Calendar time

A fast path goes outreach → onsite in ~10 days; manager-first variants can run a 30-minute manager conversation before a longer technical screen. Verdicts are commonly delivered within 1–24 hours of each round. The full loop including take-home and onsite frequently closes in under three weeks. Conversely, take-home submissions sometimes sit untouched for a week before a silent rejection — turnaround at this stage is the loop's biggest variance.

## Verdict signals

- Reject emails are blunt and offer no feedback.
- Recruiters move fast on hires and slow on rejects; silence past 48 hours after a round is usually a soft no.
- A surprisingly large share of candidates report being cut at the 15-minute screen with no obvious failure mode ("answered everything, secured a verbal yes from the interviewer, rejected one hour later"). Treat the 15-minute round as a gating round, not a formality.

## Exceptional SWE new-graduate variant (2026 Q3)

The new-graduate Exceptional SWE track can replace the short general screen with a **30-minute system-design technical screen and no coding**. The onsite then centers on one extended design-and-build exercise: 30 minutes of whiteboarding, 90 minutes of implementation, and a 30-minute wrap-up and demo. This format places system-design reasoning ahead of standalone algorithm drills. A rejection can be delivered immediately after the onsite, followed by a six-month cooldown before reapplying.

## Non-AI product-engineering roles (2026 Q4)

Traditional product-engineering roles outside the AI org run a different, shorter loop:

1. **Recruiter call.** Recruiters for these roles know the team well and can describe its scope in detail.
2. **Team-lead conversation.** A strong TL chat can skip the phone screen entirely and go straight to onsite.
3. **In-person onsite, three rounds:**
   - **Project presentation.** Prepare slides in advance. The audience mixes engineers and PMs who interrupt with questions throughout, and the expectations for depth and detail are higher than at most companies running a similar round.
   - **Coding without running code.** A data-structure design problem built around state transitions, answered in pseudo-code rather than compiled code.
   - **Product system design**, e.g. a scheduled / delayed-tweet feature for X.

No lunch is provided at the onsite (there is no cafeteria). Rejections come by email without feedback, even when the recruiter collected the candidate's feedback on the interviewers beforehand.

One interviewer described the pace as "more startup than a startup", citing a feature about to launch straight to 100% of traffic with no gradual ramp. Expect "how would you ship this safely?" to land differently here than at larger companies, and prepare to reason about rollout risk in system-design answers.

description: Walmart's engineering loop runs through Karat / HackerRank phone screens followed by a three-to-four round virtual or in-person onsite covering coding, system design, behavioral, and an extended Team Fit phase. Coding bars are moderate but heavily weighted toward Java / Spring Boot fluency, and the system-design slot leans toward retail and logistics prompts (membership, delivery, ticketing, sensor ingestion). The Team Fit phase that follows technical approval is unusually long and team-shopping in nature, and is responsible for a meaningful share of loop attrition.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
The Walmart Labs path typically opens with a recruiter screen (10-15 minutes, role + sponsorship + salary expectations) followed by either a Karat-proctored phone screen or a HackerRank online assessment. Karat phone screens run 60 minutes and pack two to three coding problems plus a few Spring Boot / OOD verbal questions. The OA is take-home, 60-90 minutes, with hidden test cases and proctoring that monitors for extra screens.

The onsite is three to four rounds, run virtually or as an in-person hiring event in Sunnyvale or Bentonville. Senior SDE loops are usually a coding round, a system-design round, and a behavioral / HM round; some loops add a project deep-dive or a code-review round. Hiring events compress the same content into a single day with a laptop-based coding round.

After the loop, candidates enter a Team Fit phase that is unique among comparable companies: the recruiter shops the candidate across multiple teams, each running its own one-to-three round Team Fit conversation (BQ-heavy, sometimes an extra coding or design slot). This phase can take four to eight weeks and is a frequent point of attrition even after a strong onsite. Recruiter response latency is also a known frustration — candidates routinely report multi-week silences and ghosting between Team Fit rounds.

Total pipeline length is commonly six to ten weeks for FTE roles; contractor / GenAI contractor pipelines are faster but follow a different track.

By late July 2026, a Bay Area physical hiring event placed roughly a dozen candidates in one venue and rotated each person through HM / behavioral, coding, and system-design rooms. Check-in included a return trip to the parking area for a permit, room changes lacked clear wayfinding, and one transition required recruiter intervention after the candidate waited in the wrong room. Buffers can be tight: the system-design round began about 15 minutes after coding, and the day ran past 1:30 p.m. without a meal break. Arrive early, confirm the complete room sequence at check-in, save the recruiter's phone number, and bring food and water rather than assuming onsite logistics will cover them.

As of fall 2026, Bay Area onsites still follow the three-round coding / system-design / HM-behavioral shape, but the code-review segment can be folded into the tail of the system-design round rather than run as its own slot: after the design discussion, the interviewer hands over a code snippet to review. Budget the last part of the design hour for reading and critiquing code, and keep the design walkthrough tight enough to leave room for it.

An internal referral from another team's manager can skip the screens entirely and go straight to a mid-week onsite of three rounds: an HM conversation on the org's systems plus behavioral prompts, a single coding round, and a second coding round with two shorter problems. Positive informal feedback does not guarantee an offer — rejections can arrive about two weeks after the loop.

briefings.title: Loop Structure and Role Differences
briefings.body:
HRT does not have one assessment format shared across all engineering and research positions. A software-engineering process used a four-question CodeSignal assessment with a 70-minute limit. A quantitative-research process used two C++ exercises in 45 minutes. An internship account described a single 75-minute class-based exercise together with timed games. These are different hiring paths; their question counts and timings should not be combined into one expected test.

Phone interviews also vary. A C++ internship process included two screens before the later interview rounds, while other candidates describe dedicated technical-knowledge screens. A process can move from OA to a first and second technical interview over several weeks. Full completion of an OA does not guarantee further progress: one Algo Dev internship candidate received a rejection despite passing the assessment tests.

The Algo Dev internship onsite can contain four one-hour rounds: programming, data analysis, system design, and mathematics. One candidate attended two sessions in the morning, with two further sessions planned after lunch. The company could end the onsite after the morning results, and that candidate was told at lunch that the remaining sessions would not proceed. The order of the four sessions can differ between candidates.

The programming part of that onsite used an existing C++ codebase, while data analysis used a dataset and notebook-style tools. This breadth matters: the process can test both familiarity with a larger program and practical data exploration. It is not enough to infer the entire onsite format from the first coding assessment.

Interview formats vary by role and over time. A format from an earlier internship cycle should not be treated as a new company-wide process. Use the particular role, assessment invitation, and round description to interpret the timing and sequence. These formats show the range candidates can encounter rather than a single guaranteed company-wide pipeline.

One 2027 new-grad C++ software-engineering process ran a 70-minute, four-question OA followed about a week later by a 30-minute live coding interview. The first two OA problems were short; the last two carried most of the difficulty. A perfect OA score led to the coding interview, but it did not carry the candidate past that round, and the rejection after the interview arrived within a few days.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Round Format
briefings.body:
## Pipeline

- **Recruiter catch-up:** a short (around 15-minute) HR call before the virtual onsite that outlines what each round will cover.
- **Virtual onsite:** a sequence of **45-minute** rounds. Two shapes show up:
  - **Coding-heavy:** two coding rounds plus one system-design round.
  - **Resume + coding + HM:** a round that opens with a resume deep dive and then two coding problems, a second round of several algorithm problems where explaining the approach matters as much as code, and a final **30-minute hiring-manager round**.
- **Hiring-manager round:** behavioral questions built from the projects on your resume. Answers are expected to stay consistent with what the resume says.

## What the coding rounds look like

- Coding rounds often pack **two or three classic problems** into 45 minutes: array search, tree, graph-connectivity, string-parsing, and cache-design problems are all in rotation.
- Some rounds are a single **practical object-design problem** in the payments domain, such as a banking simulator with ranking queries and a scheduling stretch goal.
- Speed is the main differentiator. Candidates who do well on most rounds still get rejected, which suggests a bar set by the strongest candidates in the pool rather than by passing each round.

## Decisions

- Decisions can come quickly after the final round, and a positive-feeling loop is no guarantee of an offer.

description: Zoox runs a remarkably stable loop: a language-trivia plus object-oriented coding phone screen, then an onsite where fast-paced coding sits alongside a hand-calculated math and physics round. Execution speed under tight time limits matters more than novelty, while design and deep-dive rounds shift sharply by team — from robotaxi backend to ML, GPU, and simulation.

Follow-up: make new coaster types and rule changes pluggable without touching the core loop. Usually preceded by ~15-20 minutes of language / OOP trivia.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Pipeline

1. **Recruiter call** (often a LinkedIn reach-out), sometimes followed by a **30-minute hiring-manager call** before the onsite is scheduled.
2. **Phone screen (~60 min, CoderPad):** about 15-20 minutes of language / OOP trivia, then a ~45-minute object-oriented coding problem. The roller-coaster scoring problem dominates; an airline-ticket pricing OOP problem occupies the same slot for some candidates. Some teams use a domain screen instead (SQL for Data Engineering, a research-focused HM screen for 3D simulation).
3. **Onsite (4-6 rounds).** Typical building blocks:
   - **Math & physics** — short hand-calculated questions; present in nearly every loop regardless of role.
   - **Coding** — one hour, often three problems (stock profit with a multi-threading follow-up, y = mx + n, nickname-to-team assignment, moving-vehicle interception), sometimes as many as six rapid-fire questions.
   - **System design** — team-dependent (see Role-Specific Tracks).
   - **Project deep dive + behavioral** with a staff engineer or the hiring manager.
   - **Role-specific round** — ML skills, ML system design, GPU fundamentals, or a programming round that repeats the trivia + roller-coaster format.
4. **Leadership interview** — a 30-minute conversation with a director (self-introduction + deep dive) can follow the onsite.

An onsite described as "in person" may still have most rounds run over Zoom from a conference room.

## Timeline and outcomes

- Phone-screen results can arrive the same afternoon.
- Onsite decisions range from about 7 business days to a month.
- Headcount is a frequent deciding factor: candidates have been stopped after a passed phone screen because the role was filled, and after positive onsite feedback because the director-level step chose another candidate.

## What it feels like

Candidates describe Zoox as a loop where *every* round has to go well — there is no throwaway round. Time pressure is high throughout: coding rounds leave little or no room for debugging, and every solution is expected to come with a Big-O analysis.

## Recent format (late 2026)

In-person onsites may be split across two days. Day one holds only the language trivia + coding round (roller-coaster scoring is still the coding problem). Day two holds the remaining five rounds: math & physics, system design, a cross-functional behavioral interview with someone outside the hiring team, a project retrospective, and a behavior & communication interview with the hiring manager.

description: Expedia Group runs short loops — usually three to four virtual rounds — that pair one or two LeetCode-style coding rounds with design prompts drawn directly from the interviewing team's travel-domain work, such as partner connectivity, payments, and property data. Most rounds open with an Expedia-values question, and behavioral judgment carries as much weight as coding at senior levels.

questions.title: Maximum Hole Area After Removing Prison Bars
questions.overview: A grid is formed by n horizontal and m vertical bars; given the indices of horizontal and vertical bars to remove, return the area of the largest hole after removal. Key subtlety: the given numbers index the bars between cells, not the cells themselves. Sort each direction's removed indices, find the longest run of consecutive removed bars per direction, and multiply the two resulting gap sizes.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Pipeline

Most Expedia Group software loops follow the same shape:

1. **Recruiter call** — logistics, background, and work-authorization check.
2. **OA** (role-dependent) — HackerRank, typically two DSA problems; some pipelines include a prompt-engineering section graded by tests.
3. **Phone / tech screen** (45-60 min) — usually one LeetCode-style coding problem, sometimes followed by a short BQ. For some senior and SDE III roles the screen is instead run by the hiring manager and consists entirely of a team-specific system-design exercise on HackerRank.
4. **Virtual onsite** — three to four rounds, which is short compared with most large tech companies. Typical mixes:
   - Senior SWE: project deep dive + coding + BQ (three rounds), or coding + HM/BQ + coding + system design (four rounds).
   - Coding + system design + operational excellence + HM.
   - Two system-design rounds + one coding + one BQ.
   - MLE: four rounds of past experience plus ML system design, no coding.

Most rounds open with self-introduction and a short Expedia-values behavioral question before the technical portion begins, so effective technical time is shorter than the slot length.

## Timeline and Recruiting Logistics

Scheduling is the least predictable part of the process. Common patterns:

- Recruiters go quiet for one to two weeks between stages; results sometimes arrive only after the candidate emails to ask.
- The gap from phone screen to onsite can stretch to about a month.
- Recruiter handoffs happen mid-process (a new recruiter takes over without notice), and some candidates only discover this after following up.
- Final decisions typically arrive within one to two weeks of the last round.

Follow up proactively if you have not heard back within a week or two.

## Team Matching

Interviews are run by the hiring team, and prompts — especially system design — are often drawn directly from that team's current work (payments, partner connectivity, property data, notifications). Hiring managers sometimes interview on behalf of other teams when their own headcount is full, so an onsite does not always map to the team in the job posting. Some newer ML teams have opened with sizable headcount and a lighter coding bar.

## Work Authorization

Recruiters may screen on visa status after the OA. At least one recruiter required **three years of remaining H-1B time** and declined to move forward otherwise, citing an internal rule rather than a written policy. Candidates on H-1B with limited remaining time should confirm this at the first recruiter call before investing in preparation.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
SIG runs two clearly separated pipelines: one for quantitative roles (Quant Research, Quant Trading, Quant Systematic Trading) and one for software engineers (including C++-heavy developer roles).

### Quant (QR / QT / QST)

1. **Online assessment** — a 17-question timed math and logic test (see the OA briefing). This is the main filter.
2. **Recruiter / HR round** — not purely logistics: expect several verbal probability questions in green-book style (dice, conditional probability, waiting times).
3. **Quant phone interview** — a quant asks technical questions that can span econometrics (deriving OLS and its efficiency condition), probability puzzles, and verbal algorithms questions even when the recruiter says there is no coding.
4. **Data task** — a multi-day take-home on a trading dataset (three days, any language), followed by a virtual review with two quants, one hour each.
5. **Onsite** — the final round, which candidates describe as including coding and data analysis.

A typical PhD-level timeline: OA in November, recruiter round late December, quant phone early January, data task at the end of January, review in mid-February. For QR internships, the round after the OA is a one-hour Zoom with three probability questions.

A more recent QR intern pipeline ran: OA → HR call (two or three easy probability questions) → one-hour phone screen (algorithms, probability, linear regression, a brainteaser) → HR call introducing the data task → multi-day data project → two-round data interview (data processing, then strategy) → onsite. The data interview is a real filter: intern candidates have been cut there after clearing the phone screen.

### Software Engineering

1. **Recruiter call** — resume walk-through and motivation ("why this role", "what does it mean to you").
2. **Phone screen** — live coding on CodeSignal. The most common prompt is a movie-catalog filter class; C++ roles instead get a container-implementation screen (implement `std::vector`) and sometimes a second 90-minute C++ screen.
3. **Virtual onsite** — two or three one-hour rounds: an algorithm round (ticker extraction from headlines), an OOD round (grocery checkout with inventory and live profit), and sometimes a resume deep dive.
4. **Team-fit onsite** — back-to-back conversations with several teams (30–45 minutes each, no breaks), virtual or at the Philadelphia office, followed by recruiter questions on compensation, location, team preference, and other deadlines.
5. **Offer** — verbal offer by email, then an offer call with the recruiter, future manager, and tech lead.

One successful SWE timeline ran about six weeks end to end: application in late April, phone screen invite within a week, recruiter call, CodeSignal screen, virtual onsite, positive feedback with a request for a team-fit onsite, team-fit day, verbal offer the next day, and an offer call within a week.

### Pacing and communication

- Scheduling after a recruiter reach-out moves quickly; recruiters often book the feedback call at the same time as the interview.
- Some candidates find recruiter communication impersonal — emails without human replies, a missed recruiter call followed directly by an onsite invite. Rejections can arrive within a week, sometimes after a nudge.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
### Pipeline

1. **Recruiter call** (about 30 minutes, Google Meet). Recruiters often reach out first, for example on LinkedIn. The call covers work authorization, your recent work, the culture you want, and a product demo.
2. **Online assessment** (some pipelines). A 90-minute CodeSignal industry coding assessment with four gated levels; a level unlocks only after the previous one passes.
3. **Phone screen** (about 60 minutes). One coding problem, sometimes a main problem plus a follow-up problem. Problems lean toward implementation-heavy simulation (board games, scheduling across workers, timed networks) and classic data-structure problems. The ML phone screen is described by recruiters as standard data structures and algorithms.
4. **Onsite** (in person at the San Francisco office for some candidates). One ML-track onsite contained:
   - **ML Design** — 60 minutes.
   - **AI Assignment** — 75 minutes, building a small system with an AI coding assistant.
   - **Coding** — 60 minutes, a multi-part problem where finishing every part is not required.

### Timeline and outcomes

- Rejections after a phone screen can arrive as quickly as the next day.
- Feedback is typically not shared after an onsite rejection.
- Passing a phone screen does not guarantee moving forward: when a team's headcount fills during the wait, recruiters try to match the candidate with other teams, which can take weeks.

### What decides the phone screen

Clean, finished code on every part of the problem matters. Candidates who covered only part of the required behavior (for example, one of several directions or cases) were rejected, and even candidates with a working solution have been turned down, so communication, testing, and handling follow-up discussion all count.

### Phone screen notes (2026 Q4)

- Tech-lead-manager candidates also start with a coding phone screen; the timed-train-network problem has appeared there.
- Phone screens can mix the coding problem with project questions, so manage time to leave room for the follow-up discussion.
- Some interviewers ask which topic area you want (for example graphs) and then pick the problem themselves, which may not match the area you named. Design-flavored prompts such as a chess backend can be narrowed mid-round to one concrete function, so confirm scope before writing scaffolding.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Atlassian screens can enter through either Karat-style interviews or company-run HackerRank / interviewer-led screens. A common experienced-hire path is recruiter contact, technical screen, then a virtual onsite split across coding, system design or craft, and two behavioral rounds. Some candidates describe the onsite as separable across days; when the first coding round fails, the remaining system-design rounds may not continue. MLE / MLSE loops often add a first-stage project or ML-design discussion, then a second stage with backend coding, ML coding, and ML system design, followed by values and management rounds.

Phone screens are often compressed: 45 minutes can include introduction, about 20 minutes of coding, and about 15 minutes of design. Karat formats vary, but candidates repeatedly see a system discussion plus two coding questions. Time control matters because the coding portion can be short even when the total interview is one hour.

Scheduling and feedback can be uneven. Some rounds move within one or two days, while later values / management, team match, HC, or waitlist phases can stretch for weeks. Candidates also mention pauses in process and recruiter silence around hiring slowdowns, so the practical preparation stance is to keep interviewing elsewhere until a written offer is in hand.

### BCNY ML/AI product engineering — September 2026

The acquired BCNY team uses a team-specific sequence: a coding phone screen, followed by onsite system design, a project deep dive, and leadership / behavioral interviews. One candidate completed the process in about two weeks; this timing is specific to that interview experience.

### Phone screens — October 2026

Some recent phone screens are run directly by Atlassian engineers instead of Karat. A 45-minute backend screen can pair a two-part coding task with a whiteboard design discussion on the same topic, and each coding part is expected to come with simple tests. Recruiters who reach out on LinkedIn can move fast — an interview invite can arrive the same day as the first call — so leave enough preparation time before booking the technical screen.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Common Pipeline

Most entry-level, intern, full-stack, backend, AI, and .NET applications begin with an automatically triggered HackerRank assessment. The common OA length is 60 minutes for two questions, with some backend variants using 45 minutes for a code + SQL package. Several candidates receive the assessment immediately after submitting the application or after confirming an assessment link.

## After the OA

The post-OA step varies by team. Some SDE co-op and intern loops move to a 40-60 minute interview with two interviewers covering behavioural questions, resume projects, role motivation, and light technical-stack discussion. Red Hat / AI-infrastructure roles run a more specialised live technical screen, usually one hour, with immediate coding plus follow-up discussion.

## Timing Signals

A typical co-op timeline can run roughly one month from OA to HR outreach, then a few days to interview scheduling. Auto-triggered OA links do not guarantee a recruiter follow-up; treat them as a screening step rather than a strong hiring signal.

## Preparation

- Treat the OA as a screen: practise two timed problems in one sitting, then review hidden-test failures rather than only solving untimed drills.
- For follow-up interviews, prepare concise stories for ownership, preparation, missed deadlines, and role motivation, with outcomes and measurements ready.

## September 2026 Internship OA Variant

An internship OA variant allows 80 minutes for two tasks: an algorithm problem and debugging an existing Django/Redis application. This assessment is unproctored. The candidate recommends spending 15–20 minutes on the algorithm task and reserving most of the remaining time for navigating and repairing the project. This timing and tooling apply to this variant, rather than every IBM OA.

## Recorded Competency Screen — September 2026

A September 2026 recorded competency screen uses six questions, with one minute to prepare and three minutes to answer each. An earlier AI Engineer internship screen used five questions with the same per-question timing. Check the invitation for the format assigned to your application.

## Experienced-Hire Phone Screen and Sales Engineer OA — Autumn 2026

Experienced-hire SWE phone screens can use an incremental class-design coding prompt: a small API is specified up front, and a second part extends the matching rules once the first part works. Expect hand-written test cases rather than a hidden-test harness.

The Sales Engineer pipeline uses a 75-minute, two-question coding OA, followed by a separate behavioural assessment. Passing the coding OA does not carry the application on its own — the behavioural step is a real filter, so prepare it with the same care as the coding round.

## November 2026 OA Timing

A November 2026 OA also uses the 75-minute, two-question format. One task is a known array/log-processing problem; the second is a harder rearrangement problem that needs an extra optimisation step, which the candidate described as manageable after practising the underlying pattern. Finish the first task quickly to leave time for the second.

description: Visa's software loop pairs a strictly proctored HackerRank assessment with a one-day virtual interview event in which every round opens with a resume project deep dive. At Staff level the assessment itself is the main filter, built on twisted DP and graph variants; at Senior, project depth (especially AI work) and system design decide the outcome, and team match after the onsite is a real technical step.

questions.title: Project Deep Dive (Every Onsite Round)
questions.overview: Each of the three virtual-onsite rounds starts with a project walkthrough chosen from the resume. Follow-ups cover latency reasoning, practical AI use and prompt engineering, and — for AI/RAG projects — how the knowledge base is sourced and built, down to the APIs used.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Pipeline

Visa's software engineering pipeline usually follows this sequence:

1. **Online application → HackerRank OA.** The OA invite arrives about a week after applying. Every level takes an OA, including Staff.
2. **Recruiter outreach.** A recruiter contacts you roughly a month after the OA to schedule interviews.
3. **Virtual interview event.** The onsite runs as a batched "virtual interview event": three back-to-back rounds on one day.
4. **Result.** The decision can come as soon as the next day.
5. **Team match.** HR matches you to a team, and the hiring team holds a "casual conversation" with you.

## The virtual onsite

Every round has two halves: a **resume project deep dive** followed by either **coding** or **system design**.

| Round | First half | Second half |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Project chosen by the interviewer from your resume; latency follow-ups | Coding (LeetCode-style, e.g. Jump Game) |
| 2 | Your most recent project; questions on how you use AI at work and on prompt engineering | Coding (LeetCode-style, binary-search expected) |
| 3 | Another recent project, with implementation-level follow-ups | System design (e.g. a global, low-latency ride-hailing matcher) |

Candidates rate the coding difficulty for a Senior loop as fairly low. The project segments, especially for AI-related work, are where interviewers push hardest.

## After the onsite: team match is not a formality

- **Location and team can change.** A candidate who applied for a Bellevue role was interviewed for Austin, and the offer track switched to a GenAI team after the onsite.
- **The "casual conversation" is technical.** It covered AI concepts and included a system-design question. Prepare for it like another interview.
- **Matching can stall.** If no team match is found, HR may go quiet for a week or more. Passing the onsite doesn't guarantee an offer until a team signs on.

## Practical advice

- Ask the recruiter early which location and team the event is hiring for. Locations shift between application and interview.
- Prepare three distinct project stories, since each round opens with one.
- After passing, keep your system-design and AI-concept preparation fresh for the team-match conversation.

briefings.title: Loop Structure
briefings.body:
## Overview

Abnormal Security's loop has **no LeetCode-style questions**. Every round is a custom exercise, and almost every round splits in two: roughly 20-30 minutes on an open discussion question, then the remaining time on a hands-on task (coding, code review, live debugging or system design).

## Phone screen (60 minutes)

- SWE candidates get the same phone-screen problem; recruiters have said all screens use one question. It is a duplicate-image detection problem: ~20 minutes of discussion, then ~30-40 minutes of coding against files on disk.
- The MLE screen is different: a CSV parsing and aggregation task, plus an NLP discussion (feature engineering and metric choice for sentiment analysis).

## Onsite rounds

The loop has four rounds in total, and the exact set has changed over time.

**2025 loop (four rounds):**

1. Duplicate-image coding problem (discussion + coding).
2. Hiring manager chat: conversation only, centered on your proudest recent project and its business impact.
3. Code review of pre-shared code, then system design (a lookup service).
4. Coding (a Hangman solver), then a presentation of a problem domain and your solution.

**2024 loop (phone screen + three onsite rounds):**

1. Senior staff engineer: ~30 minutes on a topic you choose (past project, any system or technology), then behavioral questions.
2. Code review of code sent the day before, then writing code with a focus on exception handling, edge cases and testing.
3. Production-debugging questions, hands-on debugging in a live AWS environment, then ~30 minutes of system design improving an API from a diagram.

## What carries the loop

- Practical engineering judgment: reading other people's code, debugging real infrastructure, defending design choices.
- Clear, focused communication. In the discussion halves, interviewers steer toward their intended problem; at least one candidate found them unreceptive to long lists of clarifying questions.

briefings.title: Loop Structure and Format Changes
briefings.body:
## Entry and technical screening
Applied Intuition commonly begins with a recruiter conversation before a technical coding screen. The order of hiring-manager contact varies. In one robotics process, a short recruiter introduction was followed by a thirty-minute manager call and then a CoderPad screen lasting roughly an hour. Other candidates had the technical screen first and met the prospective team lead afterward. A separate software process included an hour-long manager conversation before the virtual onsite. Team contact can therefore happen at different points in the sequence.

Some early-career routes also include a timed online assessment. One CoderPad assessment used three questions, with eight minutes for each of the first two and twenty-five minutes for the last. Another candidate described two short easy questions followed by a medium question. These timings belong to those assessment formats; the live technical screen is a separate step, commonly scheduled for forty-five minutes.

In October 2026 phone screens, the 45-minute slot opened with about five minutes of introductions and closed with about five minutes of Q&A, leaving roughly 35 minutes of actual coding. Given that budget, settle requirements and outline the approach quickly before writing code.

## Traditional onsite structure
Older software loops include three technical interviews and a lead conversation, usually in forty-five-minute slots. A virtual version occupied approximately three and a half hours overall. Another onsite had a thirty-minute group introduction followed by system design, two coding interviews, and a manager discussion. The introduction let interviewers explain their work and meet the candidate together before the individual rounds. Interviewers need not all belong to the hiring team.

## AI-assisted formats in 2026
By June 2026, a recruiter described a newer virtual format pairing system design with roughly two hours of Claude-assisted implementation in a production-like environment. A July onsite used an AI-assisted project, a prepared project deep dive, and architecture discussion tied to the same project. A September account describes a three-hour AI-assisted web application exercise. These are distinct arrangements, so establish the agenda and project duration for the specific interview.

As of October 2026, one onsite ran as four parts: a 30-minute panel where the introduction mattered less than explaining interest in the company's mission; a 45-minute system design on a real-time 3D playback system for vehicle logs; a two-hour AI-assisted build of that same system on log data in S3; and a 30-minute presentation of the finished project. A 45-minute behavioral conversation on school, major, and job decisions followed as a separate call after the onsite was passed. Reading the company's published mission beforehand is useful preparation for the panel.

Passing a screen does not always secure an onsite immediately. One candidate's intended position was filled, requiring a new team match and an additional manager conversation. In-person and virtual experiences both occur. For an in-person Sunnyvale visit, candidates describe registration followed by changing into provided slippers before entering the interview area.

briefings.title: Loop Structure and Timing
briefings.body:
Squarepoint uses different interview paths for software engineering, quantitative research, and discretionary trading. An assessment is not universal: one quantitative-research path began with an HR call and went directly to a one-hour technical phone interview. A software-internship path began with an OA and then scheduled three virtual rounds. Treat the invitation for the specific position as the relevant description of the process.

The internship interviews can mix résumé questions, language fundamentals, database concepts, and coding in the same session. The first interviewer may be a junior engineer, followed by a team lead. Completing apparently straightforward exercises does not by itself establish that the round has passed. In one internship process, rejection arrived two weeks after the second virtual interview.

Risk Technology interviews can be considerably more drawn out. A Singapore candidate interviewed remotely with London engineers, using Teams and HackerRank for pair programming. The process ran from initial contact in April through an August decision. Sessions covered prior work, Linux and C++ knowledge, and practical implementation. A round described in advance as system design ultimately became another technical interview. There were also long gaps and several cancellations before the final completed session.

Quantitative-research paths can extend beyond mathematical screens. One graduate process included an initial coding and quantitative round, three interviews with different teams or offices, and a final onsite dataset exercise running from about 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. The candidate then presented to a portfolio manager and had a further conversation. That timeline belongs to the research path, rather than the software-internship format.

A junior discretionary-trader path began with HR and continued with two trader interviews. Advancement after the first technical round took several days; the final outcome required a later follow-up. Across these examples, interview scheduling and decision timing vary substantially by team and role. A quick response in one process does not imply that every subsequent round will follow the same cadence.

A DQA first round, as of 2026 Q3, was a live coding session with a current DQA. It covered three short algorithm problems: a dynamic-programming warm-up with a space follow-up, a counting problem with a modulo requirement, and an array-equalization puzzle. The interviewer was relaxed and offered hints, so the session felt like solving problems together.

Interviewer style in the DQA first round is not uniform. A later DQA first round in 2026 Q4 had two problems instead of three: a prefix-sum warm-up followed by a string problem on which the candidate got stuck. That interviewer kept the camera off, gave essentially no hints, and expected the candidate to debug independently by adding print statements. Prepare to drive the session alone, including talking through your own debugging, rather than counting on a collaborative interviewer.

As of late 2026, first rounds for the 2027 quantitative-research internship follow the same mixed format of coding plus verbal probability. If the coding environment fails to load, the interviewer may run extra probability questions in its place instead of rescheduling, and the round is still evaluated.

SoFi loops are not completely uniform across teams. A common senior or full-stack flow is recruiter or HM screen, Karat or phone technical screen, then a virtual onsite with coding, system design or frontend design, and a manager/project round. Some candidates are moved into Karat after initially expecting a direct loop, and some loops replace a scheduled system-design slot with another coding round.

Frontend loops can include four separate sessions: frontend system design, React UI coding, AI-assisted coding, and a manager conversation. Backend or general SWE loops more often show two coding rounds, one design round, and one HM round.

Scheduling can be compressed. Candidates have completed multiple rounds across two days, and one report had coding and design scheduled on the same day with only a short break. Recruiter guidance is useful, but candidates should re-check the exact round type with the coordinator and enter each session ready for either coding or design.

description: Notion's interviews are built around its own product: tables, documents with edit history, page permissions, to-do lists, and calendars. Follow-ups: serve many aggregations on immutable tables (precompute + cache, lazy cache when not read-heavy), handle mutable tables (versioned snapshots / incremental maintenance), add MAX with efficient updates, and handle tables too large for memory. A task/rows variant asks for an `applyModification` add/delete/move API.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
### Software engineering loop

- **Recruiter call → technical phone screen → virtual onsite.** The phone screen is a single coding round drawn from a small, recurring pool. Recently that has been table aggregation, the text-document undo/redo problem, page permissions, and a to-do list design.
- A **hiring-manager chat** sometimes sits between the phone screen and the onsite. Its placement varies: it's normally before the phone screen, but can land after it.
- **Virtual onsite: four rounds.** A typical mix is coding, software / system design, a domain round, and a hiring-manager / career conversation. Some loops run two coding rounds plus a design round and a behavioral round. Recent loops have also included an **AI-assisted coding** round, plus two behavioral rounds.
- Applied-AI teams (e.g. Notion AI search) can add a **leadership conversation** after the onsite, focused on team fit and what kind of work you want.

### Coding round style

Coding problems are practical and API-shaped rather than puzzle-heavy. The bar is building a clean API quickly, writing a few representative test cases yourself, and leaving time to talk about scaling and optimization. In several problems (table aggregation especially), the follow-ups decide the round more than the base code.

### Design rounds

Design prompts are product-flavored: a task queue with extensions, Google Calendar, calendar search. Expect to own the whiteboard, and in at least one case to set up and share the whiteboard link yourself.

### Timeline

Scheduling after a recruiter call can be fast, with a phone screen a week out and same-day results. Elsewhere, post-screen feedback has taken two weeks and several follow-ups to arrive. Onsite feedback can be entered very quickly: in one case, failing scores from two rounds ended the process the same day, before the remaining rounds mattered.

briefings.title: Loop Structure and Timing
briefings.body:
Upstart’s software-engineering process can include a recruiter conversation, a timed OA, additional technical screens, and an onsite. One experienced-hire path used an OA, a combined behavioral-and-coding session, another coding session, and an onsite containing a hiring-manager conversation, system design, and a local project implementation. The project session allowed AI coding.

The advertised composition of a screen may differ from how the hour is used. A candidate was told to expect behavioral questions, experience discussion, coding, a mini-design problem, and questions at the end. The actual session spent roughly thirty minutes on résumé experience, fifteen minutes on behavior, and the remaining fifteen on a technical scenario. That account does not establish a guaranteed coding segment in every manager screen.

Recruiter calls can be substantive. Candidates describe follow-ups about current projects, strengths, technical communication, and relevant experience before an OA is issued. One candidate received the assessment the next day; another did not advance past the recruiter stage. A recruiter invitation therefore does not imply automatic progression to the technical loop.

Machine-learning and research hiring follows a different technical path. A recruiter described two one-hour sessions covering probability, statistics, and Python/ML coding, followed by behavioral assessment. An MLE candidate encountered a probability-and-simulation screen, a second ML coding screen, and an onsite combining further ML work, algorithms, and behavior. That candidate later spoke with a hiring manager and a VP before being told hiring had stopped.

A research-scientist candidate moved from an initial call with statistics questions to two technical sessions about a week later. Those sessions combined probability simulation and a hands-on notebook modelling case. The final decision arrived quickly after the interviews. These timelines belong to individual processes rather than a fixed turnaround policy. The consistent distinction is between software engineering’s OA and practical-project path and the research/ML path’s heavier use of quantitative reasoning and modelling.

As of late 2026, a senior software-engineering process paired a hiring-manager discussion focused on an in-depth walkthrough of challenging past work with a virtual onsite of three rounds: system design, a coding round with two problems (one classic algorithm problem and one practical calculation task), and a project round. The candidate was rejected after the virtual onsite, so completing every session does not by itself signal a strong outcome.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Cisco SWE candidates often see an automated online assessment before any deeper team conversation. The OA format is usually three coding questions in a single sitting, with examples and hidden tests, and candidates cannot revisit a problem after submission.

Meraki and management loops are less OA-centered. A recent manager loop started with a recruiter screen, then a 45-minute hiring-manager interview, followed by four 60-minute interviews covering operational excellence, system design, Java debugging / code review, and people leadership with a skip-level manager. The manager loop can be in person.

For Meraki-style coding screens, the session can start with a brief self-introduction and move directly into one coding problem. Clarification quality matters: candidates who rushed into implementation without explaining data-structure choices found the round harder to recover from even when the final code was likely correct.

Low-level and embedded-team technical screens can devote most of the conversation to a resume and infrastructure-project deep dive when the candidate's recent work is not closely aligned with the role. The remaining technical portion may combine a straightforward coding task with basic C pointer concepts. Clear code narration matters because the interviewer may need extra explanation when an implementation differs from the most conventional form.

In September 2026, a Switch-team SWE process began with a 30-minute Webex recruiter screen about the candidate's current location and possible work locations, followed by a 60-minute hiring-manager interview centered on a reasoning puzzle. The recruiter suggested reviewing switch fundamentals, but the manager interview contained no coding, past-experience questions, or switch/networking knowledge questions. The candidate did not advance to a third round.

Software QA loops vary by team. On a team from an acquired company, interviews were conversational and focused on past experience plus open questions about testing and networking (for example, what a successful ping does and does not prove, and explaining BGP). L2/L3-style QA teams were more technical: a short Python class-implementation exercise, Python and pytest fundamentals (fixtures, decorators, generators, inheritance resolution), and test-planning questions such as handling flaky tests.

description: Flexport is a freight forwarder and customs broker building software for global trade. Its interviews lean on that domain: coding and design prompts are often framed as logistics scenarios, and design rounds put heavy weight on data modeling and API design.

questions.title: Order-to-Voyage Booking System
questions.overview: Model orders (origin/destination port, dropoff date, target delivery date) and voyages (route, departure, arrival). Part 1: `book_order` assigns to the earliest valid voyage. Part 2: per-voyage capacity. Part 3: book an order if moving a single existing booking frees room. A 2026 variant replaces Part 3 with per-ship overload percentages, preferring non-overloaded ships.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Pipeline

Flexport's software engineering process is short:

1. **First-round / phone screen (coding).** One or two LeetCode-style algorithm problems, often with follow-ups. Expect classic patterns: intervals, dynamic programming, and heap-based problems framed as practical scenarios.
2. **Onsite.** For SDE2, the loop includes:
   - **Coding.** In 2026 the onsite coding problems were largely new and not found on standard practice lists. One example is an interactive word-guessing problem where the goal is to minimize guesses.
   - **System design.** An engineering-flavored prompt from Flexport's own domain: shipping, containers, and freight. The prompt itself isn't hard, but the interviewer keeps adding requirements.

A multi-part coding problem modeling order bookings onto voyages has been a long-running Flexport staple and resurfaced in 2026 with a changed final step.

## Decisions and cooldown

- Decisions can be very fast. A first-round rejection arrived within 30 minutes of the interview, and a phone-screen rejection the same day.
- Failing even the first round triggers a **6-month freeze** before you can reapply.

## Domain framing

Problems are often wrapped in logistics vocabulary: orders, voyages, ports, containers, ships, and capacity. Get comfortable turning a business description into a clean object model quickly, because several rounds start from a domain story rather than a crisp algorithmic spec.

description: Figma builds its interviews around its own product surface and runs them as collaborative, test-case-driven pair-programming sessions where candidates pick their own language and prompts are deliberately long and under-specified. Coding signal rewards clean handling of messy object models over algorithmic trickiness; system-design rounds reward pragmatic, right-sized solutions over over-engineering. Since the IPO the bar has tightened, and final leveling is often settled in a separate executive conversation.

questions.title: Document / Layer — Apply, Undo, Commit Batch, Redo
questions.overview: Figma's signature phone-screen coding question. Build a Document made of layers, where each layer holds key/value properties. Implement applying a property to a layer and undoing operations, then extend to batched commits and redo. Algorithmically light; the challenge is a clean state model and handling the verbose, awkward spec.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Figma's pipeline is recruiter screen → phone screen → onsite, with a few extra gates near the end for senior roles.

**Phone screen.** Almost always two back-to-back rounds: one 60-minute coding round and one 30–45 minute hiring-manager / behavioral chat (order varies). The coding round is the well-known gate — pass rates here have hovered around 50%, so it is not a formality. Candidates who clear it usually hear about the onsite within about a week.

**Onsite ("VO").** Typically 4–5 rounds: one or two coding/pair-programming rounds, a project deep dive, one or two system-design rounds (or ML system + ML model design for ML roles), and an all-around / behavioral round (often with the hiring manager). For ML/AI roles the onsite runs long — five rounds is common.

**After the onsite (senior/staff).** Strong candidates can face an additional director-level BQ round plus a reference check requiring two references — explicitly one manager and one peer — collected before any offer. Leveling and final terms are frequently settled in a separate executive / VP call that is mostly behavioral.

**Communication.** Recruiters are consistently described as responsive and helpful, and Figma often provides detailed post-onsite feedback through the recruiter — a rarity. The flip side: after a rejection the recruiter typically goes quiet, so do not count on a post-mortem.

**Scheduling.** Onsite rounds are frequently booked back-to-back with no gaps, and candidates consistently flag fatigue in the later coding rounds as a cause of avoidable mistakes. When the recruiter offers scheduling options, ask for short breaks between rounds.

**2026 AI-group variant.** The first stage combines a hiring-manager project conversation with coding. The onsite then uses five rounds — coding, two system-design rounds, behavioral, and project deep dive. This five-round block can be distributed across three days rather than compressed into one day; in this schedule, the decision followed two business days later.

**Track redirects and headcount (late 2026).** A failed phone screen on one track does not necessarily end the process: recruiters have proactively redirected candidates to a different SWE track (e.g. Full Stack → AI Product), which restarts at a fresh recruiter intro and coding screen with a new recruiter. Some processes stop after a positive hiring-manager screen purely because the role's headcount closed; the recruiter frames it as non-technical and keeps the interview record on file. A Figma NDA (via DocuSign) is signed early in the process. On the AI Product track the hiring-manager screen is a 30-minute behavioral chat, and coding results typically arrive within about five days.

description: HubSpot interviews favor practical engineering over puzzle-solving: level-gated online assessments, coding rounds built around real HTTP and JSON handling in your own environment, and product-style system design. Behavioral screens are short and anchored in the company's culture values, and technical rounds are often shadowed.

questions.title: Design Netflix
questions.overview: Design a Netflix-style video platform. The interviewer supplies three core features, most often some mix of browse by genre / search, stream video at multiple qualities, save watch progress across devices, recommendations, or upload. Follow-ups focus on schema design, caching (what to do when the cache miss rate is high), and rubric questions such as SQL vs NoSQL. Back-of-envelope metrics are often not required.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Full-time SWE loop

A typical full-time process runs:

1. **Online assessment** — a 90-minute, multi-level coding assessment (see Tooling & Rules).
2. **Recruiter / phone screen** — a short, values-based behavioral screen of about 20 minutes.
3. **Virtual onsite** — usually split across several days. Rounds seen in recent loops:
   - **Coding** — either a LeetCode-style medium or the practical HTTP + JSON coding round.
   - **System design** — the long-running video-streaming design prompt, or a data-ingestion design built on a public weather data feed.
   - **Project deep dive** — discuss a past project in depth. You must send the interviewer an outline beforehand; including a diagram and listing the key technical points is strongly recommended.
   - **Behavioral** — focused on handling conflict.

Some loops schedule coding and system design back to back on the same day; one full loop ran five rounds spread over four days. Others pair a coding round and a design round in one virtual onsite session. Some loops have two system design rounds.

## Timeline

- The whole process commonly takes around two months from application to decision.
- One entry-level loop: online application in early September, phone screen about two and a half weeks later, virtual onsite roughly two weeks after that, rejection ten days later, and a feedback call the next day.
- Decisions arrive roughly one to two weeks after the final round.

## Feedback calls

HubSpot regularly offers a recruiter feedback call after a rejection. The feedback is specific (e.g. a particular part of the coding round where hard-coded logic was used instead of a proper data structure, or a design diagram that was larger than necessary), which makes it worth taking the call before a re-application.

description: Rippling's engineering loop is unusually concentrated: a small set of OOD coding prompts, two data-heavy system-design prompts, and a practical web API round account for most SWE interviews. The bar is driven by speed through multi-part prompts, clean extensible design, and whether the candidate can collaborate with AI tools without losing ownership of the solution.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
The common SWE path starts with a recruiter screen, then a 60-minute technical screen that can be either coding or system design. Full loops usually run as four rounds across one or two days: two coding rounds, one system design round, and one HM / project deep-dive round. Some backend and full-stack loops add a web API implementation round where the candidate brings their own framework and runs a small REST service live.

Phone coding is usually one of the fixed OOD prompts: Delivery Billing, Expense Rules Engine, or Camel Cards. Phone system design alternates mainly between Google News / News Aggregator and User Behavior / Metrics Monitoring. Onsite coding reuses the same bank and adds Article Voting, Music Player, Logger, Task Manager, or frontend / intern variants.

For project deep dive, prepare a 3-5 slide deck rather than an informal story. Expect questions about the original problem statement, technical trade-offs, quantified impact, mentorship, and what you would improve in hindsight. HM rounds also include standard BQ such as why Rippling, conflict, deadline pressure, scope creep, and strengths / weaknesses.

SDE-2 loops can include a broader LLD-heavy sequence: a phone screen with a filesystem-style directory manager, a coding/LLD access-control design, a distributed scheduler design, a payroll architecture round, and an HM round. Staff phone screens may also be pure system design rather than coding, with Hotel Booking and News Aggregator showing up as recent prompts.

After the virtual onsite, a recruiter debrief may add another short conversation before the final decision and may revisit motivation for joining Rippling. During the July 2026 internal summit, scheduling was noticeably slower, so candidates with competing timelines needed extra buffer that month.

As of August 2026, some full-stack and general SWE loops use three onsite rounds after the phone screen: one coding round, one system-design round, and one department or project deep dive. Confirm whether the technical screen is counted in the advertised round total when planning the interview day. Another three-round variant uses an AI-required API coding exercise, a director conversation, and a distributed-system design round.

As of late October 2026, a common SWE sequence is one phone screen (often the AI-assisted Expense Rules Engine) followed by three onsite rounds: system design (Google News, or product analytics / metrics aggregation), an AI-required Web API round inside a provided full-stack HR app, and a project deep dive with slides. The onsite invitation can arrive about three business days after the phone screen. Onsite rounds run back to back, so an earlier round running over can shorten the next one. System design is drawn on HackerRank's whiteboard rather than Excalidraw, so practice with it beforehand. The recruiter's prep document includes a mock-interview link that is a useful reference for the real format.

In November 2026, a staff phone stage ran as two rounds, a system design (News Aggregator) and an HM chat. A four-round senior onsite paired a phone screen (Task Manager / scheduler) with Logger coding, the news-feed system design, a department screen (about 20 minutes of slides on a past project plus Q&A and BQ), and a motivation conversation with a more senior leader. Recruiters lay out the full process up front, and some share feedback after each round. Decisions move fast in both directions: an onsite invitation arrived on the next business day after a Friday phone screen, and a rejection arrived the day after an onsite.

description: Tower Research Capital hires team by team across its trading groups, so the interview loop depends on the group you apply to rather than one firm-wide process. briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Tower hires team by team (mid-frequency equity, mid/high-frequency equity, newly formed groups), so the loop depends on the group and role. Common patterns by role:

### Quant Researcher (new grad, new mid-frequency equity team)

- **Resume screen**: hard to get past.
- **HackerRank OA**: 90 minutes, 7 questions.
- **Four 1-hour rounds**: two of live coding + resume, one of live coding + math, and one stakeholder round.
- **Pace**: the recruiter moves you about one stage per week. Interview slots are offered at 8:00–10:00 am or pm.

### Quant Researcher (mid/high-frequency equity team)

1. **QR round**, 45 minutes: probability and expectation questions plus resume.
2. **QD round**: 30 minutes of resume, 30 minutes of coding (a streaming / data-structure problem).
3. **PM round**, 1 hour: mixed technical and resume, with very detailed probing.
4. **C++ round**: core concepts and production-level code.

The team was small. After the final round there was no update for half a day, and nudging with a competing offer helped. The PM said a small team can't match the packages of larger groups.

### Quant Researcher (ML-focused, 2026)

- No LeetCode. Questions cover practical deep-learning training (GPU throughput debugging, weight initialization) and modeling short-horizon returns from order-book data.

### C++ Quant Developer

- **HackerRank OA**, then a **1-hour phone screen**: CV questions, then reading and debugging messy C++, interrupted by brain teasers and CS-fundamentals questions about every 5 minutes.

### Data Engineer (mid-frequency team)

- **No HackerRank** for this group. After the resume screen comes a first technical stage of two rounds:
  1. Peer coding: an easy problem, graded on robustness.
  2. DE manager: no coding; experience plus HFT-flavored data scenarios.
- Decisions can be fast: a rejection came about 12 hours after the second round.

### Machine Learning Engineer (2026)

- Teams (pods) recruit independently: they share company-wide infrastructure but keep their strategies separate. A rejection from one team does not rule you out elsewhere; another pod can pick up a candidate who failed a QR loop.
- Some MLE openings are closer to ML infrastructure than to modeling. Screening questions cover LLM serving topics such as prefill/decode disaggregation and KV caching, while the team also applies learning-based methods to find trading signals.
- **Shape**: at least three initial rounds, then one or two coding rounds, then a round with a PM that includes math and statistics questions.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Bobyard is a small, early-stage startup building AI-assisted takeoff and estimating software for landscaping and construction contractors. The SWE / full-stack loop is built around a single project, a comment system, which you first build at home and then extend live.

## Pipeline

1. **Intro / recruiter screen.** A resume walk-through with a technical recruiter, plus rapid-fire frontend and backend fundamentals. Typical questions: "The frontend loads slowly. How do you fix it?" and "You find a production bug. How do you handle it?"
2. **Take-home.** Build a comment feature (YouTube-style) end to end: frontend, backend and database, with CRUD. Some candidates get a 2-hour timed version; others get an untimed one due in 2–3 days.
3. **Live coding on your take-home.** One or two rounds that extend the same comment system:
   - *Sort* (~30 min): by timestamp and by userId, ascending and descending. Persisting the choice across a refresh earns extra credit.
   - *Nested comments* (~45 min): the data gains a `parentId` field and you render threaded replies. Frontend only, mock data is fine. Extra credit: filter the tree to show matched comments and their children.
   - Some loops run sort/filter and nesting as successive feature requests within one session. A round billed as a walk-through of the take-home can turn into live coding.
4. **Onsite final.** A panel (PM, CEO, engineering manager, senior engineer) followed by a manager 1:1. See the final-panel briefing.

## Timeline

Gaps between rounds can be long. A month or more between the first live-coding round and the next invitation is not unusual, and an unfinished live-coding solution has still been advanced. Recruiting communication is generally described as friendly and clear. Candidates rejected for one role have been re-approached for a different opening.

description: Palantir interviews combine practical implementation, work with unfamiliar code, and discussion of how candidates make decisions. Company motivation and fit for the specific role can matter from the first recruiter conversation.

questions.title: Session Manager

briefings.title: Loop Structure and Timeline
briefings.body:
## Recruiter contact and the technical screen

Recruiter contact can begin with a short background conversation, but motivation deserves preparation before that first call. In an SWE process, the recruiter spent approximately ten minutes on the résumé, background, and why Palantir before moving the candidate to a technical screen. Another candidate was rejected after an initial recruiter conversation that emphasized company knowledge and reasons for joining. Read the company material included in the recruiter’s outreach and be ready to connect it to your own reasons for applying.

A 60-minute technical screen can combine a résumé discussion, coding, and candidate questions. Two SWE screens allocated approximately the first 15 minutes to the résumé or a selected project. One allocated about 40 minutes to coding; another reserved the final five minutes for candidate questions. The project conversation can emphasize methodology and decisions rather than only implementation details. Company motivation may come up again during the screen.

## Onsite and learning formats

An experienced-hire SWE onsite included three technical rounds: coding, code review, and system design. Each also included some behavioral questions or discussion of résumé projects. Keep project explanations ready throughout the technical loop, rather than assuming there will be a single separate slot for them. A different onsite included an explicit behavioral/values discussion.

Learning interviews use a different format: the interviewer introduces unfamiliar concepts or code, supplies supporting explanations, and asks the candidate to reason through progressively introduced material. Distinguish this format from the conventional coding screen when confirming the interview schedule.

## Confirm the sequence for your application

FDSE recruiter conversations emphasize both company and role motivation. FDE internship applications can also include a multipart online assessment. These formats belong to different application paths; they should not be treated as one mandatory sequence for every candidate. Ask the recruiter to identify the scheduled round types, their order, and the expected time commitment for your position. The concrete timings above describe individual rounds, not a promised end-to-end hiring timeline.

## FDSE sequence (2026)

An FDSE process can start with a 20-minute screen run by a practicing FDSE, not a recruiter. It combines motivation questions, résumé and project discussion, and one or two technical questions. A few days later, the next two rounds are scheduled together: a learning round, then a decomposition round. The decomposition round is gated: you only get it if you pass the learning round. As of late 2026, the FDSE learning round can run 45 minutes, with roughly 15 minutes of behavioral questions before a 30-minute exercise. Earlier versions appear to have run a full hour. Interview slots can be rescheduled at the last minute, so confirm timing close to the date.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Baseten's loop is short and engineering-heavy. Its exact shape depends on the team and role.

### General SWE

- **Recruiter call.** Recruiters often reach out first.
- **Hiring manager call:** background plus behavioral questions.
- **Technical phone screen:** one coding problem in parts, such as a parallel chunked file download built on starter code, an XOR-based random number generator used to encrypt a tree document, or a filesystem-backed key-value store.
- **Virtual onsite, four rounds:** coding (for example a single-pass S-expression parser), system design (for example an observability logging system), a project deep dive, and a stakeholder-focused behavioral round.

A decision came about two weeks after the onsite.

### Infra / LLM-serving leaning loop

After a coding phone screen (a byte-oriented key-value store with locking, sharding, a WAL and tombstone deletes), the onsite has five parts:

- Concurrency coding: convert sequential API calls to a thread pool.
- LLM inference system design.
- LLM fundamentals, mainly transformer internals.
- Debugging a GPU profiling program.
- A conversation with a founder.

### System-design phone screens

Some teams screen with system design instead of coding. The screen opens with an easy, interviewer-guided design, then moves to a team-specific prompt such as a CI/CD pipeline, and candidates have failed at that second step. Design topics tend to match what the team is hiring for.

### Data engineering

- **Hiring manager, one hour:** a project deep dive and a walk-through of the team.
- **SRE, one hour:** two data engineering scenarios, messy freeform alert history and bad-pod detection against sibling replicas.

A rejection arrived within hours, and the recruiter shared specific feedback.

### ML-systems leaning onsite (five rounds)

One recent onsite had five rounds:

- A timing estimate for a linear projection, starting with the basic case and extending to Mixture-of-Experts and expert-parallel variants.
- Analysis of two PyTorch profiler traces of the same model at different batch sizes.
- Coding: S-expression parsing in three parts.
- An ML deep dive.
- A behavioral round.

Five rounds in one day is a heavy load; one candidate asked the recruiter to spread the onsite over two days.
