briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Pipeline

1. **Recruiter call (~30 min).** Background, visa / sponsorship, one project, motivation questions. For some roles (e.g. senior Python) the recruiter also asks language-specific technical questions. Candidates have been moved on right after this call, so don't treat it as a formality.
2. **Technical screen / phone screen (~60 min).** Usually one coding problem. Some interviewers spend the first half on your project background and leave only about 30 minutes for coding. The problems are mostly practical rather than puzzle-style (iterators, evaluators, parsers, crawlers), though a hard algorithmic question does occasionally show up.
3. **Onsite (about 5 rounds).** A typical general SWE loop:
   - **Code review / debugging**: a large block of code to debug, mostly multithreading issues
   - **System design**: a storage-flavored design that drills down into data structures and read scaling
   - **Concurrency coding**: implement something concurrent, such as a finite web crawler
   - **Hiring manager**: a deep dive into your past projects
   - **Director**: an "exciting project" story plus behavioral questions; the director also pitches the team and org

## Low-level / systems team variant

Low-level teams run a different loop with **behavioral questions in every round**. The coding rounds focus on concurrency primitives (read-write lock, connection pool, LRU cache with a concurrency follow-up). The design slot becomes a deep investigation of a concurrent server's performance: event loops, blocking vs non-blocking I/O, multiplexing, `epoll` vs `io_uring`. The HM and director rounds are mostly behavioral.

## Timeline and outcomes

- Decisions are fast: rejections after a phone screen often arrive the next day.
- Some screens end with "role closed" or "the team received positive feedback but is not moving forward". Positions open and close quickly, so a positive screen does not guarantee a next step.

## First technical round: concurrency + DB internals (late 2026)

At least one team has run the first technical round as a two-part interview: a short multithreading coding problem (such as implementing a read-write lock) followed by an oral database-internals discussion covering the query lifecycle, the buffer cache and the optimizer. In that case the recruiter described the format in advance, so ask what your first round covers. Two engineers may run it together, and the decision can come back the same evening.

## Atlas Growth loop (late 2026)

The Atlas Growth team runs a product-engineering loop in **TypeScript / JavaScript**: recruiter call → one phone screen → three virtual onsite rounds → a hiring-manager round.

- **Phone screen**: a string-handling library problem where most of the discussion is about edge cases and error-handling design (throw vs. an alternative you choose).
- **Code review**: about 200 lines of TypeScript plus a design doc. You leave review comments only, without changing code: null / undefined handling, interface definitions, business-logic bugs measured against the design doc, and whether the tests are adequate.
- **Coding**: implement a core JavaScript primitive from scratch, in plain JavaScript only.
- **Backend design**: explicitly *not* a classic system-design round. It centers on business logic and database schema for a file-storage product backend.
- **Hiring manager**: a detailed resume deep dive plus behavioral questions. The HM probes deeply, so a loosely told story can turn into mixed feedback.

briefings.title: Loop Structure and Scheduling
briefings.body:
## Assessment and first interview
WeRide's early-career routes can begin with an online assessment before a recruiter arranges the first live interview. One new-graduate candidate applied near the end of September, received recruiter contact roughly three weeks after the assessment, and scheduled the first interview for the following week. The candidate had not passed every assessment test case, so incomplete assessment results did not automatically prevent a live interview in that process. This example does not establish a universal passing threshold.

An internship assessment contained three coding questions in 120 minutes. Another campus assessment also contained three questions, although its duration was not specified. Live interviews are separate from these assessment formats and usually include discussion of prior experience alongside the coding work.

## General software loops
One experienced software candidate had five remote interviews, each divided into approximately thirty minutes of résumé discussion and thirty minutes of coding. They were arranged on China time, allowing the candidate to interview in the evening. Another new-graduate process had three technical interviews followed by a team-match manager conversation. The first two interviewers were based in the United States and the later interviewers in China.

Team matching does not necessarily mean the evaluation is finished. In that new-graduate process, the manager conversation included extensive résumé discussion and a technical concept question, and the candidate was rejected afterward. There was no coding exercise in that final manager conversation.

## Specialist and internship variations
A frontend candidate had a technical screen followed by a virtual round combining discussion of AI use, résumé questions, frontend fundamentals, and coding. A domestic research-and-development internship route included at least three interviews: the first combined experience discussion, coding, and five minutes for candidate questions; the next two again began with past work before coding.

There is no single round count across these examples. Confirm the team, interview locations, time zone, and remaining evaluation steps when receiving the schedule. Follow-up speed also varies: one candidate received a rejection two days after a screen, while another was still awaiting a result a week after the second interview.

briefings.title: Senior SWE Loop Structure
briefings.body:
Docker's senior software engineer process can start with recruiter outreach on LinkedIn rather than a cold application. After the recruiter stage, the loop is four rounds, each with a distinct focus:

1. **Director behavioral.** A conversation with a director about ownership, working in a small team, collaboration and motivation. Docker is a small company, so this round carries real weight: concrete stories with numbers and trade-offs matter more than polished generalities.
2. **Coding.** An expression-evaluation problem in the calculator family: parse a string and evaluate it with the right operator precedence. Expect the precedence version (multiplication and division alongside addition and subtraction), and be ready for parentheses as an extension.
3. **System design.** A design centred on Docker's own domain, such as an image storage and distribution service. It may be framed loosely, for example "like Dropbox, but for images", so you have to set the scope yourself: push, pull, listing, deduplication of shared layers, and bandwidth.
4. **Technical project discussion.** A candidate-led round that works like a presentation or a sprint demo of a project you owned, with technical questions throughout.

### How to prepare

- The system design round is set in Docker's own domain, so read up on how images are built, layered and distributed before the onsite.
- Prepare one project you can present end to end, ideally with a diagram, and know the reasoning behind each major decision.
- Have specific behavioral stories ready for the director round; it is a full round, not a formality.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Harvey runs a compact, stable loop. A recruiter — often reaching out directly after an application or via LinkedIn — starts with a friendly intro call, then schedules a technical phone screen quickly.

- **Phone screen** (~45-60 min): a single coding problem drawn from a small, well-known rotation — text highlighting / citation tagging, an in-memory file system, or a spreadsheet / formula engine. Recruiters frequently run a prep call beforehand and may preview the coding question.
- **Onsite** (typically 4 rounds): coding, system design, project deep-dive, and a Harvey Values / behavioral round. Some loops split the onsite into a virtual portion (coding + values) and an in-office portion in SF (system design + experience deep-dive).
- Decisions and feedback usually arrive within ~1-2 weeks of the onsite. Rejections frequently come without detailed feedback, and candidates are sometimes passed over for a "more background-matched" applicant despite a positive loop.

The coding bank is small and stable — candidates repeatedly note the rotation is tight — so drilling the handful of recurring problems covers most of the coding surface.

Agent-focused roles can use a leaner three-round onsite: agent system design, Colab/RAG coding, and project deep-dive. The phone-screen-to-onsite transition may happen within hours.

A September 2026 Research Engineer loop used a separate sequence: hiring-manager outreach and a background/technical conversation, a cofounder conversation about prior model-training experience and team size, then two onsite discussions with different leads about research projects and training design.

As of October 2026, some loops open with a hiring-manager screen built on behavioral prompts (recent ownership, tough feedback, spotting a problem outside your own scope) before the technical screen. Passing the technical screen generally requires completing every part of the coding problem; candidates who left the final part unfinished have been rejected on that basis.

As of November 2026, staff-level agent loops follow a similar shape: the phone screen is the spreadsheet / formula engine problem; the virtual onsite has three rounds — a RAG implementation in a notebook, a project deep-dive, and a contract-review agent design — followed by a bar-raiser round that is a second RAG-focused system design. Recruiters at this level signal willingness to compete with outstanding offers. Standard virtual onsites in the same period ran four rounds: citation-tagging coding, an AI-assisted coding round on the in-memory file system, a Google-Drive-style system design, and behavioral.

briefings.title: Interview Process & Timeline
briefings.body:
Cursor runs its interview loop **sequentially**: each round is scheduled only after you pass the previous one. That makes the process long. Candidates who went through five rounds describe it as stretching over many weeks.

### Typical pipeline

1. **Recruiter outreach / screen.** Many candidates are sourced directly by recruiters.
2. **Technical screen (coding), 45–60 minutes.** Almost always the repository hash-tree problem. It is practical and runs against real files, unlike a LeetCode-style puzzle.
3. **Second technical screen.** Either a coding round with a design flavour (a multi-level notification rate limiter, or an in-memory transactional KV store as an OOP class design) or a system-design round. Design prompts are practical and product-adjacent: a job scheduler (sometimes introduced as "design CI/CD"), or storing and syncing IDE settings across users and teams.
4. **Project deep dive.** Walk through one project you built in depth.
5. **Hiring-manager conversation.** An all-around chat covering your path into computing, university projects, and career choices.
6. **In-person work trial.** Candidates who clear the virtual rounds are told the final stage is about **two days of back-to-back pair work at the SF office**.

Some candidates describe the virtual stage as "three rounds plus a one-day onsite pair-working session." In practice, the number of virtual rounds varies. One candidate did five virtual rounds and was never scheduled for the work trial.

### Decisions and speed

- Rejections can arrive the next day, sometimes after a round where the candidate felt the conversation went well.
- The coding bar is about **execution, not just correctness**. Finishing with a couple of bugs fixed during testing has still ended in rejection. Expect to need a clean, complete, tested solution within the hour.

### 2026 acquisition and reorg

In the second half of 2026, Cursor was acquired by SpaceX / xAI, and some candidates now hear the company referred to as SpaceXAI. Candidates who were mid-loop at the time saw:

- A pause of a week or more with no updates right after the announcement.
- Teams being re-prioritized. A candidate with positive feedback across all rounds was moved to a new priority team and had to pass a **new hiring-manager behavioral round** with a co-founder, which ended in a rejection.

If you are interviewing during this period, ask the recruiter which team you are interviewing for and whether it is stable, and expect possible re-matching late in the process.

briefings.title: Loop Structure
briefings.body:
Oscar Health's software engineering process is short: one coding screen, then a two-round onsite loop.

### Screen

- A single coding round over video (phone screen / "screening").
- Problems here are LeetCode-style: classic or lightly adapted problems such as Morse code conversion with an all-decodings follow-up, a longest-chain problem on a DAG, or a standard medium tree traversal.
- Some screening problems recur across candidates, so recent problems are worth drilling.

### Onsite loop (2 rounds)

| Round | What to expect |
|---|---|
| Coding (DSA) | A **custom** problem drawn from Oscar's health-insurance domain — e.g. checking whether members are covered by a provider network given specialties, locations and a maximum distance. Not a LeetCode copy, but the algorithm is approachable once the rules are read carefully. |
| System design | A domain-flavored prompt, such as a physician-facing telehealth queue or an internal sales outreach tool. Delivered as a short written brief. |

### Domain themes

Expect prompts built around Oscar's own business: members and providers, medical specialties, geographic coverage, state-by-state physician licensure, and member outreach. Knowing these concepts at a basic level makes the custom questions faster to parse.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Vanta runs a compact, stable loop: a recruiter touch, a technical phone screen, then a virtual onsite, with a hiring-manager conversation in the mix. Before the onsite, the recruiter may provide a detailed Google Doc describing what each round evaluates.

**Phone screen.** One coding problem in ~50–60 minutes (often ~50 minutes of actual solve time after intro). The question is drawn from a small rotation — most commonly a task-dependency topological sort or the employee training-status / group-aggregation problem; earlier loops used the Word Pattern / meta-pattern backtracking problem. You write and run code locally (see the tooling briefing).

**Onsite (VO).** Typically four rounds:
- **Practical Coding** — almost always the `uniq` (unique-lines-in-a-file) build, run locally with file-system I/O. A frontend track (React/TypeScript against a provided API) exists for frontend candidates.
- **System Design** — usually the internal DAU/MAU analytics system; occasionally "design Pastebin." Applied-AI candidates instead receive an AI Technical Deep Dive.
- **Project Deep Dive** — technical walkthrough of your largest project. Applied-AI loops may frame this slot as a high-level leadership interview focused on impact and decision-making rather than technical detail.
- **Principles / Leadership** — scenario-based behavioral plus a manager round on a project you led.

A hiring-manager conversation covers Vanta's product (and, for applied-AI roles, their AI product specifically). Decisions can come quickly — the loop has been cut after the first two onsite rounds when an early round goes poorly. Recruiter feedback after a rejection is frequently sparse.

A September 2026 loop ended before the next day's scheduled interviews, with this written recruiter feedback:

> Overall the team appreciated your strong technical capabilities with regards to bug-free code and requirements gathering. At this time the team has decided to prioritize candidates who had stronger, complete solutions and justifications for their technical decisions.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Scale AI starts with a recruiter or hiring-manager screen, then moves quickly into a practical first technical round. Recent recruiter guidance describes a changed first-round format: coding plus a 30-minute HM conversation. Several candidates see the coding prompt in advance or can infer the prompt family from the scheduling email, but the round still requires passing provided tests in the interview environment.

For SWE and NG candidates, the full loop commonly includes five rounds split across two days: a LeetCode-style or matrix coding round, a debugging round over an unfamiliar codebase, a backend practical round, and two behavioral or values rounds. The behavioral rounds can feel overlapping; one focuses on standard experience questions, while another may probe side projects, strengths, weaknesses, and work style.

For MLE and LLM-facing candidates, the virtual onsite is more specialized: ML coding or training debugging, LLM theory, a behavioral or credo round, and a presentation or project deep dive. Senior FDE loops can include system design, credo, ML conversation, AI coding, and HM conversation. Recruiters can also explain compensation and level as outcome-dependent rather than fixed before the loop.

As of July 2026, the recruiter screen can be a 30-minute conversation centered on company motivation and project depth. Candidates applying to multiple openings may be matched from their résumé to the closest team before the technical loop. Recruiter guidance describes a one-hour, non-LeetCode-style technical screen followed by a five-round virtual onsite mixing technical, system-design, and behavioral evaluation.

As of October 2026, a senior backend virtual onsite can consist of four rounds: a slide-based project deep dive, an API coding practical, a credo behavioral round, and a system-design round built around the embedding-plus-classification API prompt. The process is well structured and the individual prompts are not considered hard, so pacing and reading each prompt's contract carefully matter more than raw difficulty.

As of late October 2026, a full SWE loop can run a phone screen on the task-processor prompt, then a five-round virtual onsite: project deep dive, the embedding-plus-classification API design, the CSV-to-JSON backend practical, credo behavioral, and a closing HM conversation. Nearly every prompt comes from a known, recurring family, so preparing the established question set covers most of the loop. New-grad candidates can also receive an online assessment built on a tree hierarchy with a single-query part and a batched part. Recruiters may press for compensation expectations before the onsite, including whether an offer below competing numbers would be acceptable; it is reasonable to defer that conversation to the offer stage.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
Qualcomm loops vary a lot by team and role family, and each team sets its own format.

**Software (generic SWE):** applications submitted in early May led to interviews scheduled by mid-June. Rounds are LeetCode-style coding (one easy binary-search problem, then a medium tree problem). Teams can cancel later rounds at short notice: one candidate's third round was cancelled after it had been scheduled, with a plain "not moving forward" message.

**Compiler Engineer:** a long process, with seven conversations in total: an HM screen, an HR screen, and five technical interviews. The technical interviews cover:
- an easy coding question (not the focus),
- a resume deep-dive on past projects and their details,
- a large volume of compiler knowledge questions (compilation theory, optimization algorithms, LLVM backend, C/C++),
- a general, system-design-like round on how to optimize a given program.

Interviewers are courteous and the overall experience is positive.

**GPU compiler:** all coding happens in C++ in a Google Doc. A session can mix C++ semantics, an algorithm (A* on a maze), and GPU kernel performance and power questions.

**RF hardware (new grad):** a recruiter reaches out within a couple of weeks of the application, followed by an HM phone screen of about 45–60 minutes. About two weeks after the screen, the recruiter collects salary expectations, relocation, and timeline before scheduling a virtual onsite. Follow-ups after that point can go unanswered.

**Research Scientist intern:** two back-to-back rounds, an HM round on your research and an engineer round with ML fundamentals plus a distributed-training design question. Scheduling can be rigid: when a team is rushing to finish all candidates, it may offer only a single time slot.

briefings.title: Loop Structure and Round Types
briefings.body:
Temporal's software engineering process is short and leans heavily on system design and concurrency.

**Phone screen.** One loop opened with two technical conversations: a system-design chat on migrating a live database with zero downtime, and a coding question on a concurrent web crawler. Another phone screen was a log-parsing coding exercise (normalize links, aggregate error counts) paired with a design question on firing a large volume of delayed events accurately.

**Onsite.** A full onsite ran four rounds:

- Concurrency coding, considered easy if you are comfortable with Python's `ThreadPoolExecutor`.
- A hiring-manager / behavioral round with standard questions.
- A second coding round on a well-known LeetCode problem.
- System design on a task scheduler, with the discussion centered on the database layer and error handling.

A different loop started with a one-to-one chat system design round followed by a concurrent-programming coding round.

**What repeats.** Design prompts cluster around scheduling, durable state, and failure handling — task schedulers, delayed events, live data migration — which mirrors Temporal's own product area. Coding rounds repeatedly test concurrent programming, so treat thread pools, futures and early-exit patterns as core preparation rather than an extra.

**Recruiting logistics.** Recruiter availability can be tight, and rescheduling a recruiter call may be misread as withdrawing. Confirm explicitly that you are still in process whenever you move a slot.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Round Formats
briefings.body:
## Research Scientist (Yahoo Mail)
The phone screen is a single 60-minute round split into two parts:

- **Coding in NumPy** — a short, recommendation-flavored exercise over embeddings. The code is small (under ten lines), so the round is about clean vectorized thinking rather than algorithmic difficulty.
- **ML knowledge** — standard conceptual questions such as overfitting, underfitting, bias–variance, class imbalance and missing data.

Candidates describe this screen as one of the easiest coding interviews they have seen, with a friendly interviewer. The final minutes are open Q&A.

## Lead ML Engineer (Yahoo News)
Round 1 runs about an hour and is conversational: a background walk-through, a deep dive into one project chosen from your résumé, and behavioral questions such as how your manager would describe you. Expect follow-up questions on architecture, trade-offs and measurable impact rather than a coding exercise.

## SDE / Full-Stack Intern
- **Technical rounds vary by team.** One team asked a non-LeetCode question — drag-to-draw rectangles on a whiteboard by filling in mouse-event handlers — where pseudo-code plus a dry run was expected rather than a running program. Another team's round was a simplified LeetCode 995. The hiring manager ran a behavioral round with standard questions.
- **Full-stack intern video interview:** roughly the first 30–40 minutes are a CS-fundamentals and résumé check (Node.js libraries, practical uses of a stack, merge vs insertion sort, structured vs unstructured data, OOP), followed by a short anagram-grouping coding question. The questions are simple; hesitant answers are the main risk.

## What to Expect Overall
Yahoo's ML screens lean practical: applied recommendation and ranking ideas, textbook ML fundamentals, and ownership of real production work. Prepare clean, quantified project stories and fluent NumPy before anything exotic.

briefings.title: Loop Structure and Interview Paths
briefings.body:
Datadog software interviews can begin with a coding screen before an onsite loop. A senior backend-oriented process included two coding rounds, one system-design round, and one combined hiring-manager and behavioral conversation. Another candidate split four onsite rounds across two consecutive days to accommodate an existing job. The round grouping and scheduling can therefore vary even when the broad components are similar.

Some loops include separate project-experience and values discussions. One candidate described two coding rounds, system design, and two conversations focused on prior work and behavior. These discussions can be substantial assessment stages rather than short closing questions after coding. The practical implication is that a successful implementation does not resolve the entire interview decision.

Frontend hiring uses a distinct path. A fullstack candidate was directed into frontend by the recruiter and encountered general coding, a practical React exercise, project experience, values, and frontend system design. The React round began with a configured project, while the design conversation concerned a user-facing product interface. This differs from the backend sequence even when the general coding problem overlaps.

AI-oriented and distributed-systems opportunities can also diverge during the process. A candidate interviewing for an AI-agent role performed well in coding but received feedback that the LLM design discussion lacked depth. The candidate was then redirected to a distributed-systems role and scheduled for an onsite. This is evidence of one role change during hiring, rather than a guarantee that another team will always be offered after a mismatch.

The introduction of AI-assisted coding has changed some interview formats, but it has not made all earlier formats disappear at once. Candidates continued to encounter established coding exercises while others received a new practical AI-assisted session. Read the specific invitation and role description closely. The available experiences support several coexisting paths, with different combinations of coding, architecture, project discussion, and role-specific evaluation, rather than one fixed sequence for every Datadog position.

Engineering-manager hiring starts differently. After the recruiter call, the first step is a one-hour conversation with the hiring manager. It covers your background, your own technical contribution to past work, and how you handle friction within a team. This conversation is a real filter: a candidate who felt it had gone smoothly was still rejected at this stage.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Timeline
briefings.body:
## Pipeline

Chime's software engineering process is short and moves quickly:

1. **Recruiter outreach.** Many candidates are contacted directly, often on LinkedIn. The recruiter call is conversational and usually leads straight to scheduling.
2. **Phone screen (coding).** One well-known data-structure design problem plus two or three extension follow-ups. Pass/fail notices can arrive the next day.
3. **Virtual onsite.** Four rounds:
   - **Coding.** A string / number puzzle in two parts, where the second part removes a simplifying assumption.
   - **System design.** A fixed, finance-domain design prompt. Recruiters have said every candidate gets the same one.
   - **Cross-functional (XFN) behavioral.** Standard behavioral questions with a partner-team interviewer.
   - **Hiring manager.** Standard behavioral questions and a discussion of past projects.
4. **Decision.** Results come fast. A Friday onsite can have an answer by Monday.

## Alternate format

Some backend loops replace the standard structure with **two back-to-back calls**. One is a hiring-manager project conversation. The other is a "fundamentals + coding" round that can turn into a fundamentals discussion plus behavioral questions with no coding at all. Ask your recruiter which format you are getting, but prepare for both.

## Things to know up front

- **Sponsorship.** At least one San Francisco backend role stated up front that it would not sponsor a green card (PERM). If you need sponsorship, confirm the policy with the recruiter before you invest prep time.
- **Feedback.** Rejections sometimes come with no feedback. When feedback is given, it is short and focuses on dimensions (coding, design, communication) rather than specific mistakes.
- **Pipeline competition.** Candidates have been turned down right after interviews because the pipeline held "more fitting" candidates. The bar is relative to the current pool, not only absolute.

description: Parafin is a fintech company that offers embedded financing, such as merchant cash advances, to small businesses through partner platforms.

briefings.title: Loop Structure & Round Formats
briefings.body:
## Pipeline

The software engineering loop is short: **technical screen → onsite**. The onsite combines a system design round, a coding round, and several behavioral / cross-functional conversations. Candidates turned down in an earlier loop have later been invited back straight into team-match conversations without repeating the loop.

## Technical screen

- A practical coding problem rooted in Parafin's own domain: merchant financing, sales-based repayments, fees, and similar money-flow bookkeeping. Expect structured input (businesses, daily figures, schedules) and a computed output, not a puzzle-style algorithm question.
- The same prompts recur, so problems already circulating among candidates are worth drilling.
- The interviewer is collaborative: when the logic has a gap, they nudge with hints and let the candidate patch it step by step. Talking through edge cases out loud pays off.

## Onsite

- **Location.** Bay Area candidates are invited to the San Francisco headquarters. Remote candidates may be offered an in-person option, but scheduling does not always work out; a virtual onsite is the fallback.
- **System design.** The prompt is built around Parafin's core business: embedded financing for small businesses through partner platforms. One concrete version is a loan application system. Requirements start deliberately vague, and clarifying questions narrow the scope sharply. Read up on what Parafin's products do (offer → application → underwriting → funding → repayment from sales) before the day. A standard framework (requirements → API → data model → high-level design → deep dives) works well here.
- **Coding.** Candidates choose a frontend or backend track. The backend version calls a real public API (for example a payments provider's API), fetches data, and processes it. The task itself is not hard; the risk is spending too long hunting for hidden traps and running out of time. The round closes with "what would you change before this code goes to production?" A good answer covers modularising the processing logic into components, error handling, retries, and tests.
- **Behavioral / cross-functional.** Separate conversations cover leadership and management, collaboration with product (a PM-led round), and resolving technical conflict within a team. Treat the PM round as a real evaluation, not a formality: show how you push back on and shape product requirements, not only how you execute them.

## Preparation

- Learn Parafin's product end to end, especially how merchant cash advances are offered, underwritten, funded and repaid as a percentage of sales.
- Practise a timed API-integration exercise: fetch paginated JSON from a public API, aggregate it, and handle errors under a self-imposed time limit.
- Prepare stories for leadership, PM disagreement, and technical conflict resolution.

briefings.title: Frontend Internship Assessment
briefings.body:
The SDE Frontend summer-internship assessment contains three coding problems in 90 minutes. The candidate found each problem moderately difficult or harder and spent about thirty minutes interpreting the long statements.

The exercises cover different algorithmic tasks despite the frontend role title. One candidate completed only the first problem and still encountered a time-limit issue. This is an individual outcome, not an established passing threshold.

The available experience does not specify the assessment platform, allowed languages, documentation or AI rules, subsequent interview rounds, or a leveling policy. Those details cannot be inferred from the three coding tasks.

questions.title: Position Canvas and Viewport-Pinned Widgets on an Infinite Board
questions.overview: Given a viewport (size, pan, zoom) and a list of widgets that are either canvas-pinned or viewport-pinned with a normalized 0–1 anchor, return each widget's top-left screen position. Canvas widgets use the pan-zoom transform; viewport widgets interpolate the anchor against the viewport size minus the widget size so they stay fully visible.
